3632.name: Geography in secondary school
3632.outcome: I can describe the knowledge and skills I will learn in geography at secondary school.
points: Geography is the study of places around the world and the relationships between people and their environments.
Physical geography is the study of the Earth's natural features and processes.
Human geography is the study of how societies, cultures and economies differ around the world.
Environmental geography studies the relationships between people and the environment.
keywords: Environmental geography is the study of the human impact on the natural environment.
Human geography is the study of societities, cultures and economies.
Locational knowledge is knowledge which is about places and the features within those locations.
Physical geography is the study of the natural world, for example landforms such as rivers and coastlines.
tips: Ask students what geography they think they have learnt in primary school.

3633.name: Locational knowledge of the world
3633.outcome: I can describe the location of places using maps at different scales.
points: There are seven continents and five oceans around the world.
Each continent has different characteristics in terms of size, population and physical features.
The UK is in the continent of Europe, which has 44 countries in total.
Locations can be described using the acronym CLOCC.
keywords: A continent is a large land mass on Earth and there are seven: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Oceania.
an imaginary line running east to west around the Earth's surface that is used to show how far north or south a place is
An ocean is a very big area of salt water between the continents.
tips: Bring different examples of maps into school for pupils to look at or use an atlas to show the difference between political and physical maps.

3635.name: Using a GIS to locate and analyse places around the world
3635.outcome: I can use a geographic information system (GIS) to locate places around the world and find out their size and distance from the UK.
points: A GIS allows us to store and display data on a digital map.
Different layers of data can be added on a GIS which allows us to investigate spatial patterns.
A GIS can be used to locate places around the world and investigate their size and distance from other places.
Decisions are taken when using a GIS to analyse data which can lead to differences in results.
keywords: a map that can be used on a computer, tablet or smartphone
a GIS (geographic information system) is a computer system that captures, analyses and displays geographic data to help understand spatial patterns
a separate, transparent sheet within a digital canvas used to organise elements of an artwork
tips: Use computers or tablets to allow students to look at different examples of digital maps such as Google Maps or Google Earth.

3634.name: Latitude and longitude
3634.outcome: I can use latitude and longitude to locate places around the world.
points: Lines of latitude are horizontal circles on Earth, measured in degrees north or south of the Equator.
Lines of longitude are vertical circles on Earth, measured in degrees east or west of the Greenwich Meridian.
We can use coordinates to locate places around the world.
GPS uses coordinates in communication and transport systems to help society function.
keywords: The Equator is an imaginary line encircling Earth at 0° latitude and is an equal distance from the North Pole and the South Pole.
The Prime Meridian is the line of longitude at 0 degrees, from which the other lines of longitude are measured east and west.
A hemisphere is half a sphere.
tips: Use a globe to show the major lines of latitude and longitude.

3640.name: Different map projections
3640.outcome: I can describe how different map projections show the world.
points: The representation of Earth on a globe shows landmasses in the correct shape and relative size.
World maps project the spherical world (three dimensions) on to a flat surface (two dimensions).
Some projections distort shape, others distort latitude and/or longitude.
keywords: the representation of an approximately spherical world as a flat map, necessarily involving distortion
something that has height, width, and depth
the shape and height of the land
a list or array that has both columns and rows of values
tips: Bring a globe in and compare country sizes to a two-dimensional map.

3636.name: Features of an OS map
3636.outcome: I can use a key on an OS map to identify features and landforms.
points: OS maps use symbols to show human and physical features.
A key is used to explain what each symbol represents.
The details around the outside of the OS map give locational information such as the three norths.
Symbols differ between a 1:25 000 and 1:50 000 map.
keywords: the national mapping agency for Great Britain
a tool or device used to show direction, helping you find North, South, East West and the bearings in between
the specific set of notes that a piece is based on (e.g. C minor)
the shape and height of the land
tips: Bring in paper OS maps and a map key for students to have a look at.

3639.name: Showing height and relief on OS maps
3639.outcome: I can use contour lines on OS maps to describe the height and shape of the land.
points: Contours show the height of the land on a map.
Spot heights give the exact height of a place in metres.
Contours that are far apart show an area of flat land.
Contours that are close together show steep land.
Features such as spurs and valleys can be shown on a map.
keywords: Lines on an OS map that show areas of equal height.
The average level of the world’s oceans, which we use as a baseline to measure the height of the land.
Elongated ridges that extend downwards from a hill or mountain.
Lower-lying areas of land between two higher areas of land.
tips: Use local area maps to do some of the exercise in the lesson so that pupils can visual the landscape and find out more about their local area.

3638.name: Four and Six Figure Grid References
3638.outcome: I can use four and six-figure grid references to locate features on an OS map accurately.
points: Maps have grid lines that help us locate places on a map.
Horizontal lines are called northings and vertical lines are called eastings.
Each grid square has two sets of numbers, giving a four-figure grid reference.
To increase location accuracy, features can be located using six-figure grid references.
keywords: numbered vertical lines found on maps
a number which combines northings and eastings to help you to locate a feature on an Ordnance Survey map
numbered horizontal lines found on maps
tips: Bring in an OS map so students can have a look at the gridlines on a physical OS map and see where they are labelled.

6774.name: Scale and distance on OS maps
6774.outcome: I can use maps at different scales to investigate an area and measure distances.
points: The scale of a map explains how large an area shown on the map is in real life.
Small-scale maps show a large area but have little detail, e.g. a world map.
Large-scale maps show a smaller area in more detail, e.g. a town or local area.
A scale bar shows how distances between areas in real life compare with the distances shown on a map.
keywords: the specific set of notes that a piece is based on (e.g. C minor)
a word, object, or image that represents a bigger idea or meaning beyond itself
tips: Bring different OS maps in to show the students.

3641.name: Fieldwork: Planning and collecting survey data
3641.outcome: I can complete an environmental quality survey on my school site.
points: Fieldwork enquiries allow geographers to investigate a place or changes over space.
Geographical enquiry includes asking questions, collecting data, presenting data, analysing, conclusions and evaluation.
Key questions or hypotheses can be used to frame a geographical enquiry.
Surveys can help geographers to find interesting patterns of data at their field site.
keywords: Data collection is when you collect the data for your investigation using a range of methods.
An environmental quality survey is a type of survey which assesses different factors that affect the environment in one location such as cleanliness and green space.
An enquiry is an investigation to find out more about something.
Fieldwork is investigating the outdoors using geographical tools and thinking to gather information or data.
an idea, for example an idea about an outcome of an experiment, based on observations and understanding
tips: An environmental quality survey gives students an excellent opportunity to work collaboratively and to listen to the opinions of others before reaching a decision on a score.

guidance.label: Risk assessment required - outdoor learning
guidance.description: Fieldwork.

3642.name: Fieldwork: Presenting survey data
3642.outcome: I can present survey data using a range of data presentation techniques.
points: Fieldwork data can be presented using graphs and maps.
Where a comparison is needed, the data presentation technique needs to allow any comparison to be seen.
Spatial data is best shown on a map.
All graphs need a title and labelled axis so that they can be read easily.
keywords: Data presentation is the graphical way that data is shown to help the reader better understand it.
A radial graph is a type of data presentation in which scaled data can be presented.
A bar chart (bar graph) is a graph consisting of bars visually representing the frequency of objects or groups.
data that is assigned to a specific location
tips: Model the drawing of graphs in real time with students so they can appreciate the time and attention to detail required.

3643.name: Fieldwork: Analysing, concluding and evaluating survey data
3643.outcome: I can analyse and reflect on my survey data to create meaningful conclusions and an evaluation.
points: Analysis is the process which makes sense of the data that has been collected.
Analysis can involve looking for patterns and relationships in the data.
Conclusions aim to answer the key questions or disprove hypotheses.
Geographers evaluate their fieldwork to learn lessons for future studies.
keywords: Subjective data is data that is based on opinion rather than facts.
the process of examining the elements or structure of something
the closing paragraph of a non-fiction text
making a judgement or comment about something
tips: Support students who are new to field work by allowing there to be a group discussion that evaluates the data before individual students record their own thoughts.

3675.name: Weather and climate
3675.outcome: I can understand the difference between weather and climate, and use climate graphs to compare different climates.
points: Weather is the day to day atmospheric conditions whereas climate is the average weather conditions over 30 years.
Weather can be seasonal which means our weather changes throughout the year, such as in the UK.
Climate graphs show us the precipitation and temperature of a place over a calendar year.
Analysing climate graphs can help us describe patterns of the climate.
keywords: the average weather conditions in a region over a long period of time
shows the amount of precipitation and the temperature each month for a location.
Precipitation is water, in the solid or liquid state, which falls from the atmosphere to Earth’s surface.
the day-to-day conditions of the atmosphere at a particular place, e.g. temperature, rainfall
tips: A great way to help students remember the difference between weather and climate is by using the phrase "weather is what we get, and climate is what we expect!"

3677.name: World climate zones
3677.outcome: I can describe the pattern of climate zones and know some of the factors that affect climate, such as latitude.
points: Climate zones are areas with a similar climate.
Factors such as alititude, latitude and distance from the sea affect the weather and climate of a location.
The height above sea level affects the temperature.The higher above sea level, the cooler the temperature.
Coastal areas tend to have warmer winters than inland areas as water takes longer to warm up.
keywords: height above sea level or ground level
Climate zones are areas that have similar weather conditions and climate, e.g. the tropics.
an imaginary line running east to west around the Earth's surface that is used to show how far north or south a place is
a measure of how hot a substance is; it is related to the kinetic energy of the individual particles
tips: It would be useful for students to have a world map or an atlas for this lesson. It's also helpful to reinforce that it is hot and wet at the equator.

3676.name: The UK's climate
3676.outcome: I can understand the reasons why the climate of the UK varies.
points: The UK has a temperate maritime climate, which means that it is mild with lots of rainfall.
The south of the UK is warmer than the North.
The west of the UK is wetter than the east.
The east of the UK is warmer in summer and colder in winter.
keywords: height above sea level or ground level
an imaginary line running east to west around the Earth's surface that is used to show how far north or south a place is
Precipitation is water, in the solid or liquid state, which falls from the atmosphere to Earth’s surface.
a climate with moderate rainfall, mild to warm summers and cool to cold winters
tips: Ensure that students know the UK includes England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland so they understand where we are referring to.

3679.name: Fieldwork: Planning and collecting microclimate data
3679.outcome: I can collect microclimate data on my school site.
points: A microclimate is the local climate and will differ from place to place.
Land use and aspect can affect the microclimate, increasing or decreasing the temperature.
The microclimate can be measured using weather instruments such as thermometers and anemometers.
We can use our knowledge of microclimates to generate questions that we can study in our fieldwork enquiry.
keywords: the position of a feature in relation to the sun
the purpose or function of land, for example: residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural or recreational use
the climate of a small area which is likely to be influenced by local factors
the most frequent wind direction a location receives
tips: Collecting microclimate data gives learners an excellent opportunity to handle simple quantitative data and think about degrees of accuracy.

guidance.label: Risk assessment required - outdoor learning
guidance.description: Fieldwork.

3682.name: Fieldwork: Presenting microclimate data
3682.outcome: I can present microclimate data using a range of data presentation techniques.
points: Data can be presented to make it easier to analyse.
To compare data it might be possible to represent it on the same set of axes.
Presenting data on a map can help geographers see spatial patterns.
All data presentations need to conform to particular standards (such as having keys and labels) to make them readable.
keywords: a line around which the body can turn
the single variable that is measured or observed in an investigation
the single variable that is changed in an investigation
how distance from, or proximity to, a geographical feature influences data
tips: Make a checklist of common graphical conventions that one would expect to see on a graph or map and ask students to check their own work against these.

7428.name: Fieldwork: Analysing, concluding and evaluating microclimate data
7428.outcome: I can analyse and reflect on my microclimate data to create meaningful conclusions and an evaluation.
points: Analysis can involve looking for relationships between independent and dependent variables.
Conclusions discuss the most likely or most common relationships.
Geographers are careful not to assume a reason for a relationship.
Geographers often need to collect more than one sample of each data type to be sure of their conclusions.
keywords: what a geographer believes to be true, rather than what they have evidence for
how we explain or find meaning in what we see
the number of individual pieces of data that are studied in a geographical enquiry
tips: A practice analysis of a photograph can help students first recognise the difference between assumptions and interpretations.

3678.name: Types of rainfall
3678.outcome: I can describe how rain forms and understand different reasons for its formation.
points: Relief rainfall occurs when warm moist air from the ocean rises up over mountains.
Convectional rainfall occurs when the sun heats up the land, when it cools and condenses it forms rainclouds.
Frontal rainfall occurs when a warm front meets a cold front.
The west of the UK is generally wetter than the east.
keywords: a change of state from a liquid to a gas
Precipitation is water, in the solid or liquid state, which falls from the atmosphere to Earth’s surface.
a sculptural technique where the designs are raised above a flat background
a change of state of a substance from a solid directly to a gas; e.g. iodine.
tips: Ensure that students are familiar with the hydrological cycle before starting this lesson.

3683.name: Anticyclones
3683.outcome: I can explain the weather associated with an anticyclone, and its impact on people and the environment.
points: High pressure systems, when air is sinking, are called anticyclones.
Anticyclones are characterised by dry, stable weather.
Anticyclones have very gentle winds shown by widely spaced isobars on a weather map.
Anticyclones can bring summer heatwaves and very cold conditions in winter.
keywords: a prolonged period of abnormally hot weather
have a strong effect on someone or something
applying defensive intensity to an opponent in possession of the ball
tips: High-pressure systems cause air to move outward and downward in a clockwise direction (in the Northern Hemisphere) or counterclockwise (in the Southern Hemisphere). You could use a spinning top to demonstrate the rotational motion.

3684.name: Depressions
3684.outcome: I can explain the weather associated with a depression.
points: Depressions are areas of low pressure where air is rising.
Warm air and cold air meet at depressions causing changeable temperatures and rain.
Depressions bring windy conditions shown by closely spaced isobars.
Typically the passage of a depression over the UK can last between 1 and 5 days.
keywords: a mass of air with the same levels of temperature, humidity, and pressure
in this context, a period of economic hardship in which there is very little business activity and not many jobs
a front refers to the line where opposing armies meet in battle
applying defensive intensity to an opponent in possession of the ball
tips: Students may remember the weather associated with depressions if you say "depressions are depressing, because it rains!"

3685.name: Weather and climate forecasting
3685.outcome: I can describe and read a weather forecast.
points: Weather forecasts can be displayed on synoptic charts.
Air pressure is shown on weather maps by isobars indicating areas of equal air pressure.
Symbols are used to indicate the type of weather that can be expected.
Weather fronts are shown on weather forecasts, these are cold and warm fronts.
keywords: force exerted by the weight (or mass) of the column of air above a place
a front refers to the line where opposing armies meet in battle
lines on weather maps that join areas with the same air pressure
strategy that involves anticipating what the answers might be by listing relevant French words or phrases
tips: You could show students a TV weather forecast for their local area to make this lesson relatable.

3687.name: Past climate change
3687.outcome: I can describe different types of evidence of past climate change.
points: Climate change is the long-term shift in temperatures and weather patterns.
The Earth's climate varies naturally and continuously over time.
Climate change can involve both global warming and global cooling.
Evidence of climate change comes from analysing ice cores, tree rings and the instrumental record.
keywords: a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
the information from a text that can support or justify our reasoning
the increase in Earth’s global temperature, likely caused by higher levels of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere
being dependable and consistent in performing your role, ensuring that teammates can count on you during competition
tips: Reinforce the use of the word evidence where possible.

3686.name: Causes of climate change
3686.outcome: I understand the physical and human causes of climate change.
points: There are both human and physical causes of climate change.
Volcanoes, sunspots and Earth's changing orbit around the sun can change the climate.
Human activity since the industrial revolution has been blamed for climate change.
Greenhouse gases absorb energy from long-wave radiation and re-emit it back into our atmosphere.
keywords: a belief, goal, or movement that someone cares about deeply and is willing to support and defend
a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
the effect of some gases in the atmosphere that keep Earth’s surface warmer than it would be without them
a gas that contributes to global warming by reducing the amount of radiation leaving Earth’s atmosphere
tips: Reinforce that climate change is not just caused by humans, and that we do expect climate to change naturally over time.

3688.name: Impacts of climate change on the UK
3688.outcome: I can understand the impacts of climate change on the UK.
points: Extreme weather events are becoming increasingly common due to climate change.
Climate change effects include higher temperatures in summer, fewer cold spells in winter and an increase in heavy rain.
Extreme weather events have social, economic and environmental effects.
keywords: a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
when a weather event is significantly different from the average or usual weather pattern
have a strong effect on someone or something
tips: Refer to scale in this lesson as impacts can vary depending on scale.

7469.name: Actions to tackle climate change
7469.outcome: I can describe how we can mitigate against and adapt to climate change.
points: There are a range of things we can do to measure our impact on the planet.
Living more sustainably can help tackle climate change.
We can mitigate against climate change by: planting trees, international agreements, and using alternative energy.
We can adapt to climate change by: adapting agriculture, considering water supply, and protecting the land from erosion.
keywords: An adaptation is a feature that organisms have to help them live in a particular place.
the total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases released into the atmosphere by an individual, product, process, country, etc
actions to reduce or prevent the emission of greenhouse gases
development that meets the needs of people today without damaging the environment or reducing resources for future generations
tips: It's useful to use real-world examples to make the distinction between adaptation and mitigation clear. For example, show images of wind farms or electric cars to represent mitigation and flood barriers or drought-resistant crops to illustrate adaptation.

3657.name: Our global population
3657.outcome: I can describe global population change over time.
points: Our population is growing and has reached 8 billion people.
Our population has changed over time, but icnreased most rapidly since the 1800s.
Population growth is slowing down, but is still expected to hit 9 billion by 2037.
keywords: the number of births for every 1000 people in a population per year
number of deaths per 1000 people per year
when the death rate is higher than the birth rate over a period of time
the difference between the birth rate and the death rate of a population; occurs when the birth rate is higher than the death rate
A group of organisms of the same type in the same place is called a population.
tips: A good place to find up-to-date data on population stats is Our World in Data

3659.name: Population density
3659.outcome: I can explain why population density differs across the globe.
points: Population is unevenly spread across the world.
Human and physical factors can affect population density.
A sparse population means that an area has few people relative to its size; rural areas have sparse populations.
A dense population means that an area has a large amount of people relative to its size; cities are densely populated.
keywords: an area with a high number of people living in it
how something is spread out over a geographical area
the number of people living in a defined area, e.g. 300 people per square kilometre
an area with relatively few people living in it
tips: Get pupils to move around the classroom to demonstrate densely and sparsely populated areas.

3660.name: GIS: Analysing the distribution of the world's population
3660.outcome: I can use a geographic information system (GIS) to investigate population data and alayse world popluation distribution.
points: A GIS allows us to store and display data on a digital map.
A GIS can be used to investigate population data within a country and across the world.
Maps of the world's ‘human footprint’ show us information on where people live and where has been impacted by humans.
GIS can be used to help explain the world’s human footprint.
keywords: a GIS (geographic information system) is a computer system that captures, analyses and displays geographic data to help understand spatial patterns
the number of people living in a defined area, e.g. 300 people per square kilometre
describes how the people in that population are spread out across the area
tips: It is straightforward to adapt the practice tasks to focus on areas of the world that pupils study as part of their geography curriculum.

3661.name: The population of the UK
3661.outcome: I can explain where people live in the UK and how topography influences population distribution.
points: The UK has a population of around 67 million people.
The population of the UK is unevely distributed with around 10 million people living in and around London.
The population distribution of the UK is affected by the topography, with fewer people living in mountainous areas.
keywords: the number of people living in a defined area, e.g. 300 people per square kilometre
describes how the people in that population are spread out across the area
a sculptural technique where the designs are raised above a flat background
tips: Get pupils to move around the room to demonstrate migration.

3663.name: Population structure
3663.outcome: I can interpret and analyse population pyramids.
points: A population pyramid shows the age and gender balance for a country.
A wider base on a pyramid means that there is a high birth rate.
The taller a pyramid is, the greater the life expectancy.
Bulges in population pyramids show years where there was a baby boom.
keywords: the number of births for every 1000 people in a population per year
the average number of years a person is expected to live
an age-sex graph used to present the structure of a population (that may resemble a pyramid)
tips: Give students some figures and graph paper to draw their own population pyramids.

3662.name: GIS: Analysing the population of the UK
3662.outcome: I can use a GIS to analyse the distribution and structure of the UK's population.
points: A GIS can be used to visualise and analyse the UK population.
A GIS can allow us to analyse the population density and age profile of the UK.
There are limitations with all GIS applications.
A GIS can be used to investigate changes in the UK population over time.
keywords: Geographical Information System: software that create maps of spatial data, as well as digital tools to analyse it
A census is the official collection of data about a whole population.
the number of people living in a defined area, e.g. 300 people per square kilometre
tips: ONS census maps allow pupils to analyse population data in England and Wales. Scotland and Northern Ireland both have freely available census maps that can be used in learning cycle 1. For learning cycle 2, all pupils should use the England and Wales census map or another GIS platform.

3665.name: Migration around the world
3665.outcome: I can describe the reasons for migration and differentiate between types of migrants.
points: Migration is the movement of people from one location to another, this can be permanent or temporary.
Push factors are the reasons why someone wants to leave a place such as war, famine, lack of jobs and hazards.
Pull factors are the reasons for someone moving to a place such as improved job prospects, education and safety.
There are different categories of migrants such as economic migrants, refugees and asylum seekers.
keywords: moving from one place to another with the intention of staying there
Pull factors refer to the attractive aspects or opportunities that draw individuals to a new destination.
negative things that make people want to leave an area, for example, war
tips: Get students to move around the room to demonstrate migration. Set up the classroom with regions representing different areas (e.g., safe zones, resource-rich places). Simulate migration based on push/pull factors like food or safety.

3666.name: Migration in the UK
3666.outcome: I can describe some of the impacts of migration on the UK.
points: Migration brings opportunities for a country but can also lead to challenges.
Migration can increase diversity within a country, leading to changes in fashion, food and culture.
People may choose to move away from the UK for different work or lifestyle opportunities.
keywords: anything to do with money, jobs, and resources
the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
a person who moves from one place to another
moving from one place to another with the intention of staying there
payments sent home by migrants to members of their family or community
tips: Discuss the benefits of migration by highlighting places in your local area that have come about or grown due to migration, such as international food outlets.

3667.name: Diversity and change in the local area
3667.outcome: I can describe the impact of migration on a local area in the UK.
points: Migration makes our population more diverse.
Diversity within the UK has led to changes in local communities and culture.
Local areas can change over time as a result of changes in population.
keywords: A census is the official collection of data about a whole population.
the shared ideas, customs, and art of a group of people
when a group has people with different backgrounds and experiences; this can be differences in nationality, ethnicity, culture, religion, language, identity, interests, skills and perspectives
tips: Use the internet to research other ways migration has influenced culture, food and fashion in the UK.

3664.name: Population challenges: ageing populations
3664.outcome: I can describe the features and impacts of ageing populations globally.
points: Life expectancies around the world are increasing due to better healthcare and disease prevention.
Many higher income countries such as the UK, Germany and Japan have ageing populations.
An ageing population leads to the government having to invest more in pensions and healthcare.
keywords: anything to do with money, jobs, and resources
services provided to individuals to treat and prevent illness
the average number of years a person is expected to live
a regular payment made during retirement from an investment fund
tips: A good place to find up-to-date data on population stats is Our World in Data.

3668.name: Population challenges: overpopulation and underpopulation
3668.outcome: I can describe overpopulation and underpopulation and responses different countries take to these challenges.
points: Overpopulation is where there are not enough resources to meet the needs of the population.
China's population grew rapdily in the twentieth century, resulting in the One Child Policy.
Underpopulation is where there are not enough people for the resources available.
The Australian government felt the country was underpopulated after WWII and encouraged people to live there.
keywords: moving from one place to another with the intention of staying there
describes how the people in that population are spread out across the area
anything that can be used for a human need
tips: Use 'Our World in Data' website to see how the populations of different countries have changed over time.

3670.name: The future of the world's population
3670.outcome: I can describe different theories of population change and understand that climate change will impact population change.
points: There are different theories about how population will change in the future.
The population of some places around the world is likely to significantly increase.
The population of some places around the world is likely to decrease.
Climate change will have an impact on the movement of people around the world.
keywords: a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
moving from one place to another with the intention of staying there
the number of people living in a defined area, e.g. 300 people per square kilometre
tips: Use Our World In Data website to explore population changes and projected changes across the globe.

3644.name: The UK's coastline
3644.outcome: I can explain what the coast is and describe how we use the UK's coastline.
points: The coastline is where the land meets the sea.
The United Kingdom is a range of islands, each with their own coastline.
Some parts of the coastline have a beach whereas other parts have cliffs.
The coastline has many uses, for example for fishing and tourism.
keywords: area of land between low and storm tide marks made up of beach materials like sand, mud and stones
A coastline is the boundary between the land and the sea or ocean.
the business of attracting and taking care of visitors to a place
tips: Ask students if they have ever visited the coast before and if so can they share their experiences. What was it like? What did they do there? Alternatively, if you live at the coast, ask students to talk about what your local area is like. Does it have a sand or shingle beach, or cliffs?

3645.name: Waves and tides
3645.outcome: I can explain what waves and tides are and I can identify and describe different types of waves.
points: Waves are powered by the wind and tides are controlled by the gravitational pull between the moon and Earth.
The stretch of open water over which the wind blows is called the fetch.
Constructive waves have a powerful swash and a weaker backwash.
Destructive waves have a powerful backwash and a weaker swash.
keywords: the distance over water that wind blows, which affects the size and energy of waves
the regular rise and fall of sea levels caused by the Moon’s and Sun’s gravity pulling on Earth’s oceans
ripples in the sea caused by wind blowing over the surface of the water
tips: Be careful with swash and backwash - students will often say 'backswash' by putting the two terms together. Highlight and correct this straight away if it does happen, even if you have to do so multiple times, this should ensure the mistake doesn't become embedded.

3646.name: Processes shaping the coastline
3646.outcome: I can name and describe processes that help to shape our coastlines.
points: Natural processes that happen at the coast help to shape coastlines.
There are four types of erosion: abrasion, hydraulic action, attrition and solution.
There are four types of transportation: traction, solution, suspension and saltation.
The process of deposition occurs when waves have lost their energy and can no longer carry their load.
keywords: when material being carried is dropped due to loss of a river’s energy
the wearing away of rocks along the coastline
a series of steps or actions taken to achieve a result
When objects are moved from one place to another, it is called transportation.
tips: Use flashcards or matching games to help to consolidate understanding of new geographical terms.

3648.name: Erosional coastal landforms
3648.outcome: I can explain erosional processes and describe the coastal landforms they create.
points: There are four types of erosion: abrasion, hydraulic action, attrition and solution.
The geology of a coastline will have an impact on the rate of erosion.
Coastal landforms, such as arches, are formed through erosional processes over millions of years.
The sequence from a headland to a stump is: headland, cave, arch, stack, stump.
keywords: the wearing away of rocks along the coastline
the study of the Earth and its physical structure
a natural feature created by a process such as erosion or deposition
a measure of how much change occurs per unit of time
tips: If you have some small samples of different types of hard and soft rock to pass around the room, students can feel how they are all 'solid', even though some of them are 'hard' and some of them are 'soft'.

3649.name: Depositional coastal landforms
3649.outcome: I can explain depositional processes and describe the coastal landforms they create.
points: Longshore drift is the lateral movement of sediment across the beach through swash and backwash.
Longshore drift creates depositional landforms such as spits, bars and tombolos.
Spits are long narrow ridges of sand or shingle which project from a coastline into the sea.
Salt marshes may form behind spits, as these are low energy zones.
Spits can change direction due to the prevailing wind, which makes them curve into a hook.
keywords: when the water from a wave retreats back into the sea
when material being carried is dropped due to loss of a river’s energy
A material deposited by water, wind or ice, such as pebbles or sand.
when a wave rushes up the beach
When objects are moved from one place to another, it is called transportation.
tips: Use internet software to look at satellite images of spits and other depositional landforms around the UK, and in other places around the world. Ask students to compare them and talk about similarities and differences. This will help them to identify the features of the landforms.

3650.name: Threats to the UK's coastline
3650.outcome: I can describe how the UK's coastline is at risk from threats such as rising sea levels.
points: The UK's coastline is at risk due to sea level rise as a result of climate change.
Rising sea levels are speeding up rates of erosion, leading to the east coast of England eroding quickly.
When cliffs erode quickly they put homes and buildings on top of the cliffs at risk of falling into the sea.
Some parts of the UK's coastline are eroding at a rate of more than 2 metres a year.
keywords: a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
the wearing away of rocks along the coastline
the increase in Earth’s global temperature, likely caused by higher levels of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere
Something that increases the chance of something harmful happening.
The average level of the world’s oceans, which we use as a baseline to measure the height of the land.
tips: Use old and new maps to work out distances of settlements from cliffs in different time periods as evidence of coastal retreat. Students could also track and list buildings, roads or entire settlements that have been lost to the sea as a result of coastal erosion.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3651.name: GIS: Visualising and Analysing coastal erosion
3651.outcome: I can visualise and analyse coastal erosion using GIS platforms.
points: Aerial imagery can be used to visualise coastal erosion using GIS.
Old and new maps can visualise coastal erosion using GIS.
Analysing maps and aerial imagery using GIS can help us explain patterns of coastal erosion.
keywords: a GIS (geographic information system) is a computer system that captures, analyses and displays geographic data to help understand spatial patterns
to form a picture in your mind or imagine how something looks
tips: It is easy to extend this lesson using the same GIS applications and let the pupils complete an enquiry project about coastal erosion the Holderness coast.

3652.name: Protecting the UK's coastline
3652.outcome: I can describe how different methods of hard and soft engineering protect the UK's coastline from erosion.
points: Hard engineering is the building of fixed structures to slow down the waves and the rate of erosion.
Soft engineering is working with nature to reduce the risk of flooding and erosion.
Examples of hard engineering include groynes, sea walls and gabions.
Examples of soft engineering include beach replenishment and dune stabilisation.
keywords: area of land between low and storm tide marks made up of beach materials like sand, mud and stones
the wearing away of rocks along the coastline
A disturbance that travels, like a ripple on water.
tips: You can demonstrate some coastal defences using small models and water. Take a thick piece of card representing a cliff, and another representing a sea wall. Stand them parallel in a watertight container and throw water at the sea wall. Which piece of card gets wettest and deteriorates quickest?

3653.name: Coastal management
3653.outcome: I can explain why different stakeholders have varying views about coastal management.
points: Management plans are in place in order to protect the coast.
In England and Wales, local councils work with the government to implement Shoreline Management Plans.
Hard and soft engineering can be used to help protect coastal areas from erosion.
There are different groups of stakeholders in coastal areas.
Different stakeholders support different coastal management plans.
keywords: using artificial structures to protect coastlines from erosion and flooding
Something that increases the chance of something harmful happening.
making use of natural processes to reduce erosion and flooding in a way that minimies environmental impact
anyone who has an interest in or is affected by a decision or issue
tips: Try role play to allow students to put themselves in the shoes of different stakeholders. Encourage them to think about the individual needs or concerns of stakeholders and how coastal management plans could impact them particularly.

3654.name: Tuvalu: An island nation
3654.outcome: I can describe aspects of the physical and human geography of Tuvalu.
points: Tuvalu is an island nation in the Pacific Ocean with 9 main islands including some atolls.
Some of the islands are made from coral, seawater bubbles up through the coral causing flooding.
Many Tuvaluans rely on subsistence farming, the saltwater is poisoning the soil.
Tuvalu experiences drought and water scarcity due to lack of natural freshwater.
keywords: a type of coral reef shaped like a ring with a water body in the middle
tiny marine organisms that accumulate to form coral reefs in tropical waters
a country that does not share any land borders with other countries
the body of water in the middle of an atoll
farming that is done to feed oneself and one’s family, not for profit
tips: Coral reefs are among some of the most beautiful and unique ecosystems on Earth as well as the most fragile. Encourage students to investigate the risks of human activity for coral reefs and find out how some areas are mitigating or managing those risks.

3655.name: The impacts of climate change on Tuvalu
3655.outcome: I can explain why some people in Tuvalu are at risk of becoming displaced due to climate change.
points: Tuvalu is a low elevation coastal zone.
Building coastal defences for small island nations can be challenging due to their low elevation.
The residents of Tuvalu could become displaced as a consequence of climate change.
A displaced person is someone who is forced to move due to something outside their control such as flooding.
keywords: a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
The average level of the world’s oceans, which we use as a baseline to measure the height of the land.
to be forced to move due to something outside human control such as flooding
tips: Have a class 'sweep' to guess what your location's elevation is. You can find out your elevation exactly using a phone app or the internet. Encourage students to think about the local topography and landscape when making their guesses. How high above sea level are you? Who guessed closest?

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3656.name: The future of global coasts
3656.outcome: I can explain the risks associated with climate change for coastal communities and describe how countries are taking action to combat them.
points: Climate change is putting millions of people across the world at risk from sea level rise and flooding.
Island nations and coastal cities and communities are trying to mitigate the risk with built structures.
There are different actions taking place to find solutions and try to prevent further global issues.
keywords: a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
Something that increases the chance of something harmful happening.
tips: Climate change and its impacts is a hotly debated topic in society. Allow space for students to express their opinons and ideas, to share their concerns and give them opportunity to debunk myths about climate change they may have picked up from social media.

3689.name: The forests of the world
3689.outcome: I can explain why forests are important and describe the global distribution of different types of forest.
points: Forests have a range of important functions and benefits.
There are different types of forest across the world, e.g. tropical rainforests, boreal forests and temperate forests.
Different types of forests are located in specific parts of the world.
keywords: a large-scale ecosystem with specific climate, plants and animals
the average weather conditions in a region over a long period of time
a large area full of trees
the increase in Earth’s global temperature, likely caused by higher levels of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere
A habitat is the place where an organism lives. It must provide food, shelter and a place to reproduce.
tips: A nice way to help students understand biome locations is to describe how the vegetation would change if you walked north from the equator.

3690.name: The tropical rainforest biome
3690.outcome: I can describe and explain the location of tropical rainforests and identify their key features.
points: Tropical rainforests are located in the tropical climate zone.
Tropical rainforests are home to millions of species of plants, animals, insects, birds and humans.
There are four layers to the forest; the emergents, the canopy, the understory and the forest floor.
keywords: a large-scale ecosystem with specific climate, plants and animals
the average weather conditions in a region over a long period of time
energy radiated from the sun via electromagnetic waves
the region north and south of the Equator, between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn lines of latitude
tips: Every time you can it is good to emphasise that the climate of the rainforest is hot, potentially ask the students to imagine how they would feel if they were in a rainforest, what they would wear etc. This helps remove misconceptions before they arise.

3691.name: People's use of the rainforest
3691.outcome: I can describe different ways people use tropical rainforests and explain the impacts of deforestation.
points: Indigenous peoples have been living in tropical rainforests for thousands of years.
People use rainforests in a variety of ways including farming, mining, medicine and homes.
Deforestation is rapidly reducing the size of rainforests to make way for human activity.
Deforestation has negative impacts: loss of carbon sinks, loss of habitats, soil erosion and the displacement of people.
keywords: a land use category used for areas that trade goods and services
economy is the way people, businesses and governments make and spend money
the wearing away of rocks along the coastline
indigenous people are the original inhabitants of a specific area
tips: There is the potential to discuss what jobs students would want in the rainforest.

3693.name: Protecting the tropical rainforest
3693.outcome: I can describe how tropical rainforests can be protected using the example of Costa Rica.
points: Costa Rica is a small country in central America which once experienced the highest rate of deforestation in the world.
Costa Rica was the first tropical country in the world to reverse deforestation.
Wildlife corridors enable species such as the jaguar to move through the rainforest undetected.
National parks, selective logging, small-scale agroforestry and ecotourism have protected the rainforest.
keywords: the variety of species found in a habitat
large-scale removal or clearing of forests
A habitat is the place where an organism lives. It must provide food, shelter and a place to reproduce.
the purpose or function of land, for example: residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural or recreational use
tips: There is the potential to use GIS to compare forested area over time.

3694.name: The temperate deciduous forests
3694.outcome: I can locate the temperate deciduous forests, describe their climate and explain the role of the nutrient cycle.
points: Temperate forests are distributed across Europe, Asia and North America, within the temperate climate zone.
The temperate forests have an average annual temperature of 10 degrees Celsius.
There are four layers in a temperate deciduous forest; the canopy, sub-canopy, herb layer and the ground layer.
The nutrient cycle means the soil in the temperate deciduous forest is nutrient rich.
keywords: the region between the tropics and the polar areas
to change, or to alter something, to suit different conditions.
the average weather conditions in a region over a long period of time
chemical substances found in all biotic features which are important for survival
Food that is seasonal is only harvested at certain times each year.
tips: It would be useful for students to have access to a world map with country names.

3695.name: Animals and plants in the temperate deciduous forests
3695.outcome: I can describe how animals and plants in temperate deciduous forests adapt to the climate.
points: Animals such as squirrels, hedgehogs, and birds, such as nightingales, can be found in temperate deciduous forests.
Plants such as oak trees, beech trees and bluebells can be found in temperate deciduous forests.
Animals and plants adapt to living in seasonal conditions in different ways.
keywords: Climate zones are areas that have similar weather conditions and climate, e.g. the tropics
to migrate is to move from one place to another
An organism is a living thing.
the temperate climate zone is the region between the tropics and the polar areas
tips: Task A allows for drawn or written responses or both.

3696.name: The boreal forest biome
3696.outcome: I can locate boreal forests and explain their climate and adaptations.
points: The boreal forest is the world's largest land-based biome.
The boreal forest is also known as the taiga; they are found at high latitudes.
There is little rainfall in the boreal biome due to the high latitudes and temperature.
Boreal forests contain many coniferous trees which are normally evergreen and so don’t drop their leaves.
keywords: a large-scale ecosystem with specific climate, plants and animals
A hemisphere is half a sphere.
an imaginary line running east to west around the Earth's surface that is used to show how far north or south a place is
Producers make their own food using a series of chemical reactions called photosynthesis. The reaction includes taking in carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
energy radiated from the sun via electromagnetic waves
tips: If any trees are visible from the window or are well known to students locally, these can be discussed alongside christmas trees to relate the coniferous, evergreen, deciduous definitions to students' own lives.

3697.name: People's use of the boreal forest
3697.outcome: I can describe how people live in the boreal forest, human activities there and the impact of these activities.
points: Communities such as the Saami live in parts of the boreal forest, they are traditionally reindeer herders.
Traditional ways of life in the boreal forest are being threatened.
Deforestation is rapidly reducing the size of boreal forests to make way for human activity.
Deforestation has led to the fragmentation of the woodland caribou habitat.
keywords: the world’s largest land biome, found in the Northern hemisphere
indigenous people are the original inhabitants of a specific area
moving from one place to another with the intention of staying there
Rural means something to do with the countryside.
relating to a city or town; often busy, built-up areas with lots of human activity
tips: There is the potential to set a research task as homework to investigate how a specific boreal forest is changing.

3698.name: Climate change and the forests
3698.outcome: I can explain how deforestation contributes to climate change and how climate change impacts forests.
points: Global temperatures are increasing because of climate change.
Forests remove carbon dioxide from Earth's atmosphere and replace it with oxygen.
Deforestation is a major contributor to climate change.
Climate change can cause changes to species in a forest; the spread of pests and diseases and more and worse wildfires.
keywords: a compound with molecules that each contain one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms
When a substance decomposes it undergoes a decomposition reaction.
large-scale removal or clearing of forests
gases in the atmosphere that keep it warmer than it would be without them
energy radiated from the sun via electromagnetic waves
tips: A homework task linked to this topic could involve students calculating their own carbon footprint using an online calculator.

3699.name: The Siberian wildfires
3699.outcome: I can say why wildfires occur and talk about the impact of the Siberian wildfires.
points: Wildfires are uncontrolled fires that spread fast through vegetation, e.g. forests, grasslands or shrublands.
Wildfires have both natural and human causes.
Climate change is making the conditions needed for wildfires to spread more likely.
The carbon dioxide emitted from wildfires was a huge contribution to carbon emissions in 2022.
The 2022 Siberian wildfires had devastating impacts on people and the environment.
keywords: the world’s largest land biome, found in the Northern hemisphere
a natural or artificial system that absorbs more carbon dioxide than it releases
the increase in Earth’s global temperature, likely caused by higher levels of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere
A habitat is the place where an organism lives. It must provide food, shelter and a place to reproduce.
tips: There is potential to relate this content to the increased wildfire risk in the UK. A HW research task to create a poster on "How to avoid accidental wildfires" could be beneficial.

3700.name: Mangroves: forests of the seas
3700.outcome: I can describe the role of mangrove forests and talk about the impact of forest loss in the Sundarbans.
points: Mangroves are shrubs and trees which grow in coastal waters.
Mangroves help protect the land from flooding, caused by tropical storms and tidal surges.
The Sundarbans in India and Bangladesh are an example of a mangrove forest.
Mangroves face a variety of threats including coastal developments, farming and sea level rise.
The impacts of mangrove loss include: coastal flooding, loss of biodiversity, resources and income.
keywords: the variety of species found in a habitat
an unusual rise in sea level above the normal level of high tide
the regular rise and fall of sea levels caused by gravity from the moon and the sun pulling on Earth’s oceans
a powerful low-pressure weather system that forms in tropical regions
a rise in the proportion of people living in urban areas
tips: There is potential for students to research the actions people are taking to protect the mangroves as homework.

3701.name: The future of our forests
3701.outcome: I can describe ways in which forests are being protected for the future.
points: Sustainable management of the forests is vital for the health of Earth and for future generations.
Reforestation and afforestation schemes help absorb carbon dioxide and improve biodiversity.
Agroforestry can help people farm more sustainably and reduce forest clearance.
Stronger laws and the use of technology help to combat deforestation and illegal logging.
keywords: introducing forest to land which has not been forested for a long time/ever
trees, crops and/or livestock occupy the same land
large-scale removal or clearing of forests
the wearing away of rocks along the coastline
Reforestation is the act of planting trees on an area of land that has become empty or spoiled.
tips: There is potential for students to use GIS further to investigate deforestation as homework.

3702.name: GIS: Visualising the human and physical geography of India
3702.outcome: I can use a geographic information system (GIS) to visualise the human and physical geography of India.
points: GIS can be used to visualise the human and physical geography of India.
India is located just north of the Equator in southern Asia.
India is similar in size to Greenland although looks much smaller on some projections of the world map.
Different layers of data on a GIS show that the population of India is very high.
Visualising the landscape using GIS shows that India is a very diverse country.
keywords: Geographical Information System: software that create maps of spatial data, as well as digital tools to analyse it
a separate, transparent sheet within a digital canvas used to organise elements of an artwork
to form a picture in your mind or imagine how something looks
tips: Teachers may want to use two lessons rather than one to explore the themes in more detail.

3704.name: The climate of India
3704.outcome: I can use climate graphs to investigate what India’s climate is like and how it varies from place to place.
points: Most of India has a tropical monsoon climate and has three seasons.
Cherrapunjee in India is one of the wettest places on Earth, it receives 12 metres of rain a year.
The average annual temperature in India is around 27.4 degrees celsius.
The highest recorded temperature was in Delhi in 2024 and it was 53.2 degrees celsius.
India has a varied climate because of its large size and diverse landscape.
keywords: height above sea level or ground level
the average weather conditions in a region over a long period of time
all the visible features of an area of land, often considered in terms of their visual appeal
an imaginary line running east to west around the Earth's surface that is used to show how far north or south a place is
a measure of how hot a substance is; it is related to the kinetic energy of the individual particles
tips: Investigate climate data from other locations in India and make comparisons with climate data from the UK.

3705.name: Monsoon season in India
3705.outcome: I can explain how monsoons are formed and why they are important.
points: Monsoons lead to distinct wet and dry seasons.
The north-east monsoon occurs in the winter months and the south-west monsoon occurs during the summer.
The change in wind direction during the monsoon is caused by a difference in pressure over the land and ocean.
The monsoon is very important to India’s people and its economy.
Climate change is causing the monsoon rains to become more erratic and unpredictable.
keywords: a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
economy is the way people, businesses and governments make and spend money
electricity created by water flowing downhill turning a turbine
a seasonal change in wind direction that brings a very rainy season or a very dry season
applying defensive intensity to an opponent in possession of the ball
tips: Investigate news reports about the impacts of the monsoon season in India and other countries.

3706.name: The biomes of India
3706.outcome: I can list some of India’s biomes and use a geographic information system (GIS) to investigate one of these biomes.
points: A biome is a large community of vegetation and wildlife adapted to a specific climate.
India has a range of biomes including desert, savanna and forests.
The Great Thar desert is one of the largest deserts in the world and part of it is found in India.
The tropical forests of the Western Ghats are one of the most biodiverse places on Earth.
A geographical information system (GIS) can be used to investigate biomes in India.
keywords: Geographical Information System: software that create maps of spatial data, as well as digital tools to analyse it
a large-scale ecosystem with specific climate, plants and animals
the temperate climate zone is the region between the tropics and the polar areas
the tropical climate zone is the region between the Tropic of Cancer in the north and the Tropic of Capricorn in the south
tips: Use GIS or atlases to investigate other biomes in India.

3707.name: Coastal India: the Sundarbans
3707.outcome: I can describe what the Sundarbans are like, explain why they are important and list some ways in which they are being protected.
points: The Sundarbans are a mangrove forest found in north-east India and south-west Bangladesh in the Bay of Bengal.
The Sundarbans are known for their wide range of animals included the royal Bengal Tiger and the estuarine crocodile.
The Sundarbans are one of the largest remaining areas of mangroves in the world.
The Sundarbans face challenges such as climate change, overuse of resources, and conflict between people and wildlife.
There are three wildlife sanctuaries in the Sundarbans to help conserve its unique and varied biodiversity.
keywords: the variety of species found in a habitat
a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
a shrub or tree that grows in coastal water and has roots that grow above ground
an area where wild animals and plants and their habitats are protected
tips: Use other sources of information to further investigate the benefits of mangrove forests and the challenges they face.

3708.name: The population of India
3708.outcome: I can describe population growth in India and explain why population distribution is uneven across the country.
points: The population of India is over 1.4 billion and has overtaken China as the largest population in the world.
India has a high average population density of 479 people per square kilometre.
The population of India is unevenly distributed because of different physical and human factors.
keywords: moving from one place to another with the intention of staying there
A group of organisms of the same type in the same place is called a population.
the number of people living in a defined area, e.g. 300 people per square kilometre
describes how the people in that population are spread out across the area
tips: Use GIS to investigate how population density varies across India.

3709.name: Rural to urban migration in India
3709.outcome: I can describe reasons why people migrate from rural areas to cities in India and identify benefits and challenges of this migration.
points: Each year thousands of people move from rural areas to cities in India.
There are different reasons why people migrate from rural to urban areas.
The migration of people from rural to urban areas has benefits and brings challenges.
keywords: the variety of cultural and ethnic groups within a society
economy is the way people, businesses and governments make and spend money
moving from one place to another with the intention of staying there
Pull factors refer to the attractive aspects or opportunities that draw individuals to a new destination.
negative things that make people want to leave an area, for example, war
tips: Drama and role play could be used to further explore the thoughts that a young person might have about whether to move from a rural area to the city.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

3710.name: Mumbai: A global city
3710.outcome: I can use images to investigate the geography of Mumbai and explain why Mumbai is called a global city.
points: A global city is a well-connected city with good transport and financial links across the world.
Mumbai has a population of around 22 million people and is the financial capital of India.
Property in Mumbai is becoming some of the most expensive in the world due to Mumbai being a thriving global city.
Mumbai accounts for 25% of India's industrial output.
Bollywood is a major film industry in India and it is based in Mumbai.
keywords: a city that is a major centre for trade and communication with other places around the world
the total value of goods produced by a country's industry
the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
a city with a population of 10 million people or more
the number of people living in a defined area, e.g. 300 people per square kilometre
tips: There are many different ways to use images in investigate the geography of places. Other possibilities include asking learners to generate questions about an image; imagine what people in an image might be thinking or saying; and extending a cropped image.

3711.name: Opportunities in Mumbai
3711.outcome: I can describe ways in which Mumbai has developed over time and identify opportunities in living and working in this global city.
points: Mumbai was once a small fishing port however it has grown significantly over time.
Mumbai’s population has increased; more and more land is becoming built up and infrastructure has developed.
Mumbai’s rapid growth and status as a global city provides a wide range of opportunities.
Many large transnational corporations are based in Mumbai such as Tata and the State Bank of India.

the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
ways in which to help, support and / or serve the public

3712.name: Challenges in Mumbai
3712.outcome: I can identify some of the challenges facing Mumbai and describe some ways in which the lives of people living there are unequal.
points: There are high levels of inequality in Mumbai.
It is estimated that around 1.2 million people earn less than 20 rupees a day.
Mumbai's transport system is incredibly busy and overcrowded.
Some people live in informal settlements, however these are some of the happiest settlements in India.

areas of makeshift housing where the people who live there don’t own the land or have access to services like clean water, power, sanitation
presence of harmful substances in the environment, such as in the air, water or soil, which can damage ecosystems and human health
poverty is the state of being extremely poor
ways in which to help, support and / or serve the public
tips: Cut up a cake or share out stickers unfairly to illustrate what inequality means.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

3713.name: Evaluating India's status as a global superpower
3713.outcome: I can describe ways in which India is changing and explain why the country is called a global superpower.
points: India has the fifth largest economy in the world.
India's economy was worth $3.6 trillion in 2023.
Global superpower is used to describe a country that has a lot of power or influence over other countries in the world.
Different indicators can be used to measure how India has changed over time.

tips: Learners could collaborate in groups for Task A. The activity could be made less challenging by using a selection of the questions instead of the full set.

3715.name: Climate change in India
3715.outcome: I can describe some impacts of climate change in India and give examples of ways in which the country is taking climate action.
points: Some people and places are more impacted by climate change than others.
Droughts, flooding and heatwaves in India are becoming more frequent and severe because of climate change.
People around the world are taking action against climate change but a lot more action is needed.
India is taking action in different ways to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to climate change impacts.

3716.name: GIS: Visualising the human and physical geography of China
3716.outcome: I can use a geographic information system (GIS) to visualise the human and physical geography of China.
points: GIS can be used to visualise the human and physical geography of China.
China is located in the Northern Hemisphere in the continent of Asia.
China is the fourth largest country in the world by area although it looks smaller on some projections of the world map.
Different layers of data on a GIS show that the population of China is very high.
Visualising the landscape using GIS shows that China is a very diverse country.
keywords: a GIS (geographic information system) is a computer system that captures, analyses and displays geographic data to help understand spatial patterns
a separate, transparent sheet within a digital canvas used to organise elements of an artwork
to form a picture in your mind or imagine how something looks
tips: Teachers may want to use two lessons rather than one to explore the themes in more detail.

3717.name: The climate of China
3717.outcome: I can use climate graphs to investigate what China’s climate is like and how it varies from place to place.
points: China’s climate varies considerably because of its large size and diverse landscape.
Much of China has a monsoon climate with dry winters and wetter summers.
Temperatures in part of China can reach more than 50oC in the summer.
China’s lowest recorded temperature was -53oc in Mohe, the country’s northernmost city.
Some places in China receive heavy rainfall; other places have an arid climate.

the average weather conditions in a region over a long period of time
an imaginary line running east to west around the Earth's surface that is used to show how far north or south a place is
a seasonal change in wind direction that brings a very rainy season or a very dry season
a measure of how hot a substance is; it is related to the kinetic energy of the individual particles
