3718.name: The biomes of China
3718.outcome: I can list some of China’s biomes and use a geographical information system (GIS) to investigate one of these biomes.
points: A biome is a large community of vegetation and wildlife adapted to a specific climate.
China has a range of biomes including desert, grassland and forests.
The Gobi desert is one of the largest deserts in the world and part of it is found in China.
The tropical forest of Xishuangbanna is one of the largest forests in Asia.
A geographical information system (GIS) can be used to investigate biomes in China.
keywords: Geographical Information System: software that create maps of spatial data, as well as digital tools to analyse it
a large-scale ecosystem with specific climate, plants and animals
the temperate climate zone is the region between the tropics and the polar areas
the tropical climate zone is the region between the Tropic of Cancer in the north and the Tropic of Capricorn in the south
tips: Use GIS or atlases to investigate other biomes in China.

3719.name: The Gobi Desert
3719.outcome: I can describe what the Gobi Desert is like, explain why it is growing in size and give examples of action that is being taken to reduce this desertification.
points: The Gobi Desert is a large, cold desert that covers parts of northern China and southern Mongolia.
The Gobi Desert is a rain shadow desert and is formed by the blocking of rainfall by the Himalayas.
Different factors make the Gobi Desert a challenging environment to survive in.
Human activities are causing the Gobi Desert to increase in size.
Different actions are being taken to try and reduce desertification in and around the Gobi Desert.
keywords: a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
an area of land that is extremely dry and receives less than 25 centimetres of rain per year
the process by which land becomes desert due to climate change, deforestation, or inappropriate agriculture
the wearing away of rocks along the coastline
a seasonal change in wind direction that brings a very rainy season or a very dry season
tips: Use GIS and other sources of information to investigate the Gobi Desert in more detail. Comparisions could also be made with other major deserts in the world.

3720.name: Population change in China
3720.outcome: I can describe population growth in China and explain why population distribution is uneven across the country.
points: The population of China is more than 1.4 billion; China is the second most populous country in the world.
China’s population increased rapidly after the Second World War but its population is now declining.
Falling birth rates and an ageing population are contributing to the decrease in China’s population.
The population of China is unevenly distributed because of different physical and human factors.
keywords: the number of births for every 1000 people in a population per year
number of deaths per 1000 people per year
A group of organisms of the same type in the same place is called a population.
the number of people living in a defined area, e.g. 300 people per square kilometre
describes how the people in that population are spread out across the area
tips: Use GIS to investigate how population density varies across China.

3721.name: Rural to urban migration in China
3721.outcome: I can describe reasons why people migrate from rural areas to cities in China and identify benefits and challenges of this migration.
points: Each year millions of people move from rural areas to cities in China.
More than 64% of people in China live in urban areas and this proportion is increasing rapidly.
There are different reasons why people migrate from rural to urban areas.
The migration of people from rural to urban areas has benefits and brings challenges.
keywords: the variety of cultural and ethnic groups within a society
economy is the way people, businesses and governments make and spend money
moving from one place to another with the intention of staying there
Pull factors refer to the attractive aspects or opportunities that draw individuals to a new destination.
negative things that make people want to leave an area, for example, war
tips: Drama and role play could be used to further explore the thoughts that a young person might have about whether to move from a rural area to the city.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

3722.name: Beijing: A global city
3722.outcome: I can use images to investigate the geography of Beijing and explain why Beijing is called a global city.
points: A global city is a well-connected city, this means that there are good transport and financial links across the world.
Beijing is the capital of China and has a population of around 22 million people.
Beijing is a major centre for finance and industry, both in in China and globally.
Beijing is important for its rich history and culture; millions of tourists visit the city each year.
keywords: economy is the way people, businesses and governments make and spend money
a city that is a major centre for trade and communication with other places around the world
the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
a city with a population of 10 million people or more
a set idea that people have about what someone or something is like
tips: There are many different ways to use images in investigate the geography of places. Other possibilities include asking learners to generate questions about an image; imagine what people in an image might be thinking or saying; and extending a cropped image.

3723.name: Opportunities in Beijing
3723.outcome: I can describe ways in which Beijing has developed over time and identify opportunities of living and working in this global city.
points: Beijing is one of the oldest cities in the world with a history dating back around 3000 years.
Beijing’s population has increased; more and more land is becoming built up and infrastructure has developed.
Beijing’s rapid growth and status as a global city provides a wide range of opportunities.
Many large transnational corporations have bases in Beijing.
keywords: a city that is a major centre for trade and communication with other places around the world
the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
ways in which to help, support and / or serve the public
TNCS are large companies that operate in several countries; they often have headquarters in one country and factories or offices in others
a rise in the proportion of people living in urban areas
tips: Use GIS tools to explore how land use in Beijing has changed over time.

3724.name: Challenges in Beijing
3724.outcome: I can identify some of the challenges facing Beijing and describe some ways in which the lives of people are unequal.
points: There are high levels of inequalities in Beijing and many other places in the world.
Beijing is one of the wealthiest cities in the world but many people struggle to meet their daily living needs.
Beijing’s high population density puts strains on housing, infrastructure and services.
Poor air quality in Beijing is harmful to people and the environment.
keywords: when things are not fair or equal for everyone
areas of makeshift housing where the people who live there don’t own the land or have access to services like clean water, power, sanitation
the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
presence of harmful substances in the environment, such as in the air, water or soil, which can damage ecosystems and human health
ways in which to help, support and / or serve the public
tips: Cut up a cake or share out stickers unfairly to illustrate what inequality means.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

3726.name: China: The workshop of the world
3726.outcome: I can explain why so many things are made in China and describe some of the impacts of this on people and the environment.
points: More than a quarter of the products manufactured globally are made in China.
China manufactures a wide range of products such as electronics, clothing, toys and machinery.
Cheaper labour, good infrastructure and a large population are some of the reasons why so many things are made in China.
Manufacturing in China impacts people and the environment in different ways.
keywords: economy is the way people, businesses and governments make and spend money
a gas that contributes to global warming by reducing the amount of radiation leaving Earth’s atmosphere
manufactured items are items produced by a machine
moving from one place to another with the intention of staying there
The starting materials used to make products are known as the raw materials. Wood, metal and crude oil are examples of raw materials.
tips: Spend more time discussing possible impacts of manufacturing in China. Some impacts, such as rural to urban migration, are investigated in other lessons in this unit. If possible, complete the consequence wheel in groups. Simplify the activity by considering just one of the manufacturing impacts.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

3727.name: Evaluating China's status as a global superpower
3727.outcome: I can describe ways in which China is changing and explain why the country is called a global superpower.
points: China has the second largest economy in the world; it was worth US$17.8 trillion in 2023.
Global superpower is used to describe a country that has a lot of power or influence over other countries in the world.
Different indicators can be used to measure how China has changed over time.
China’s political system affects some of the rights and freedom that Chinese people have.
keywords: economy is the way people, businesses and governments make and spend money
the money a person or government earns
when things are not fair or equal for everyone
poverty is the state of being extremely poor
tips: Learners could collaborate in groups for Task A. The activity could be made less challenging by using a selection of the questions instead of the full set.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

3728.name: Climate change in China
3728.outcome: I can explain why some people and countries contribute more to climate change than others and describe some ways in which China is taking action to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions.
points: A carbon footprint is a measure of the amount of greenhouse gases something releases into the atmosphere.
Some people and countries contribute more to climate change than others.
Tackling climate change needs a huge reduction in the world’s greenhouse gas emissions.
China is taking action in different ways to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
keywords: a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
gases in the atmosphere that keep it warmer than it would be without them
energy that comes from moving water such as fast-flowing rivers, waterfalls and waves at sea
energy from natural sources that are constantly replenished, like wind and solar
tips: Create a positive climate news board with examples of ways in which people are taking climate action.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

3730.name: Globalisation: An introduction
3730.outcome: I can explain what globalisation is.
points: Globalisation is the way in which the world has become more interconnected.
Globalisation is not a new concept. Colonisation and exploration both led to the sharing of ideas and cultures.
Globalisation can lead to a diverse society where there is a wide variety of people, religions and different cultures.
keywords: the global exchange of goods and services
the increased interconnectedness of the world, economically, politically and culturally
different parts or things being linked or related
tips: If the students are struggling to annotate the map they could work in small groups or pairs.

3731.name: The globalisation of jeans
3731.outcome: I can explain how various countries contribute to the production of a single product.
points: Materials to make jeans come from a number of countries and they may be made and exported from another country.
Fashion is a global industry and jeans are sold all over the world.
There are issues with sustainability in the manufacture of jeans.
keywords: A component refers to a part of something, e.g. a tyre on a car.
the increased interconnectedness of the world, economically, politically and culturally
Trade is the exchange of goods, commodities and services.
tips: Get students to look at the labels of their clothes to see where they have been made.

3732.name: Food production and supply chains
3732.outcome: I can explain what a supply chain is and how this impacts the food we eat.
points: Supermarkets are the main way that people shop for food.
Many supermarkets in the UK are global companies and operate in different countries around the world.
Supermarkets sell many different goods and food items which all have their own complex supply chains.
keywords: goods and services sold to another country
goods and services brought in from another country
making changes to a food’s natural state, e.g. cooking beans in tomato sauce and preserving them in tins
The starting materials used to make products are known as the raw materials. Wood, metal and crude oil are examples of raw materials.
all of the stages involved in producing goods, transporting them and selling them to customers
tips: Bring in a variety of packaging from food items to see where they have come from. Could set this as a homework for students too.

3733.name: The drivers of globalisation
3733.outcome: I can explain what drives globalisation.
points: There are different drivers for globalisation and these include transport and commnications.
Other drivers for globalisation include economic activity, trade of goods, supply and demand.
Political factors and changes in technology also drive globalisation.
keywords: the act of giving and receiving information between people, companies and countries
the increased interconnectedness of the world, economically, politically and culturally
the action of putting forward money, time or effort with the aim of making a profit or other benefit
Trade is the exchange of goods, commodities and services.
tips: Ask students how they connect with people around the world. What devices can they use to do this?

3734.name: The importance of trade
3734.outcome: I can explain what trade is and why countries trade with each other.
points: Global trade involves exporting goods from one country and importing them to other countries.
Commodities are raw materials which can be bought and sold.
Manufacturing uses raw materials to make other goods for sale.
Import and export data can be used to show the types and amounts of things that countries trade around the world.
keywords: goods and services sold to another country
goods and services brought in from another country
compulsory charges to citizens and businesses by government to finance some of its spending
Trade is the exchange of goods, commodities and services.
tips: Bring in an example of a commodity and manufactured good to show the difference.

3736.name: The UK's imports and exports
3736.outcome: I can describe the UK's main imports and exports and can explain why we trade those products.
points: The UK trades goods and products with countries around the world.
The UK imports food, products and other goods that it does not produce itself.
The UK exports goods and manufactured products produced here to other countries that want to buy them.
keywords: goods and services sold to another country
goods and services brought in from another country
the making of goods on a large scale, often using machinery
Trade is the exchange of goods, commodities and services.
tips: Make clear to students that you can import and export services. For example, you can sell an educational course.

3737.name: Global transport routes
3737.outcome: I can describe global transport routes and explain the importance of the Suez Canal in global trade.
points: Container ships transport products across the world.
Many container ships take products from eastern China to western Europe through a series of 'choke points'.
The Suez Canal is an important route for global trade from Asia to Europe.
In 2021 the Ever Given became stuck in the Suez Canal, delaying global trade.
keywords: goods carried by ships, road, rail and aircraft
narrow passageways of water in global transport routes
using containers to transport goods by ships, road and rail
the exchange of goods, money and services between countries
tips: Start the lesson by asking pupils to use atlases to work out what route ships will use to transport products from China to the UK. This will help pupils engage with the content as they may see the chokepoints for themselves.

3738.name: Transnational corporations
3738.outcome: I can explain what a transnational corporation is and describe some of their activities in different countries.
points: A transnational corporation is a company that can be found all over the world such as Nike and McDonalds.
Transnational corporations can bring about glocalisation, where products and ideas are adapted to local cultures.
keywords: transnational corporation. A company that operates in more than one country
the shared ideas, customs, and art of a group of people
the increased interconnectedness of the world, economically, politically and culturally
when TNCs adapt their product or service to suit the local market better
tips: Get students to think of companies they have seen in other countries of the world either in person or on TV shows and social media.

3739.name: TNCs: Advantages and disadvantages
3739.outcome: I can explain the advantages and disadvantages of TNCs for both high and low income countries.
points: Transnational companies can bring benefits and disavantages to countries.
Benefits from TNCs include the creation of jobs, new trade markets and better education to produce skilled workers.
Disadvantages of TNCs can include exploitation of the host country, poor treatment of workers and environmental damage.
keywords: the new country which the TNC has set up a new factory, office or shop in
the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
More people have jobs so have more money to spend, giving other businesses more money so they expand and employ more workers
the level of necessities and comforts of daily life that is available to and affordable by a person
tips: Explain to students that often the advantages of TNCs are economic while a lot of the disadvantages tend to be environmental. Socially, people can be at an advantage or disadvanatage.

3740.name: Analysing patterns of globalisation using digital maps and data
3740.outcome: I can analyse patterns of globalisation and explain why some countries are more interconnected than others.
points: Some places of the world are more interconnected than others.
Digital maps and graphs can help us visualise and analyse patterns and trends in globalisation.
The wealth and size of the country can influence economic and social globalisation.
keywords: the way people, places, and things are linked together through movements of people, goods, money, information, and ideas
to form a picture in your mind or imagine how something looks
tips: This lesson can easily be expanded to investigate a greater range of evidence showing interconnectedness. Pupils may like to choose maps to investigate to see if they can see patterns of globalisation.

3741.name: Globalisation opportunities
3741.outcome: I can explain the opportunities associated with globalisation.
points: Globalisation can be good for businesses as they can sell products around the world.
Globalisation can be good for consumers as they can buy products from around the world.
People are exposed to fashion, food, music and culture from around the world.
Technology and ideas can spread quickly around the world leading to improvements in people's quality of life.
keywords: a person who purchases a good or service
the shared ideas, customs, and art of a group of people
the increased interconnectedness of the world, economically, politically and culturally
wellbeing of individuals or groups of people measured by criteria other than wealth such as housing, employment and environmental factors
tips: Ask students to think of ways they have benefitted from globalisation.

3742.name: Globalisation challenges
3742.outcome: I can explain the challenges associated with globalisation.
points: Globalisation can have severe environmental consequences and can increase global warming.
Local businesses are often out-competed by foreign businesses leading them to close down.
Globalisation has been blamed for creating a more uniform culture around the world.
keywords: transnational corporation. A company that operates in more than one country
the shared ideas, customs, and art of a group of people
coal, oil, and natural gas, formed from the remains of ancient plants and animals over millions of years
the increase in Earth’s global temperature, likely caused by higher levels of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere
gases in the earth's atmosphere that trap heat, leading to climate change
tips: Explain to students the difference between local and global scale.

3743.name: Geological timescales
3743.outcome: I can explain how geological time is divided, and identify the current period and epoch we live in.
points: Geological timescales are measured in millions of years.
A period is a basic unit of geological time and they last for millions of years.
An epoch is a subdivision of a geological time period.
We are currently in the quaternary period in the holocene epoch.
keywords: the largest division of geological time, lasting hundreds of millions to billions of years
the smallest measurement of geological time, a subdivision of a period, lasting thousands to millions of years
1st and 3rd person singular of the irregular verb 'ser' in the imperfect tense
A period is a row on the periodic table that corresponds to the number of electron shells in an atom.
tips: You could teach students to remember the order of the older geological time divisions with the mnemonic: Camels, Often, Sit, Down, Carefully. Perhaps, Their, Joints, Creak.

3744.name: The rock cycle
3744.outcome: I can identify the three main types of rocks, and recognise how they are formed by different processes.
points: There are three types of rock; igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic.
Igneous rocks are volcanic rocks and examples include basalt, obsidian and granite.
Sedimentary rocks are formed from sediments and examples include sandstone, limestone and chalk.
Metamorphic rocks are formed through heat and pressure and examples include slate, gneiss and marble.
keywords: the wearing away of rocks along the coastline
applying defensive intensity to an opponent in possession of the ball
a series of steps or actions taken to achieve a result
A rock is a solid substance, which is a mixture of minerals. It composes any solid portion of Earth.
the breakdown or disintegration of rocks at or close to the surface
tips: You could use rock samples or edible models (e.g. crumbled cookies for sedimentary rocks, melted chocolate for igneous rocks, and compressed marshmallows for metamorphic rocks) to help students understand the differences between the rock types and how they change over time.

3746.name: The geology of the UK
3746.outcome: I can explain the formation and distribution of rocks in the UK, and understand how past tectonic activity shaped the landscape.
points: The UK has a rich and varied geology with igneous, metamorphic and sedimentary rocks present.
England's lowland geology is dominated by sedimentary rocks, such as limestone.
Scotland's geology is dominated by metamorphic rocks with areas of igenous rock.
In the past, Britain was close to a plate boundary, and there was volcanic activity.
keywords: how something is spread out over a geographical area
rocks formed due to intense heat and pressure
rocks formed from layers of compressed sediment
the structure of Earth’s crust and how it was formed
tips: Use real-world examples and physical rock samples (if available) to help students connect abstract geological concepts to evidence.

7239.name: GIS: Visualising the geology of the UK
7239.outcome: I can use GIS to visualise and analyse the UK's geology and the way this creates contrasting landscapes.
points: Understanding the UK’s geology is important, especially for building, mining and managing our energy and water supplies.
The British Geological Survey is a government-funded organisation that studies the UK’s geology, resources, and hazards.
GIS can be used to show the south-east to north-west pattern in the UK’s geology.
The UK’s varied geology leads to contrasting landscapes.
keywords: rocks formed due to intense heat and pressure
rocks formed from layers of compressed sediment
tips: You may choose to project your use of the Geography Visualiser rather than using the video modelling in the slide deck.

3747.name: Weathering and rocks
3747.outcome: I can explain the different types of weathering.
points: There are three types of weathering; biological, chemical and physical weathering.
Biological weathering is when rocks are broken up by the roots of plants or from animals burrowing into them.
Chemical weathering is when rocks are broken up by acids in rainwater or when air reacts with minerals in the rocks.
Physical weathering is when rocks are broken up by changes in temperature, such as when ice forces apart cracks in rock.
keywords: relating to the interaction of substances
the breakdown or disintegration of rocks at or close to the surface
tips: If teaching this lesson in person, you could bring in small rock samples or use a visual demonstration to show how weathering works. For example, use sugar cubes to illustrate chemical weathering by dissolving them in vinegar or place wet sponges in a freezer to mimic freeze-thaw weathering.

3749.name: Limestone landscapes
3749.outcome: I can identify the key features of limestone, and describe different limestone landscapes.
points: Limestone is a sedimentary rock made of calcium carbonate.
Grykes are deep cracks on the surface on limestone formed by chemical weathering.
Clints are exposed blocks of limestone separated by grykes.
Limestone landscapes include limestone pavements, such as Malham Cove, and limestone caves, such as Gough's Cave.
keywords: deep cracks on the surface of limestone pavements
a way to successfully solve a problem or overcome a challenge
tips: A helpful way to remember what clints and grykes are, is: clints are clumps, and grykes are gaps.

3750.name: The importance of soil
3750.outcome: I can explain what soil is made of, how it forms, and understand its importance.
points: Soil is made up of minerals, dead plants and animals, water and living organisms.
Soil takes hundreds of years to form.
There are three main particle sizes in soil, clay, sand and silt.
Soil is important for farming; infertile soil can make growing crops very difficult.
Soil is an important carbon store and protecting it can help us reduce global warming.
keywords: something that absorbs and holds carbon
the wearing away of rocks along the coastline
Soil is ground up rock mixed up with plant and animal remains.
the breakdown or disintegration of rocks at or close to the surface
tips: You could use different types of chocolate to represent different soil: dark chocolate chunks represent rocky soil, white chocolate shavings can represent sandy soil, which is light and crumbly, milk chocolate fudge can represent clay soil, which is sticky and holds moisture well.

3748.name: Fieldwork: Planning a soil enquiry and collecting data
3748.outcome: I can collect soil texture data on my school site.
points: Soil texture can potentially affect the rate of water infiltration.
A fieldwork enquiry can be used to find the extent to which soil texture effects infiltration.
Geographers can use a combination of data collection techniques to investigate the characteristics of soil.
keywords: the process by which water on the ground surface enters the soil
how porous soil structure is (i.e. the size and quantity of spaces between soil particles)
characteristics of soil, such as how large the soil particles are, or how large the pores (spaces) between the particles are
tips: Introduce students to the fieldwork equipment they are going to be using beforehand in the classroom. This will help them to remember the names of equipment and increase their confidence in handling it.

guidance.label: Risk assessment required - equipment
guidance.description: Use of equipment that may require supervision for safety, e.g. scissors in KS1, needles, paint, knives, cooking.

guidance.label: Risk assessment required - outdoor learning
guidance.description: Fieldwork.

3751.name: Fieldwork: Presenting soil data
3751.outcome: I can present soil texture data using creative techniques.
points: Data made up of three parts can be shown on a triangular graph.
Proportional shapes or symbols can be used to compare the size of data values.
All forms of data presentation need to conform to particular standards and use conventions to make them readable.
keywords: data that is the relative amount of something when considered as part of a whole
a symbol on a map or in a graph that shows a value of data by the size at which it has been drawn
a graph with three axes used to display proportional data with three constituent parts
tips: If you have access to a visualizer, use this to structure and plot the points on a triangular graph in real time. This tricky skill is often easier to comprehend when it is modelled to students.

7429.name: Fieldwork: Analysing, concluding and evaluating soil data
7429.outcome: I can analyse and reflect on my soil data to create meaningful conclusions and an evaluation.
points: Analyses of data can sometimes reveal data that does not seem to fit with the general pattern.
Geographers should try to find explanations for anomalous data.
Geographers look for evidence that their data is both valid and reliable.
keywords: a value within the data set that does not appear to follow the general pattern or trend
data that could be replicated if the data collection were to be repeated
data that is able to answer or partially answer an enquiry question
tips: Listing the geographical variables that were not measured in the data collection stage can be a good way of helping students to formulate sensible reasons for anomalies.

3752.name: Mass movement
3752.outcome: I can understand mass movement and know how gravity causes sediments to move downhill.
points: Mass movement is the downhill movement of sediment under the influence of gravity.
The main types of mass movement are rockfall, sliding, and slumping.
Slumping is common on coastlines.
Weathering and erosion lead to mass movement when combined with wet weather conditions.
keywords: the wearing away of rocks along the coastline
the downhill movement of material under the influence of gravity
the breakdown or disintegration of rocks at or close to the surface
tips: Use real-life examples, such as famous coastal cliffs or landslide events, to make the topic more relatable. Show videos to highlight the dramatic effects of mass movement, and consider using physical demonstrations (e.g., using sand and water to simulate a mudflow) te exemplify.

3754.name: Geology and the economy
3754.outcome: I can explain why geological resources are important to the economy, and where they come from.
points: Mining provides valuable materials like fossil fuels, stone, and metals.
Rare earth metals are vital for modern tech like phones and green energy.
Oil and gas are found in underground reservoirs, beneath land or sea.
Oil and gas take millions of years to form.
Fossil fuels and minerals support economies through jobs and exports.
keywords: improving and building on design ideas to make them better
economy is the way people, businesses and governments make and spend money
coal, oil, and natural gas, formed from the remains of ancient plants and animals over millions of years
mining is the process of digging into the ground to remove natural resources
the process of extracting stone or other materials from a quarry
tips: This lesson can be made relatable by linking it to the technology students use. You could bring in real-world objects (like a smartphone or battery) and ask students to guess what materials it contains.

3753.name: The impacts of using geological resources
3753.outcome: I can evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using geological resources and explain how they affect people and the environment.
points: Geological resources bring money, jobs, and materials we rely on daily.
Extraction harms landscapes, wildlife, and sometimes local communities.
Mining and fossil fuels create jobs and support national economies.
Fossil fuels pollute and add to global warming despite economic value.
Sustainable alternatives are growing but aren't yet fully replacing fossil fuels.
keywords: the process of removing natural resources from the ground
coal, oil, and natural gas, formed from the remains of ancient plants and animals over millions of years
presence of harmful substances in the environment, such as in the air, water or soil, which can damage ecosystems and human health
using resources wisely so future generations can also meet their needs
tips: Encourage students to think critically by weighing up the pros and cons, rather than assuming that resources are purely good or bad.

3755.name: Inside Earth
3755.outcome: I can describe the structure of Earth and how the pattern of earthquakes and volcanoes relate to Earth's tectonic plates.
points: Earth is made up of four main layers: the inner core, outer core, mantle and crust.
Together the upper mantle and the crust form Earth’s rigid outer layer: the lithosphere.
The lithosphere is broken into large sections or tectonic plates.
Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur at plate boundaries.
keywords: The mass per cubic metre (m³) or cubic centimetre (cm³) of a material.
where two tectonic plates meet is known as a plate boundary
applying defensive intensity to an opponent in possession of the ball
a large, rigid slab of Earth's lithosphere (outer layer) that sits on the semi-solid asthenosphere beneath it
tips: A real or imaginary hardboiled egg can be used as a model: shell = crust, white = mantle and yolk = core, squeeze to crack the shell to show how the tectonic plates fit together. In addition, show students a globe and turn it round to the Pacific to demonstrate a Pacific centred map.

3757.name: The movement of tectonic plates
3757.outcome: I can use evidence to show that the continents have moved and explain how tectonic plate movement happens.
points: The theory of continental drift suggests that Earth’s continents were once joined together and later drifted apart.
Evidence for continental drift includes continents' jigsaw like shape, rock type and fossils matching across continents.
There are two types of crust; oceanic and continental crust.
Oceanic crust is dense but thin and continental crust is thicker and less dense.
Plates move by the processes of slab pull and ridge push.
keywords: A continent is a large land mass on Earth and there are seven: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Oceania.
The mass per cubic metre (m³) or cubic centimetre (cm³) of a material.
a large, rigid slab of Earth's lithosphere (outer layer) that sits on the semi-solid asthenosphere beneath it
tips: It is possible to model slab pull by using a chain or scarf hanging off the edge of a table. Let the students see how the weight of the item drags the rest of it down off the table.

3758.name: Plate boundaries
3758.outcome: I can describe what happens at plate boundaries, including the tectonic hazards that occur.
points: There are four main types of plate boundary: conservative, constructive, collision and destructive.
At a conservative plate boundary, the tectonic plates move past each other, causing earthquakes.
At a constructive plate boundary, the tectonic plates move apart, causing volcanic eruptions and earthquakes.
At collision plate boundaries, plates move together, causing earthquakes.
At destructive plate boundaries, plates move together, causing volcanoes and earthquakes.
keywords: a lot of mass packed into a small space
where two tectonic plates meet is known as a plate boundary
a large, rigid slab of Earth's lithosphere (outer layer) that sits on the semi-solid asthenosphere beneath it
tips: Focusing on the root words helps students to differentiate between the plate boundaries: conservative (land conserved), constructive (land constructed), collision (plates collide) and destructive (oceanic plate lost as it is subducted into mantle).

3759.name: Types of volcanoes
3759.outcome: I can name the key features of volcanoes and explain how composite and shield volcanoes are formed.
points: There are two main types of volcano: composite and shield volcanoes.
Composite volcanoes are usually found at destructive plate boundaries and they are highly explosive volcanoes
Shield volcanoes are usually found at constructive plate boundaries.
Some eruptions are explosive, whereas others are effusive.
keywords: The rocky, outermost layer of Earth.
a boundary where two tectonic plates move together causing volcanoes and earthquakes
Molten (i.e. melted) rock beneath the Earth's surface.
A layer of dense rock found below the crust. Parts of it behave as a fluid over very long, geological time scales.
tips: You can model viscosity by pouring honey and water onto a tray and observing which moves faster. This can be an imagined task without equipment too.

3760.name: Volcanic hazards
3760.outcome: I can explain what pyroclastic flows, ash and lahars are and relate this to real life examples.
points: Volcanic eruptions can lead to a range of hazards, such as pyroclastic flows, ash and lahars.
Pyroclastic flows are flows of hot volcanic gases, ash and rock.
Ash is made up of tiny pieces of volcanic rock and glass, this can damage lungs, machines, crops and buildings.
Lahars are mudflows caused by volcanic material mixed with water.
Mount Semeru (Java, Indonesia) erupted in 2021, triggering damaging pyroclastic flows, ashfall and lahars.
keywords: tiny pieces of volcanic rock and glass
the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
a mudflow formed when volcanic ash mixes with water
a very hot mix of lava, ash, gases and rock that flows rapidly down the side of the volcano
tips: Students enjoy imagining themselves experiencing a volcanic eruption. Try to set them up for the misconception above during discussion, this will make the learning more meaningful for them.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3761.name: Living close to volcanoes
3761.outcome: I can explain why people live near volcanoes and how to prepare for and respond to eruptions.
points: One in twenty people lives close to an active volcano due to their fertile soils, tourist income and geothermal energy.
There are risks including: pyroclastic flows, ash and lahars.
Preparation such as public education as well as the monitoring of volcanoes can reduce risks to people living close by.
Short-term responses include local and international emergency services providing aid to people.
Long-term responses include infrastructure repair/rebuild in the months and years after the eruption.
keywords: to move people away from an area with a threat or hazard to a place of safety
the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
action that focuses on rebuilding after the tectonic hazard and reducing risks from future hazards
actions that occur in the hours, days or weeks immediately after a disaster to help the basic needs of people
tips: Researcing a specific volcano, and creating an advert to encourage more visitors, could provide an inspiring homework task.

3762.name: The eruption of Mount Nyiragongo
3762.outcome: I can explain why Mount Nyiragongo erupted and the impacts of the eruption.
points: Mount Nyiragongo is a volcano located in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, on the East African Rift System.
On the 22nd May 2021, it began to erupt; this followed a deadly eruption in 2002, which reached the city of Goma.
When the eruption happened, lava poured down the sides of the volcano.
At least 450 000 people were displaced or evacuated due to the lava flows.
keywords: consequences that relate to the way money is made, lost or spent
the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
consequences that relate to people’s quality of life, e.g. healthcare
tips: It is worth researching the current state of the volcano to set the 2021 eruption in context, or asking students to find any updates for homework.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3763.name: Earthquakes
3763.outcome: I can describe where earthquakes occur and explain how they happen.
points: Earthquakes are sudden, violent movements of the ground caused by tectonic plate movement.
Earthquakes usually happen on or near plate boundaries.
At a plate boundary two plates are locked together, yet moving in different directions.
When rock fractures at a plate boundary this causes an earthquake.
Small earthquakes can also occur far from plate boundaries.
keywords: the point deep underground where the tectonic plates first break
where two tectonic plates meet is known as a plate boundary
The huge pieces that Earth’s crust is broken into are known as tectonic plates.
tips: Get up-to-date details of earthquakes in the UK and globally using the British Geological Survey and US Geological Survey websites.

3764.name: The effects of earthquakes
3764.outcome: I can categorise primary and secondary effects of earthquakes and explain why some earthquakes are more deadly than others.
points: Primary effects happen directly as a result of an earthquake, for example broken gas pipes.
Secondary effects happen as a result of an earthquake's primary effects, for example a fire.
Earthquake severity depends on the magnitude, focus depth, epicentre location, aftershocks, preparations and response.
Some of the deadliest and costliest earthquake events have occurred in high income countries.
keywords: The area of attention in a story or piece of writing.
the point on Earth's surface that is directly above where an earthquake happens underground
a measure of the energy released by an earthquake
tips: A homework task could be to research the primary and secondary effects for a case study that interests the students.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3765.name: Living in earthquake regions
3765.outcome: I can explain to what extent people can anticipate earthquakes and how they survive living in areas affected by earthquakes.
points: Scientists can calculate the probability of an earthquake happening within an area in the future.
It is not currently possible to predict exactly when or where earthquakes will occur.
Earthquake detection can only provide seconds of warning.
Drop-cover-hold is practised during earthquake drills.
Base isolators, flexible building materials, strong shapes and mass dampers help create earthquake-resistant buildings.
keywords: The probability that an event will occur is the proportion of times the event is expected to happen in a suitably large experiment.
identifying that something has just happened or is happening now
strategy that involves anticipating what the answers might be by listing relevant French words or phrases
tips: To engage students you could introduce a simple earthquake drill "When I shout earthquake you need to drop to the floor, cover under the table and hold on." For even more suspense say that you may do this at any time for the rest of the unit.

3766.name: The 2025 Myanmar Earthquake
3766.outcome: I can describe the causes, effects and recovery efforts made following the 2025 Myanmar Earthquake.
points: Stress had built up along the Sagaing faultline in central Myanmar and was released during the 2025 earthquake.
Myanmar is a low income country affected by conflict.
Few plans were in place and earthquake-resistant buildings were rare.
The 7.7 magnitude quake occurred close to large centres of population.
Many different organisations provided short-term aid for the millions of people who needed support.
keywords: total value of goods and services produced within a country, divided by its population
a smaller earthquake that follows an initial larger earthquake
a boundary where two tectonic plates move past each other, either in different directions and/or at different speeds, in the same direction
tips: The final task would work well as a homework task, especially if access to devices, in order to do research, is challenging in a classroom environment.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3768.name: The 2018 Sunda Strait Tsunami
3768.outcome: I can explain how a tsunami occurs and what happened in the Sunda Strait in 2018.
points: A tsunami is a series of large, powerful ocean waves caused by a sudden disturbance.
Undersea earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and landslides can displace sufficient water to trigger a tsunami.
In 2018, a tsunami was caused by the collapse of the Anak Krakatau volcano in the Sunda Strait in Indonesia.
Tragically, the tsunami led to the deaths of over 430 people.
The impact was devastating due to insufficient warning systems, the Strait funnelling the waves, and the time of day.
keywords: to move something from its original position, e.g. ocean water
the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
a series of large ocean waves caused by underwater earthquakes, volcanic eruptions or landslides
tips: Emphasising that the knowledge from the lesson could save their lives, can add importance to the content.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3780.name: Lives around the world
3780.outcome: I can describe some of the similarities and differences of living in different places around the world.
points: Life varies around the world in a range of different ways related to physical and human geography.
There are similarities as well as differences in how we live around the world.
There is inequality in wealth and housing within countries.
Average incomes give us perceptions about a country but they give us a limited understanding of what a place is like.
keywords: total value of goods and services produced within a country, divided by its population
the average weather conditions in a region over a long period of time
when things are not fair or equal for everyone
tips: You could easily adapt this lesson so that pupils use computers to investigate lives around the world using the dollar street website.

3769.name: Perspectives on inequality and development
3769.outcome: I can explain different perspectives on inequality and development.
points: Inequality is the uneven distribution of resources, opportunities, and living conditions.
Inequality can be categorised as economic, social, political, digital and environmental.
Inequality can vary over geographical space and between different groups.
Development refers to the improvement in people's quality of life within a country or region.
There are a variety of different perspectives on development.
keywords: improving and building on design ideas to make them better
when things are not fair or equal for everyone
development that meets the needs of people today without damaging the environment or reducing resources for future generations
tips: The lesson refers to inequality across different ethnic groups. You may consider adapting this depending upon your local context.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

3770.name: Measuring and mapping development
3770.outcome: I can describe and evaluate key indicators of development.
points: There are many different ways of measuring development.
Economic indicators of development, such as GDP per capita, are a common way of comparing countries.
Composite indicators of development, such as the HDI,are often seen as a more rounded way of measuring development.
Indicators that measure happiness and ecological footprints are important as they go beyond simply measuring wealth.
keywords: a measure that combines multiple individual indicators to give a more complete picture of development
improving and building on design ideas to make them better
a measurable piece of data used to assess and compare levels of development between countries or regions
tips: Debating over the best way of measuring development is a great opportunity for a class discussion.

3771.name: GIS: Analysing inequality at different scales
3771.outcome: I can use Geographic Information Systems to analyse patterns of inequality at different scales.
points: Digital maps and GIS help us visualise inequality globally and within the UK.
Digital maps help us analyse economic and social inequality.
GIS can be used to analyse deprivation across a transect in a city.
keywords: total value of goods and services produced within a country, divided by its population
Geographical Information System: software that create maps of spatial data, as well as digital tools to analyse it
low standard of living caused by low income, poor health and low educational attainment, sometimes described as living in poverty
the estimated average number of years lived free from disability or disease burden
when things are not fair or equal for everyone
tips: The 2nd learning cycle includes analysing deprivation across a transect across Sheffield. You may wish to replicate the instructions using a different place. Analysing deprivation within the local area is sensitive and it is important to consider what is appropriate for your setting.

3772.name: Changes in wealth and quality of life over time
3772.outcome: I can analyse trends in development indicators over time.
points: Overall the world has become wealthier over time.
GDP per capita has risen in many countries, but in some countries it has remained the same.
Statistics suggest that health and education has improved in most places around the world over time.
Despite increasing wealth, inequality has also grown in many countries.
keywords: total value of goods and services produced within a country, divided by its population
a measure of inequality on a scale between zero and one
economy is the way people, businesses and governments make and spend money
tips: The ‘Our world in data’ website can be used to find maps that show changes over time. You can add or change this lesson to use development indicators of your choice.

3773.name: Physical geography and development
3773.outcome: I can explain how physical geography influences development.
points: Physical geography can help or hinder development.
Relief, natural resources, natural hazards, climate and location may all be barriers to development.
Countries can overcome physical barriers to development in a variety of ways.
HICs are often more able to overcome physical barriers than LICs due to having more financial resources.
keywords: the average weather conditions in a region over a long period of time
being surrounded by land of other countries, having no coast
extreme natural events that have the potential to cause harm to people, property, and the environment
materials or substances occurring in nature, such as minerals, water, forests, and fossil fuels
a sculptural technique where the designs are raised above a flat background
tips: The practice task in learning cycle 2 could be made into a much larger activity where the pupils do significant research into each country and then make more extensive suggestions based on their context.

3774.name: Past and present causes of inequality
3774.outcome: I can explain how historical and present-day human factors have created and reinforced inequalities.
points: Colonialism was a system where powerful countries controlled others for power, land and resources.
Colonialism shaped modern trade and wealth gaps.
Debt and global trade rules reinforce global inequality.
Technology gaps limit opportunities in poor nations.
Historical inequalities still impact development today.
keywords: the occupation, management and control of one country by another, often involving exploitation of its people and resources
a debt is something, especially money, that is owed to someone else
goods brought in from another country
tips: This lesson deals with the difficult subject matter associated with colonialism and slavery. It is worth liaising with your school’s History department to speak about where these topics fit into their curriculum.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of discriminatory behaviour
guidance.description: Historic or outdated representations of people that may portray inequality or injustice.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

3775.name: Inequality and migration
3775.outcome: I can explain the link between migration and inequality.
points: Inequality in wealth between countries can lead to migration.
On average, people are more likely to move from lower-income countries to higher-income countries.
Inequality in safety between countries can lead to migration.
Refugees often have to flee quickly and they are likely to go to a bordering country.
Listening to people's experiences of migration helps us understand the variety of reasons people move.
keywords: when people have to move, often due to war or natural disasters
someone who has successfully sought asylum in another country and is henceforth protected by international law
when people choose to move, often for work or lifestyle
tips: Real-life stories of migration help humanise the topic. Look for videos or get people who have migrated to speak to the class to make sure that pupils understand the complexity of migration.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction of war, threats of war, death or the aftermath of war.

3776.name: Gender and inequality
3776.outcome: I can analyse the relationship between gender and inequality.
points: Women earn less than men due to unequal access to jobs, pay, and property in many countries.
Girls are more likely to miss school due to poverty, conflict, or cultural expectations.
Women are underrepresented in political leadership in most countries.
Gender inequality varies by place and is shaped by geography, culture, laws, and development.
Progress is being made in some places through laws, education, and activism, promoting gender equality.
keywords: when people have different rights, responsibilities and access to resources based on their gender
when different groups of people have a voice in government or decision-making, like being able to vote or become leaders
tips: You may wish for pupils to research the gender equality advocates from learning cycle 2.

3777.name: Climate justice and environmental inequality
3777.outcome: I can explain how climate change impacts are felt unequally and why this leads many people to call for climate justice.
points: Historically, high income countries have produced more greenhouse gases than low income countries.
Low income countries are often more vulnerable to climate change as they have fewer resources to adapt to its impacts.
Many people call for climate justice, so that poorer and more vulnerable people are not unfairly affected.
keywords: relating to, or resulting from the influence of human beings on nature.
a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
gases in the atmosphere that keep it warmer than it would be without them
tips: An extension of the final activity can be to hold a debate on the topic of climate justice. A good way to manage this is to give pupils different roles and ask them to argue from their perspective.

3781.name: Strategies to support development
3781.outcome: I can explain different ways to support development and evaluate the effectiveness of top-down strategies.
points: Strategies to support development can be top-down or bottom-up
Investment, aid, debt relief and fairtrade are all strategies to reduce the development gap
All strategies to reduce the development gap have strengths and weaknesses.
keywords: an organisation dedicated to improving the income and lives of farmers in lower income countries by making trade fairer
help given by a group or country to support development in another country or for disaster relief
when debt is cancelled or reduced
the action of putting forward money, time or effort with the aim of making a profit or other benefit
tips: The final practice activity can be developed so that pupils debate top-down aid from the perspective of different stakeholders.

3782.name: Grassroots movements and development
3782.outcome: I can describe what grassroots development means and explain how grassroots initiatives can improve people’s lives.
points: Grassroots development is when local people work together to solve problems and make their communities better.
Grassroots development focuses on community participation, local knowledge, empowerment and sustainability.
Practical Action is a charity which supports grassroots development.
Grassroots development is often seen as sustainable.
keywords: where local people are actively involved in planning, decision-making, and running projects
giving people the confidence, skills, and control they need to make decisions and improve their own lives
development that meets the needs of people today without damaging the environment or reducing resources for future generations
tips: Pupils could be given a homework on researching a charity that focusses on grassroots initiatives.

3783.name: The growth of cities
3783.outcome: I can explain the process of urban growth and describe the distribution of cities around the world.
points: The urban hierarchy explains how settlements range from small villages to global cities based on size and function.
Urbanisation is the growth of urban areas and is a phenomenon experienced globally.
The location of the biggest cities in the world has changed over time from high to low and middle income countries..
The two main causes of urbanisation are rural to urban migration and natural increase.
In 2008, for the first time in world history, over 50% of the world's population lived in towns and cities.
keywords: the difference between the birth rate and the death rate of a population; occurs when the birth rate is higher than the death rate
the movement of people from the countryside to towns and cities
a rise in the proportion of people living in urban areas
tips: Use Our World in Data to show interactive graphs on urban population growth. Let students explore how urbanisation rates differ between HICs, NICs, and LICs to visualise global trends and challenge misconceptions.

3784.name: GIS: Visualising and analysing the growth of cities
3784.outcome: I can use GIS to visualise and analyse the growth of cities around the world.
points: GIS can be used to visualise cities around the world.
India and China now have a large number of megacities.
Cities with a lower HDI often have faster growth rates than cities with a higher HDI.
GIS can be used to analyse the growth of different cities around the world.
keywords: a UN measure of development calculated using education, life expectancy and income data
a background map in a GIS
a city with a population of 10 million people or more
tips: Pupils can study the cities which are referred to in other parts of your curriculum. This will help pupils make links with other topics of study.

3785.name: Urban structure and land use
3785.outcome: I can compare different urban land use models and apply them to real-world cities.
points: Urban land use models help explain how cities are structured and how different areas serve different functions.
The Burgess and Hoyt models are examples of urban land use models.
Land use models often don’t match the land use of cities due to physical geography and local context.
Comparing urban land use models to cities such as Sheffield can help us understand the layout and function of the city.
keywords: the CBD is the commercial and business centre of a city, usually with high land values, tall buildings and a concentration of shops, offices and services
someone who lives a distance from where they work and has to regularly travel between the two locations
the purpose or function of land, for example: residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural or recreational use
tips: Although this lesson uses Sheffield, pupils could investigate a city close to them and compare it with urban land use models. The Geography Visualiser is a perfect tool to do this.

3786.name: Global cities and megacities
3786.outcome: I can explain how some cities have a global influence.
points: Global cities influence business, banking and culture around the world.
Not all megacities (10 million or more) are global cities and vice versa.
Global cities are hubs for international travel.
Global cities are diverse and multicultural.
The influence of different cities changes over time.
keywords: a city that is a major centre for trade and communication with other places around the world
a city with a population of 10 million people or more
relating to or containing several cultural or ethnic groups within a society
tips: Use well-known examples (e.g. New York, London, Lagos, Tokyo) to help students distinguish between global cities and megacities. Visuals such as maps or global company headquarters can support understanding of influence beyond just size.

3787.name: Population in cities
3787.outcome: I can explain who lives in cities and why.
points: Urban populations often have a larger share of people aged 18–40.
Migration to cities is driven by employment and educational opportunities.
Cities provide a wide range of leisure facilties which are also a draw for younger people.
Natural increase is a key factor in the growth of urban populations.
High population density puts pressure on infrastructure and services.
keywords: moving from one place to another with the intention of staying there
the difference between the birth rate and the death rate of a population; occurs when the birth rate is higher than the death rate
the number of people living in a defined area, e.g. 300 people per square kilometre
tips: Use real-life city examples (like London, Manchester, or Lagos) to illustrate why people move to cities and how different age groups use urban spaces. This helps students connect abstract ideas (like migration or population density) to places they know or have heard of.

3788.name: Benefits of living in cities
3788.outcome: I can identify the advantages of urban life.
points: Cities provide a wider range of jobs, and more opportunities in healthcare and education.
Urban areas are meeting places, reflecting diverse cultures and cultural richness.
Cities have advanced infrastructure and services.
Cities drive innovation and economic growth.
Cities provide more business opportunities.
keywords: the shared ideas, customs, and art of a group of people
the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
the process of coming up with new ideas or inventions
tips: Use examples from your local area like local transport systems, famous inventions, or cultural festivals to make these ideas concrete and memorable.

3789.name: Challenges of living in cities
3789.outcome: I can explain the challenges that people living in cities face.
points: The high cost of land can lead to overcrowding.
Pollution (air, water, noise) is a major urban issue.
The growth of cities may be faster than the growth of services.
Urban growth and traffic congestion hampers life in cities.
The poorest people may be vulnerable to environmental hazards due to the location of informal housing, e.g. landslides.
keywords: areas of makeshift housing where the people who live there don’t own the land or have access to services like clean water, power, sanitation
the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
happens when too many players gather around the ball in a small area, reducing space and limiting passing options
presence of harmful substances in the environment, such as in the air, water or soil, which can damage ecosystems and human health
tips: Use real-world examples that students can relate to. Link challenges to students' own experiences (e.g., being stuck in traffic, seeing litter or smog, crowded buses). This builds relevance and makes abstract urban issues more concrete and memorable.

3791.name: Regenerating cities
3791.outcome: I can explain how and why cities are regenerated.
points: Cities change due to economic and social factors.
Urban regeneration is often needed when manufacturing industry declines due to dereliction.
Regeneration renews the built environment, creating homes, jobs and services.
Big changes can leave some groups behind.
Community involvement is important in regeneration.
keywords: a group of people who share something in common
when buildings or land degrades into a state of poor condition, having been abandoned
a planning strategy aimed at addressing problems associated with decline, often involving improvements to infrastructure and encouraging new industries to an area
tips: Encourage students to research or discuss any regeneration projects in their own local area—this makes the topic more relevant and helps them connect lessons to real life.

3792.name: Steel cities: Tangshan and Sheffield
3792.outcome: I can compare how the cities of Tangshan and Sheffield have changed over time.
points: The changing global economy can lead to radical changes in cities.
Sheffield was once a global centre of steel, but has now transitioned to a post-industrial economy.
Tangshan is a major steelmaking city in modern China.
Industrial activities shape the landscape, environment, and identity of cities.
keywords: the increased interconnectedness of the world, economically, politically and culturally
Industry is work linked to the processing of raw materials and the manufacture of products.
term used to describe a city after it has changed from being centre of manufacturing to a place where most people work in services
tips: Encourage students to make links between the cities and their local area—for example, ask if any local industries have changed over time, or if old factory buildings have been repurposed. This helps them see industrial change as something real and relevant.

3793.name: Cities and climate change
3793.outcome: I can describe how cities cause, and are affected by, climate change.
points: Urban areas are vulnerable to climate impacts such as increasing temperatures.
Many of the world's cities are vulnerable to sea level rise.
Cities contribute to climate change through emissions.
Planners can adopt strategies that help cities mitigate the impacts of climate change and help populations adapt.
keywords: An adaptation is a feature that organisms have to help them live in a particular place.
Emissions are materials released into the environment from a particular process.
actions to reduce or prevent the emission of greenhouse gases
tips: Encourage students to link climate impacts to their own experiences (like heatwaves or flooding in the UK) to make the topic more relatable and highlight that climate change affects cities here too.

3794.name: Sustainable cities
3794.outcome: I can explain how cities can be made more sustainable.
points: Sustainable cities prioritise environmental and social well-being.
Renewable energy reduces a city's carbon footprint.
Sustainable transport reduces emissions and congestion.
Green spaces improve urban health, climate resilience, and enrich society.
Urban waste management is more sustainable if more people reduce, reuse and recycle.
keywords: the total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases released into the atmosphere by an individual, product, process, country, etc
areas of grass, trees, or plants within urban environments, like parks or gardens
using resources wisely so future generations can also meet their needs
tips: Emphasise that small actions, like using public transport or recycling, are part of wider sustainable city strategies. This helps students feel their actions matter.

3795.name: The future of cities
3795.outcome: I can explore how cities may look and function in the future.
points: Smart cities use technology to improve urban life.
Urban planning will focus on climate mitigation and adaptation in future.
Future cities will rely on renewable energy and green tech.
Advances in transport will shape future city living.
The function of cities may change as more of their traditional functions go online.
keywords: a city that uses digital technology to improve services and quality of life
using resources wisely so future generations can also meet their needs
designing and managing how cities grow and change
tips: Encourage students to connect ideas about future cities with issues in their own local area—such as traffic, pollution, or green spaces—to help them see how global trends could affect their own lives.

3796.name: GIS: Visualising the physical and human geography of the DRC
3796.outcome: I can use a geographic information system (GIS) to visualise the human and physical geography of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
points: The DRC is a country in central Africa and is one of the largest countries in Africa.
The DRC is largely landlocked, it has a very small stretch of coastline to the west.
Different layers of data on a GIS help us visualise the human geography of the DRC.
Different layers of data on a GIS help us visualise the physical geography of the DRC.
keywords: a GIS (geographic information system) is a computer system that captures, analyses and displays geographic data to help understand spatial patterns
a separate, transparent sheet within a digital canvas used to organise elements of an artwork
to form a picture in your mind or imagine how something looks
tips: There is ample opportunity to expand or reduce the use of GIS in this lesson to suit the needs of your class.

3798.name: Population of the Democratic Republic of the Congo
3798.outcome: I can describe where people live in the DRC and describe what the population structure of the DRC is like.
points: The DRC has a population distribution of around 45 people per square kilometre due to its sheer size.
Just over half of the people live in rural areas, but Kinshasa is one of the fastest-growing cities in the world.
Population pyramids represent the population structure of a given location.
The median age in the DRC is 18.8 years, however half of the population are under 15 years old.
High birth rates and low life expectancy impact population growth.
keywords: The median is the central (middle) piece of data when the data are in numerical order. It is a measure of central tendency representing the average of the values.
the number of births for every 1000 people in a population per year
the average number of years a person is expected to live
the number of people living in a defined area, e.g. 300 people per square kilometre
an age-sex graph used to present the structure of a population (that may resemble a pyramid)
tips: Compare the population pyramid of the DRC with population pyramids for other countries at various stages of development. Ask students what they notice, what is similar and what is different about the population structures of each country. Can they suggest reasons for the differences?

3797.name: Colonial history and legacy of the Democratic Republic of the Congo
3797.outcome: I can describe the impact of colonial rule on the DRC and its lasting effects.
points: The DRC was a former Belgian colony and has had multiple names over time including the Belgian Congo and Zaire.
King Leopold II exploited the country's natural resources and people, causing millions of deaths.
After independence in 1960, the DRC faced political instability and conflict.
Colonial borders and exploitation still affect the DRC today.
keywords: a colony is a country or area under the control of another country and occupied by settlers from that country
the lasting impact or things a person leaves behind for others, even after they are gone
materials or substances occurring in nature, such as minerals, water, forests, and fossil fuels
to use something for personal benefit
tips: Read a passage from Conrad's 'Heart of darkness' to get pupils thinking about the impact of colonialism in the DRC.
