keywords: proposed geological epoch that marks when human activity has had a significant impact on Earth
the mood created in a section or whole of a text
life on Earth, encompassing all living organisms (plants, animals, bacteria, etc.) and the ecosystems they form
the solid parts of Earth, including the crust, mantle, and core, as well as rocks, soil, mountains, and other landforms
includes all the water on Earth, such as oceans, rivers, lakes, glaciers, groundwater, and water vapour in the atmosphere
tips: Ask students what impact they have had on Earth.

3891.name: Evidence of the Anthropocene
3891.outcome: I can describe and evaluate key evidence that shows how humans have altered Earth's systems.
points: Atmospheric CO₂ levels have risen steeply since the industrial revolution.
Ice core data shows a sharp increase in greenhouse gases linked to human activity.
Biodiversity loss is happening faster than natural extinction rates.
Plastics and radioactive elements form geological markers of human impact.
Land cover change is visible from satellites and historical maps.
keywords: the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere at a given time, measured in parts per million (ppm)
the variety of species found in a habitat
something found in layers of Earth (like rock, ice, or mud) that shows a big change in the planet's history
a cylinder of ice extracted from an ice sheet or glacier which is used to analyse past climate conditions
the physical material at the surface of Earth
tips: Get students to look out the window and ask what evidence they can see of human impact on the environment.

3892.name: The human impact on ecosystems
3892.outcome: I can explain how human activity changes ecosystems and reduces biodiversity.
points: Deforestation reduces habitats and threatens species survival.
Pollution from agriculture and industry harms ecosystems.
Climate change alters ecosystems and species distributions.
Invasive species introduced by humans disrupt native ecosystems.
Biodiversity loss reduces ecosystem resilience and services.
keywords: the variety of species found in a habitat
large-scale removal or clearing of forests
An ecosystem is made up of all the living organisms in a place, interacting with each other and their non-living surroundings.
plants, animals, or other organisms that are brought into a new environment, usually by humans, where they don't naturally belong
tips: Ask students to research an animal which has become extinct in the last 50 years and share findings as a class.

3893.name: The impact of consumption
3893.outcome: I can describe how resource use and consumption patterns affect the planet.
points: High levels of consumption increase demand for natural resources.
Global trade increases the environmental footprint of consumption.
Richer countries consume more per person than poorer countries.
Waste from overconsumption contributes to pollution and emissions.
Fast fashion and electronics create growing environmental problems.
keywords: the mass production and sale of cheaply made clothing that is not worn often and is quickly replaced
the exchange of goods, money and services between countries
materials or substances occurring in nature, such as minerals, water, forests, and fossil fuels
when people use more resources than Earth can replace
tips: Ask students to think about how could they reduce their consumption (for example buy less clothes or buy clothes from a second hand source).

3894.name: Plastic pollution
3894.outcome: I can explain the causes, scale, and impacts of plastic pollution on people and the environment.
points: Most plastic is made from fossil fuels and is not biodegradable.
Plastic production has grown rapidly since the 1950s.
Plastic waste pollutes land, rivers, and oceans.
Microplastics enter food chains and may harm human health.
Wildlife can be injured or killed by plastic waste.
keywords: tiny pieces of plastic, usually smaller than five millimetres, that either come from the breakdown of larger plastic items or are made that size
a large area of the ocean where plastic and other waste collects, trapped by circular ocean currents
tips: Ask students to think of how they could use less plastic (for example using refillable water bottles).

3895.name: Threats to oceans
3895.outcome: I can explain the main threats to oceans and how they affect marine environments.
points: Plastic pollution harms marine life and spreads through ocean currents.
Overfishing reduces fish populations and disrupts marine food chains.
Climate change warms oceans and causes coral bleaching.
Oil spills and chemical pollution damage marine ecosystems.
Rising sea levels and acidification threaten coastal and ocean habitats.
keywords: A food chain shows the order in which living things depend on each other for food.
when the ocean becomes more acidic because it absorbs too much CO₂ from the air
continuous movements of seawater in the ocean
catching too many fish, so the breeding population becomes too depleted to recover
tips: Ask students to do some extra research on the 1996 Milford Haven Oil spill, looking at the causes and effects.

3896.name: Fieldwork: Planning an air pollution enquiry and collecting data
3896.outcome: I can collect data about air pollution as part of a fieldwork enquiry.
points: Though most air pollution is not visible to the naked eye, particulate matter can be captured using simple methods.
Questionnaires are a good way of gauging public opinion about an issue.
Secondary data can support the primary data that is collected in the field.
keywords: tiny particles held in the air such as dust, ash and soot
data that is collected in person during fieldwork
data that has previously been collected by someone, usually unknown to the person doing the fieldwork
tips: Students might like to look into how researchers collect particulate matter data and how that method compares to the one they will be using.

guidance.label: Risk assessment required - outdoor learning
guidance.description: Fieldwork.

7432.name: Fieldwork: Presenting air pollution data
7432.outcome: I can present qualitative and quantitative air pollution data.
points: Qualitative data can be presented in interesting ways, such as word clouds and proportional speech bubbles.
Choropleth shading on a map can be used to show the level of air pollution.
Emoji icons can be used to show the strength of agreement or favourability.
keywords: using density of colour on a map to show the density of data spatially
descriptive, non-numerical information focusing on opinions
numerical information that can be measured or counted
using colour conventions in data presentation to represent certain ideas
tips: To better grasp the concept of choropleth shading, show students applied examples that they may see regularly such as rainfall maps in weather forecasts.

7433.name: Fieldwork: Analysing, concluding and evaluating air pollution data
7433.outcome: I can analyse and reflect on my air pollution data to create meaningful conclusions and an evaluation.
points: Statistical tests are used by geographers to find patterns in data sets that are not obvious in their raw form.
Conclusions can be strengthened by combining the results of different data sets together.
The scale at which geographers collect data can have a significant influence over the type of conclusions they make.
keywords: a statistical test that shows the strength of any correlation between two variables
enquiries that focus on a large area such as a city or a whole country
enquiries that focus on a small area such as a street or a park
tips: Model the Spearman's rank correlation coefficient calculations in real time with students so you can ensure that no student gets lost in the process.

3897.name: Phasing out fossil fuels
3897.outcome: I can explain why fossil fuels are being phased out and what challenges this creates.
points: Fossil fuels release large amounts of carbon dioxide when burned.
Fossil fuels are non-renewable and contribute to climate change.
Some countries rely heavily on fossil fuels for energy and income.
Moving away from fossil fuels requires investment and new technology.
There is disagreement about how quickly fossil fuels should be phased out.
keywords: reducing the amount of carbon dioxide (CO₂) released into the atmosphere from processes such as burning fossil fuels
natural substances that were formed over millions of years ago from the buried remains of ancient organisms. They include coal, oil and gas
energy sources, such as fossil fuels, that cannot be replaced and will eventually run out
energy from natural sources that are constantly replenished, like wind and solar
tips: Ask students if they have seen any of the measures which are helping us to reach net zero, electric cars, wind turbines, etc.

3898.name: Alternative energy supplies
3898.outcome: I can describe alternative sources of energy to using fossil fuels, and some of their benefits and limitations.
points: Alternative energy sources include renewable energy sources and nuclear power.
Renewable energy sources produce little or no greenhouse gas emissions.
The cost of renewable technology is falling, making it more accessible.
Nuclear energy is reliable and does not produce greenhouse gas emissions.
There are disadvantages in using nuclear energy.
keywords: Geothermal energy comes from heat contained within Earth's crust.
is the energy from inside atoms which can be used to generate electricity
energy from natural sources that are constantly replenished, like wind and solar
tips: Use Google Earth with the class to look at the scale of the Bhadla solar park in India.

3899.name: Global governance
3899.outcome: I can explain how global cooperation is needed to solve environmental problems.
points: Climate change is a global issue that requires international cooperation.
Agreements like the Paris Accord aim to reduce global emissions.
Some countries pollute more and have greater responsibility to act.
Not all countries agree on climate targets or financial commitments.
NGOs and citizens can influence climate action at different levels.
keywords: a non-profit, voluntary group of citizens who work on a local, national or international level to achieve an aim; they are not controlled by the Government, but will often work closely with it
an international treaty on climate change aiming to limit global warming
a person who was born in a particular country and has certain rights or has been given certain rights because of having lived there
steps taken by people, governments, and organisations to reduce climate change and its effects
actions to reduce or prevent the emission of greenhouse gases
tips: Show students the Greta Thunberg "how dare you" speech which is available on YouTube.

3900.name: Our future climate
3900.outcome: I can describe how the climate may change in the future and what the impacts could be.
points: Climate models predict rising temperatures and more extreme weather.
Sea levels are expected to rise due to melting ice and thermal expansion.
Some regions may face drought, while others experience more flooding.
Climate change may increase migration and conflict over resources.
Actions taken now will influence how severe future climate change becomes.
keywords: a computer program that uses maths and science to predict how Earth’s climate might change in the future
when a weather event is significantly different from the average or usual weather pattern
when people lack secure access to sufficient amounts of safe and nutritious food for normal growth and development and an active and healthy life
moving from one place to another with the intention of staying there
tips: Ask students what extreme weather they have experienced and build on the fact it is more likely due to climate change.

3902.name: Sustainability: A new way of living
3902.outcome: I can explain how sustainable living can reduce the environmental impact of our everyday lives.
points: Sustainability means meeting today's needs without harming future generations.
Reducing waste and reusing materials helps conserve resources.
Choosing local and seasonal food reduces environmental footprints.
Sustainable transport reduces carbon emissions and pollution.
Individuals, communities and governments all play a role in sustainability.
keywords: Food miles are the distance between the place where food is grown or made and the place where it is eaten.
the shared use of vehicles such as trains, buses, trams and planes on routes where people pay fares
food that is grown and harvested at a specific time of year when it is naturally ripe and ready for consumption
using resources wisely so future generations can also meet their needs
tips: have a look at the riverford website as a class: https://www.riverford.co.uk/

4029.name: Using atlases
4029.outcome: I can read a variety of different styles of atlas maps.
points: Atlases present the world at the smallest scale, showing the least detail but larger patterns and relationships.
Atlases use latitude and longitude lines to locate particular places.
There are many types of atlas map that are used to show specific information.
keywords: an imaginary line running east to west around the Earth's surface that is used to show how far north or south a place is
an imaginary line running north to south across the Earth's surface that is used to show how far east or west a place is
a map that shows a particular geographical phenomenon such as population density or air temperature
tips: For an immersive experiences, give pairs of students a set of questions, the answers of which can only be found in an atlas, such as the GDP of a particular country or the nearest port to a specific city. Students can then set ever harder questions for their peers.

4030.name: Using OS maps to locate places
4030.outcome: I can use directions, grid references and scale to find precise locations and distances on a map.
points: Direction on a map can be understood by using compass points or bearings.
Four and six figure grid references are a way of finding a specific place on a map.
The scale of the map can be used to calculate the distance between two features or places.
keywords: the four main compass points (north, south, east and west)
vertical lines running north to south on a map that divide it into east and west parts
horizontal lines running west to east on a map that divide it into north and south parts
tips: Wherever possible, use OS maps or samples of maps from your local area. This will contextualise things like distance and direction and empower students to look differently at their locality.

4031.name: Using OS maps to analyse physical features
4031.outcome: I can use contour lines to identify and describe physical features on a map.
points: The height of the land can be shown on a map using spot heights and contour lines.
The shape of the land can be shown on a map by examining how contour lines relate to each other.
Distinctive patterns of contour lines show particular physical features on a map.
keywords: lines drawn on maps that connect points of equal height above sea level
a sculptural technique where the designs are raised above a flat background
a point marked on a map showing a particular height
tips: A large potato cut in half length ways will give students a 'hill' on which they can mark contours at 1cm intervals. The more misshaped the potato, the more variation there will be in the gradient and the contour line patterns produced.

4032.name: Describing landscapes using maps
4032.outcome: I can describe a landscape from a map.
points: Landscapes can be described through their relief and drainage.
Landscapes can be described through their vegetation cover and land use.
Landscapes can be described through the shape and situation of their settlements.
keywords: a description for a feature (such as a settlement) that is wrapped around a central point
how straight or curvy (sinuous) a river is
tips: Maps can be used alongside photographs of landscapes. Students can evaluate which source gives the most accurate information and which allows the viewer to make the most informed description.

4033.name: Sketch maps and cross sections
4033.outcome: I can use sketch maps and cross sections to understand what a landscape is like.
points: A sketch map is often used to show information one might not normally find on a map.
A cross section shows what the landscape would look like if we were to slice through it vertically.
Drawing a cross section can help geographers understand what a landscape looks like.
keywords: notes added to sketches to explain ideas, describe textures, or record thoughts
the inside view of a 3D object when cut straight through
each piece of data is annotated with one or more labels which provide information about that data
tips: If students wish to practise creating cross sections from a map, this is best done using maps of rural areas where there is limited development. Contour lines on maps of urban areas tend to be difficult to read as they also contain a lot of other symbols.

1196.name: Using and interpreting photographs
1196.outcome: I can use and interpret a range of photographs.
points: Geographers use different types of photographs to show different aspects of geography.
Drawing a sketch from a photograph can be a good way of highlighting certain geographical features.
Photographs rarely tell geographers everything about a place and so they use critical analysis to interpret them.
keywords: notes added to sketches to explain ideas, describe textures, or record thoughts
thinking more widely about an image to gain a deeper understanding of it
an aerial photograph where the camera is at an angle to Earth’s surface
a photograph taken straight down from the air, showing a view of Earth’s surface
tips: If possible, source aerial or historic photographs of a place the students will know well, such as the school site. These contextual images are likely to help students to better understand the differences between different types of images.

4034.name: Constructing graphs in geography
4034.outcome: I can accurately construct graphs of frequency and proportional data.
points: There are many forms of graphical data presentation but not all are appropriate for all types of data.
Frequency data can be presented using bar charts, pictograms and histograms.
Proportional data can be presented using pie charts and percentage bars.
keywords: data that sits on a continuum from low to high values
data that can be arranged into exclusive categories
data such as counts or the actual amounts of something
data that is the relative amount of something when considered as part of a whole
tips: Using a class text book, students can identify different forms of graphical representation of data and comment on the nature of the data itself, such as if the data is discrete or continuous.

4036.name: Interpreting graphs in geography
4036.outcome: I can interpret data from a wide variety of graphs.
points: Graphs of data allow geographers to understand trends and correlations.
Bivariate graphical data allows geographers to predict other values within or beyond the data set.
More complex data presentation techniques can be used to show the relationships between two or more aspects of data.
keywords: a value within the data set that does not appear to follow the general pattern or trend
data for two variables where one of those variables is believed to influence the other
estimating unknown values beyond the data set based on the pattern or trend of the known values
estimating unknown values within a data set based on other values within the set
tips: As students encounter and interpret graphs, ensure they are exposed to graphs with a variety of different scales and units. This will build their confidence in dealing with unusual values.

4037.name: Using statistical data in geography
4037.outcome: I can use some simple statistics to better understand the values in a set of data.
points: Univariate data can be statistically analysed using measures of central tendancy.
Data can also be statistically analysed by thinking about proportions and how these change.
The spread of data points across a range of values can be statistically analysed using percentiles.
keywords: data such as counts or the actual amounts of something
the number of values within a data set that fall below a certain percentage of the total number of values
data that represents values against one variable
tips: For students who lack confidence in maths, a variety of statistical calculators are available online. These can be used to check workings and show the stages of calculations.

4038.name: Using and interpreting spatial data
4038.outcome: I can interpret spatial data shown in a variety of map styles.
points: Spatial data can be shown on a map using points, lines and polygons.
Geographical Information Systems (GIS) create maps that can show many forms of spatial data.
There are some styles of maps that show spatial data in specific ways.
keywords: Geographical Information System: software that create maps of spatial data, as well as digital tools to analyse it
using density of colour on a map to show the density of data spatially
a line on a map that joins points that have the same value
data that is assigned to a specific location
tips: As students create their first map of spatial data (such as a choropleth or isoline map), keep the nature of the data as simple as possible. Once the technique has been mastered, students may like to experiment with multiple layers of data.

7595.name: Using GIS to visualise data in a webmap
7595.outcome: I can visualise data in a webmap using basemaps, filters and buffers.
points: GIS can be used to add and visualise georeferenced data in a webmap.
GIS uses a variety of basemaps which need to be selected carefully to visualise data effectively.
GIS uses filters to select data in a layer to visualise spatial patterns more clearly and avoid cluttering a webmap.
GIS uses tools such as buffers to create visualisations which support analysis of data.
keywords: a background map in a GIS
in GIS, an area generated by analysis tools for a specified distance around a point, line or polygon feature
the selection of some data in a GIS layer to visualise spatial patterns more clearly
a GIS (geographic information system) is a computer system that captures, analyses and displays geographic data to help understand spatial patterns
a digital map which is available online. It will usually be interactive or can be created or saved by the user online (‘in the cloud’)
tips: No matter what your level of experience is with GIS, go through all the steps yourself first until you feel confident and fluent. Don't worry if you make a mistake, everybody does, even experienced practitioners!

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3903.name: An introduction to natural hazards
3903.outcome: I can describe different types of natural hazards and explain their impacts on people and property.
points: A natural hazard is a natural event that has the potential to cause damage, loss of life or economic disruption.
There are several types of natural hazard, including landslides, earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.
Natural hazards pose major risks to people and property.
keywords: the likelihood that people or property will be harmed by a natural hazard
a sudden event, caused by natural and not human activity, for example an earthquake or flood
a natural event that has the potential to cause damage, loss of life or economic disruption
tips: Using interactive maps, GIS data and animations (e.g. how tectonic plates move or how tropical storms develop) can help students get a clearer understanding of the processes involved.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3904.name: Factors affecting hazard risk
3904.outcome: I can explain that several factors affect hazard risk.
points: Hazard risk is the likelihood of being affected by a natural event.
Physical factors affect risk, such as climate change.
Human factors affect risk, including poverty, urbanisation and climate change.
keywords: the likelihood that people or property will be harmed by a natural hazard
a natural event that has the potential to cause damage, loss of life or economic disruption
tips: The UN's INFORM risk assessment tool is used in this lesson. The map explorer tool is a good way of exploring the concept of hazard risk and the factors that affect it.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3906.name: Plate tectonics theory
3906.outcome: I can explain the theory of plate tectonics and the mechanisms involved in plate movement.
points: Earth's outer layer (lithosphere) is divided into a number of plates.
Gravitational sliding, involving the processes of 'ridge-push' and 'slab-pull', contributes towards plate movement.
Earth's surface provides evidence for plate tectonics theory.
keywords: a semi-solid layer of Earth's upper mantle
the transfer of heat through the movement of fluids: warmer, less dense material rises and cooler, denser material sinks, creating a circular flow
a large, rigid slab of Earth's lithosphere (outer layer) that sits on the semi-solid asthenosphere beneath it
tips: The Plate Boundaries layer on ESRI's Geography Visualiser shows the relationship between surface features and plate margins/boundaries.

3907.name: Global distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes
3907.outcome: I can explain how most earthquakes and volcanoes are located at plate margins.
points: There is a pattern in the global distribution of earthquakes.
There is a pattern in the global distribution of volcanoes.
The global distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes coincides with plate margins.
keywords: the point on Earth's surface that is directly above where an earthquake happens underground
a hotspot is a place of significant activity, danger or violence
a measure of the energy released by an earthquake
the boundary where tectonic plates meet
tips: This lesson uses AQA terminology for plate margins; for Edexcel B plate boundaries are used instead of plate margins, destructive margins are convergent boundaries and constructive margins are divergent boundaries.

3908.name: Processes at constructive/divergent plate margins
3908.outcome: I can explain the processes at constructive/divergent plate margins and the causes of earthquakes and volcanoes.
points: Constructive/divergent plate margins involve two plates moving away from each other.
Distinctive processes occur at constructive/divergent plate margins.
Earthquakes and volcanic eruptions occur at constructive/divergent plate margins and have distinctive characteristics.
keywords: a measure of the energy released by an earthquake
a long, narrow depression formed when a tectonic plate stretches and fractures at a constructive margin, causing the land to sink between parallel fault lines
a broad, gently sloping volcano formed by basaltic lava that is runny and flows easily. Eruptions tend to be effusive rather than explosive - lava flows out
tips: GIS provides useful tools for visualising the processes going on at plate margins - see the GIS lesson in this unit for some examples.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3909.name: Processes at destructive/convergent plate margins
3909.outcome: I can explain the processes at destructive/convergent plate margins and the causes of earthquakes and volcanoes.
points: Destructive/convergent plate margins involve two plates moving towards each other.
Distinctive processes occur at destructive/convergent plate margins.
Earthquakes and volcanic eruptions occur at destructive/convergent plate margins and have distinctive characteristics.
keywords: a measure of the energy released by an earthquake
the process at a destructive plate margin where a denser oceanic plate sinks beneath a less dense plate into the mantle
a series of large ocean waves caused by underwater earthquakes, volcanic eruptions or landslides
tips: Show students video clips of explosive and effusive volcanic eruption types to underline the differences between them.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3910.name: Processes at conservative plate margins
3910.outcome: I can explain the processes at conservative plate margins and relate these to the causes of earthquakes.
points: Conservative plate margins involve two plates sliding alongside each other.
Distinctive processes occur at conservative plate margins.
Earthquakes occur at conservative plate margins but volcanoes do not.
keywords: Molten (i.e. melted) rock beneath the Earth's surface.
a measure of the energy released by an earthquake
tips: Once students have learned about all three types of plate margin, they could show their understanding by comparing the processes and hazards associated with each type.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3911.name: Primary and secondary effects and responses to tectonic hazards
3911.outcome: I can explain the difference between primary and secondary effects of a tectonic hazard, and between immediate and long-term responses to a tectonic hazard.
points: Earthquakes have primary and secondary effects (impacts).
There are short-term (immediate) and long-term responses to earthquakes.
Volcanic eruptions have primary and secondary effects (impacts).
There are short-term (immediate) and long-term responses to volcanic eruptions.
keywords: action taken during and immediately after a hazard event that focuses on surviving the hazard and providing short-term relief
action that focuses on rebuilding after the tectonic hazard and reducing risks from future hazards
impacts that occur instantly and as a direct result of the earthquake or volcanic eruption
impacts that follow as a consequence of the earthquake or volcanic eruption in the hours, days and weeks that follow
tips: The first two parts of this lesson are suitable for both AQA and Edexcel B specifications, while the third part is AQA-specific.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3913.name: An example of effects and responses to a tectonic hazard in an HIC
3913.outcome: I can use a named example to discuss the effects and responses to a tectonic hazard in an HIC.
points: In March 2011, a massive 9.0 magnitude earthquake shook the Japanese island of Honshu.
Sudden slippage occurred along a destructive plate margin between the Pacific plate and the Okhotsk plate.
Primary and secondary effects of the disaster caused the deaths of more than 18 000 people.
Japan's position as an HIC influenced its immediate and long-term responses and their effectiveness.
keywords: the point on Earth's surface that is directly above where an earthquake happens underground
a measure of the energy released by an earthquake
tips: There is a range of very useful layers relating to the Tohoku earthquake and tsunami in the ArcGIS online Map Viewer, which can be accessed with or without a log-in.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3914.name: An example of effects and responses to a tectonic hazard in an LIC
3914.outcome: I can use a named example to discuss the effects and responses to a tectonic hazard in an LIC.
points: In January 2010, a 7.0 magnitude earthquake struck Haiti in the Caribbean, one of the world's poorest countries.
The earthquake was caused by slippage at the conservative margin between the Caribbean plate and North American plate.
Primary and secondary effects of the disaster caused the deaths of more than 220 000 people.
Haiti's position as an LIC influenced its immediate and long-term responses and their effectiveness.
keywords: the point on Earth's surface that is directly above where an earthquake happens underground
a measure of the energy released by an earthquake
tips: Once students have notes on both their HIC and their LIC (or NEE) example, they can compare the effects and responses using an exam-style question, such as: To what extent do the responses to a tectonic hazard vary between areas of contrasting wealth? Use two named examples in your answer.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3915.name: Reducing risks from earthquakes and volcanoes
3915.outcome: I can explain why people continue to live in areas at risk from tectonic hazards and how management can reduce the effects of a tectonic hazard.
points: People continue to live in areas at risk from a tectonic hazard.
Monitoring and prediction can reduce the risks from a tectonic hazard.
Protection and planning can reduce the risks from a tectonic hazard.
keywords: the likelihood that people or property will be harmed by a natural hazard
techniques used to reduce hazard risk, including short-term relief and long-term planning, preparation and prediction
the continuous observation and recording of atmospheric conditions to detect changes
tips: Use real-world case studies to show how simple measures - like evacuation plans and building design- make a massive difference in disaster outcomes.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

6756.name: Using GIS to visualise physical processes at different types of plate margin
6756.outcome: I can use GIS Elevation Profiles to visualise physical processes at different plate margins.
points: 3D GIS provides powerful ways to visualise what is physical at plate margins.
GIS transects can be used to create Elevation Profiles to visualise topography and bathymetry.
GIS Elevation Profiles can visualise physical processes at different plate margins.
keywords: a GIS tool which visualises changes in height above or below sea level along a transect line
the measurement of elevation for bodies of water, e.g. depth of oceans, seas, or lakes
the shape and height of the land
tips: No matter what your level of experience is with GIS, go through all the steps yourself first until you feel confident and fluent. With this lesson, deliberate practice is intentional with repetition of a task in novel situations, providing students with an opportunity to achieve fluency.

3918.name: Global atmospheric circulation model, pressure belts and surface winds
3918.outcome: I can explain that the atmosphere operates as a global system, determining pressure, winds and rainfall patterns.
points: The atmosphere operates as a global system.
The atmospheric circulation and ocean currents transfer heat around the Earth.
The atmospheric circulation determines the location of global pressure belts.
Global pressure belts affect surface winds and patterns of rainfall.
keywords: deflection of winds and ocean currents caused by Earth's rotation
the pressure of a column of air at a point on the Earth'ssurface, creating relatively high or low pressure
an imaginary line running east to west around the Earth's surface that is used to show how far north or south a place is
the movement of air from place to place, generally from an area of high pressure to an area of low pressure
tips: Show satellite or climate maps of rainfall and temperature to connect circulation cells with real-world climates.

3919.name: Tropical storms – distribution, formation and development
3919.outcome: I can explain how tropical storms develop as a result of particular atmospheric conditions and where they are found.
points: Tropical storms have distinctive structural characteristics and are widely distributed within the tropics.
Tropical storms are related to the atmospheric circulation and are formed by particular meteorological conditions.
Tropical storms form in source areas, intensify as they track over oceans and then dissipate.
Climate change may affect the distribution, frequency and intensity of tropical storms.
keywords: deflection of winds and ocean currents caused by Earth's rotation
a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
the energy stored in water vapour when it evaporates, that is released when the vapour condenses back into liquid water
the change in wind speed and direction at different altitudes
tips: The GIS lesson for this unit, Using GIS to map the track of a tropical storm, supports pupils in tracking tropical storms and identifying the factors influencing their distribution.

3920.name: Tropical storms – hazards and effects
3920.outcome: I can identify that tropical storms have significant effects on people and the environment.
points: Tropical storms have significant effects on people and the environment.
Tropical storms have primary effects on people and the environment, such as strong winds, heavy rain and storm surges.
Tropical storms have secondary effects on people and the environment, such as coastal flooding and landslides.
Some countries are more vulnerable to the impacts (physically, socially and economically) of tropical storms.
keywords: a natural or human-made event that poses a threat to people, property or the environment
the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
the rising of the sea as a result of atmospheric pressure changes and wind associated with a storm
being more susceptible or exposed to the harmful impacts of a natural disaster
tips: Make use of up to date news articles and videos to exemplify the effects in a range of places.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3921.name: Tropical storms – responses
3921.outcome: I can explain the immediate (short-term) and long-term responses to tropical storms.
points: People respond to the effects of tropical storms.
There are short-term responses to tropical storms.
There are long-term responses to tropical storms.
keywords: a non-profit, voluntary group of citizens who work on a local, national or international level to achieve an aim; they are not controlled by the Government, but will often work closely with it
immediate assistance and supplies provided to people affected by a disaster
the process of moving people from a dangerous place to safety
action taken to address the impacts of a disaster
tips: Use a time line to separate immediate (days and weeks) and long-term (months and years) responses.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3922.name: Reducing risks from effects of tropical storms
3922.outcome: I can explain how monitoring, prediction, protection and planning can reduce the effects of tropical storms.
points: Monitoring, for example using satellite technology, can reduce the effects of tropical storms.
Prediction, for example using weather forecasting, can reduce the effects of tropical storms.
Protection and planning, for example evacuation strategies, can reduce the effects of tropical storms.
keywords: use of technology to predict the likelihood of a tropical storm, including its path, intensity and speed
person who studies the causes of weather conditions using information from land, sea and the atmosphere, and creates forecasts
taking actions to reduce the effects of a tropical storm
the continuous observation and recording of atmospheric conditions to detect changes
tips: Use storm tracking information and imagery for pupils to decide how a country should prepare for the oncoming hurricane. They should take into account the type of country - high or low income - when planning.

3924.name: Example of a tropical storm
3924.outcome: I can explain the location of Typhoon Rai and understand the effects and responses to it.
points: Location and track of Typhoon Rai.
Typhoon Rai had primary and secondary effects.
There were immediate and long-term responses to Typhoon Rai.
keywords: the immediate effects of a natural disaster
action taken to address the impacts of a disaster
indirect impacts that arise after an event, they often happen because of the primary effects
a tropical cyclone occurring in the western Pacific or Indian oceans
tips: To gain a better understanding, the use of newspaper articles and video clips will help. It may also be helpful to look at the impact of a tropical storm of similar strength that made landfall in a high income country, to compare the effects and responses.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3926.name: Weather hazards in the UK
3926.outcome: I can explain that the UK is affected by weather hazards and that there is evidence that weather is becoming more extreme.
points: The weather in the UK can be hazardous.
The UK is affected by a number of weather hazards, such as strong winds, torrential rain and snowfall.
There is evidence that weather in the UK is becoming more extreme.
keywords: the average weather conditions in a region over a long period of time
when a weather event is significantly different from the average or usual weather pattern
the day-to-day conditions of the atmosphere at a particular place, e.g. temperature, rainfall
tips: Students could find out more about recent named storms and the factors that are considered when naming storms from the Met Office website. The class could potentially submit a suggestion for a storm name that meets the requirements.

3927.name: An example of a recent extreme weather event in the UK
3927.outcome: I can understand the location, causes, impacts and management strategies associated with the ‘Beast from the East’ extreme weather event in the UK.
points: Location of a named extreme weather event in the UK.
Causes of the named extreme weather event in the UK.
The named extreme weather event in the UK had social, economic and environmental impacts.
Management strategies associated with the named extreme weather event in the UK can reduce risk.
keywords: the effect of an event on the financial conditions of an area, e.g. employment, income, investment
when a weather event is significantly different from the average or usual weather pattern
Something that increases the chance of something harmful happening.
the effect on people and communities due to an event or situation
tips: There are news reports about the Beast from the East on YouTube which would be a good way to introduce the lesson, as well as detailed reports from news organisations looking back at the factors that caused this extreme weather event.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

6757.name: Using GIS to map the track of a tropical storm
6757.outcome: I can use and configure GIS to visualise the tracks of tropical storms.
points: Ready-made tropical storm layers can be configured to visualise spatial patterns more effectively, e.g. using filters.
Tropical storms can be analysed using pop-up data.
Georeferenced data about a particular tropical storm can be mapped using GIS and configured to show selected attributes.
A storm track can be visualised using temporal data, in a time-enabled GIS map.
keywords: properties or characteristics of an entity
information which has been tied to a particular location (geolocated), using an agreed system such as latitude and longitude
in GIS, a read-only display of attribute information (e.g. text, images, charts) often linked to a location
information which is tied to a particular point in time, so that data can be time-enabled (also known as spatiotemporal data)
tips: Practise the procedural steps yourself first until you achieve fluency and feel confident. Don't worry if you make mistakes - everyone does even after years of experience!

3928.name: Evidence for climate change in the Quaternary period
3928.outcome: I can identify evidence for climate change in the Quaternary period.
points: Climate has changed in the past through natural causes.
Evidence for natural climate change include ice cores, tree rings and historical sources.
Evidence can be used to reconstruct climate change from the Quaternary to the present day.
keywords: the period of geological time from 2.6 million years ago to the present
a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
a cylinder of ice extracted from an ice sheet or glacier which is used to analyse past climate conditions
tips: The GIS lesson for this topic, Using GIS to visualise climate change impacts, provides pupils with step-by-step instructions (with a video demo) for measuring and presenting evidence for climate change for themselves using GIS tools.

3929.name: Natural and human causes of climate change
3929.outcome: I can explain the natural and human causes of climate change.
points: There are natural and human causes of climate change.
Natural causes of climate change include orbital changes, asteroid collisions, volcanic activity and solar output.
Human causes of climate change include the use of fossil fuels, agriculture and deforestation.
Human causes of climate change produce greenhouse gases, enhancing the greenhouse effect and leading to global warming.
keywords: natural changes in Earth's orbit and tilt over thousands of years that influence solar energy and Earth’s climate
the increased concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere due to human activities, leading to global warming
a gas that contributes to global warming by reducing the amount of radiation leaving Earth’s atmosphere
tips: It is important to ensure a good understanding of both the natural greenhouse effect and the enhanced greenhouse effect, the use of videos and diagrams to support this is key.

3930.name: Effects of climate change on people and the environment
3930.outcome: I can explain how climate change affects people and the environment.
points: Climate change due to human activity is causing sea level rise, declining Arctic ice and more extreme weather events.
Climate change is affecting people and the environment.
With a range of projections, for example for global temperatures, there is uncertainty about future climates.
keywords: the variety of species found in a habitat
when a weather event is significantly different from the average or usual weather pattern
when people lack secure access to sufficient amounts of safe and nutritious food for normal growth and development and an active and healthy life
the effect on people and communities due to an event or situation
tips: Try to use up to date examples, news stories and where possible local/national effects to bring this concept to life, as well as more established examples and facts.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3931.name: Managing climate change – mitigation
3931.outcome: I can explain how climate change can be managed through mitigation strategies.
points: Managing climate change can involve mitigation strategies.
Mitigation strategies include alternative energy production, carbon capture and planting trees.
Mitigation can involve international agreements.
keywords: an international treaty on climate change aiming to limit global warming
actions to reduce or prevent the emission of greenhouse gases
energy from natural sources that are constantly replenished, like wind and solar
tips: Using the internet to calculate individual carbon footprint can be interesting for pupils and leads to discussion of ideas as to how they can reduce it, reinforcing the importance of individual actions.

3932.name: Managing climate change – adaptation
3932.outcome: I can understand how climate change can be managed through adaptation strategies.
points: Managing climate change can involve adaptation strategies.
Adaptation strategies include change in agricultural systems and managing water supply.
Adaptation involves reducing risk from rising sea levels.
keywords: structures built to protect land from the sea, e.g. sea walls
the process of removing salt from seawater to make it suitable for drinking and irrigation
a method of supplying water to crops to help them grow
tips: Encourage pupils to think of this at a local and individual level as well as looking at the larger scale, more complex, adapation strategies.

6755.name: Using GIS to visualise climate change impacts
6755.outcome: I can use 2D and 3D GIS to visualise climate change impacts.
points: Climate change impacts can be visualised and analysed using geospatial data.
The impacts can be visualised with georeferenced data using the GIS tool called media layers.
Configuration of media layers happens in a 2D webmap, which can be saved for even more powerful use in 3D maps.
GIS tools can support analysis of media layers including measurement tools and the Elevation Profile tool.
keywords: a GIS tool which visualises changes in height above or below sea level along a transect line
georeferenced information including quantitative data (e.g. numbers) or qualitative data (e.g. photos), which has been tied to a particular location (geolocated)
overlays of scanned maps, aerial or satellite images which can be georeferenced to visually line up with other layers
tips: Practise the procedural steps first until fluent. Optional to improve georeferencing: In ‘Layers’ for ‘Triftglacier’ layer, click three dots > ‘Show properties’: ‘Edit placed media’ > click ‘Side-by-side’ to improve accuracy using the four corresponding place holders on each side.

2926.name: Understanding small-scale ecosystems
2926.outcome: I can describe the natural processes that occur within a small-scale ecosystem in the UK.
points: An ecosystem is a natural system in which plants, animals and their non-living environment interact.
Living and non-living things interract within a small-scale ecosystem.
Food webs help us understand the interrelationships in a small-scale ecosystem.
Nutrient cycles show how nutrients transfer across different stores within an ecosystem.
keywords: A consumer is an organism that eats other organisms for food.
A decomposer is an organism that feeds on the remains of other living organisms (organic matter).
An ecosystem is made up of all the living organisms in a place, interacting with each other and their non-living surroundings.
A food chain shows the order in which living things depend on each other for food.
A producer is an organism that makes its own food.
tips: Coordinate with science colleagues about what students should already know about this topic from KS3 and KS4.

6459.name: Changes in small-scale ecosystems
6459.outcome: I can explain how natural changes and human activities affect the balance of small-scale ecosystems.
points: Ecosystems are finely balanced and can be affected by changing one component.
College Lake is the site of a range of small-scale ecosystems: lake, marshland and chalk grassland.
Natural events as well as human actions can create changes that affect the complexity and productivity of ecosystems.
keywords: the non-living elements of an ecosystem (e.g. water, nutrients)
the variety of species found in a habitat
the living elements of an ecosystem (e.g. plants, animals)
a complex interconnection of food chains within an ecosystem
A habitat is the place where an organism lives. It must provide food, shelter and a place to reproduce.
tips: Avoid using the term 'man-made' and instead utilise the phrase 'created by/as a result of human activities'.

2931.name: The distribution and characteristics of global biomes
2931.outcome: I can describe the distribution and characteristics of global biomes.
points: Ecosystems at the global scale are called biomes.
The pattern of biomes is broadly latitudinal, with tropical rainforests near the Equator and tundra near the poles.
Each biome has distinct characteristics as a result of its specific climate.
keywords: a large-scale ecosystem with specific climate, plants and animals
the average weather conditions in a region over a long period of time
how something is spread out over a geographical area
an imaginary line running east to west around the Earth's surface that is used to show how far north or south a place is
tips: Learners can practise their atlas map skills by locating the places named using the coordinates supplied in the slide deck.

2929.name: The factors affecting biome distribution
2929.outcome: I can explain how climate and local factors affect biome distribution.
points: On a large-scale, climate is the main factor affecting the distribution of biomes.
Local factors (altitude, rock and soil type and drainage) can affect local biome distribution.
Biotic and abiotic components interact within biomes, reflecting these large-scale and small-scale factors.
keywords: height above sea level or ground level
the average weather conditions in a region over a long period of time
the distribution, storage and movement of water in the environment
tips: The first learning cycle of this lesson provides opportunities for checking and reinforcing pupils' understanding of weather and climate.

6736.name: Using GIS to visualise the distribution and characteristics of global biomes
6736.outcome: I can use GIS webmaps and filters to visualise the distribution and characteristics of global biomes.
points: Global biomes can be easily mapped using shared GIS layers in webmaps.
Basemaps can be selected to improve the visualisation and links to prior geographical knowledge.
GIS layers can help to visualise the spatial distribution of global biomes more clearly.
Filters and transparency sliders can be used to toggle biome layers and explain their spatial distribution.
keywords: the selection of some data in a GIS layer to visualise spatial patterns more clearly
a GIS (geographic information system) is a computer system that captures, analyses and displays geographic data to help understand spatial patterns
the spread of information (data) across an area, creating spatial patterns which geographers attempt to describe, explain and analyse
a digital map which is available online. It will usually be interactive or can be created or saved by the user online (‘in the cloud’)
tips: You can familiarise yourself with the activities by watching the 'GIS guides' included in this lesson.

2932.name: Characteristics of tropical rainforests
2932.outcome: I can describe key abiotic and biotic characteristics of the tropical rainforest.
points: Tropical rainforests are distinctive global biomes (large-scale ecosystems).
Tropical rainforests have distinctive abiotic characteristics that result from the equatorial climate.
Tropical rainforests have distinctive biotic characteristics, including the structure of vegetation into layers.
keywords: the non-living elements of an ecosystem (e.g. water, nutrients)
a large-scale ecosystem with specific climate, plants and animals
the living elements of an ecosystem (e.g. plants, animals)
the average weather conditions in a region over a long period of time
tips: This is a good lesson for recapping and assessing pupils' skills with interpreting climate graphs.

2933.name: Plant and animal adaptations in tropical rainforests
2933.outcome: I can explain how plants and animals in tropical rainforests are well adapted to the physical conditions.
points: Tropical rainforests are home to a wide variety of plants and animals.
Plants are adapted to the physical conditions in tropical rainforests, for example, drip tips and buttress roots.
Animals are well adapted to the physical conditions in tropical rainforests.
keywords: a feature or behaviour that helps an animal or plant survive in its environment
the variety of species found in a habitat
A habitat is the place where an organism lives. It must provide food, shelter and a place to reproduce.
tips: Virtual reality tours of the tropical rainforest will allow students to better understand the adaptations of plants and animals living in each layer of the tropical rainforest. BBC Earth's 'The "busy" life of the sloth' is an engaging way into this topic, for example.

2934.name: Nutrient cycling and biodiversity in tropical rainforests
2934.outcome: I can explain that tropical rainforests have a high rate of nutrient cycling and support high levels of biodiversity and complex food webs.
points: Tropical rainforests support high levels of biodiversity.
Tropical rainforests have high rates of nutrient cycling.
Tropical rainforests support complex food webs.
keywords: the variety of species found in a habitat
when two or more biotic features, like plants or animals, depend or rely on each other to survive
chemical substances found in all biotic features which are important for survival
tips: Check with colleagues in science to see what pupils should already know about nutrient cycles and the movement of nutrients through ecosystems.

2935.name: Deforestation in the tropical rainforest
2935.outcome: I can explain the causes and changing rates of deforestation.
points: Tropical rainforests are threatened by deforestation.
Rates of deforestation are changing.
There are several causes of deforestation, such as commercial logging, agriculture and mineral resources.
keywords: the variety of species found in a habitat
large-scale removal or clearing of forests
farmers that grow only enough food for themselves
tips: The GIS lesson in this unit, 'Using GIS to visualise and analyse deforestation', gives pupils the opportunity to use GIS tools to engage with causes and impacts of deforestation.

2936.name: Deforestation in Indonesia’s tropical rainforest
2936.outcome: I can describe the location, causes and impacts of deforestation in Indonesia.
points: The majority of Indonesia’s rainforests are located in Borneo, Papua and Sumatra.
Causes of deforestation in Indonesia include subsistence and commercial farming, logging, energy and population growth.
Impacts of deforestation in Indonesia include erosion, pollution, habitat loss, carbon emissions, economic development.
keywords: the variety of species found in a habitat
large-scale removal or clearing of forests
farmers that grow only enough food for themselves
tips: The GIS lesson in this unit, 'Using GIS to visualise and analyse deforestation', gives pupils the opportunity to use GIS tools to engage with causes and impacts of deforestation.

2937.name: Value of tropical rainforests to people and the environment
2937.outcome: I can explain the value of rainforests to people and the environment.
points: Tropical rainforests are special ecosystems.
Tropical rainforests are of value to people at all scales.
Tropical rainforests are of value to the environment at all scales.
keywords: a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
physical resources or products that can be directly harvested or used by people and animals
natural processes or benefits that rainforests provide to support life on Earth, often indirectly
tips: The lesson in this unit called "Using GIS to visualise and analyse deforestation" gives students opportunities to explore and measure deforestation using accessible GIS tools.

2938.name: Sustainable rainforest management
2938.outcome: I can explain how local and global actions can help manage rainforests in a sustainable way.
points: Sustainable management means using resources in a way that allows future generations to use them in the same way too.
Local actions, such as alternative livelihoods, enable tropical rainforests to be sustainably managed.
Global actions can contribute to sustainable management of tropical rainforests.
keywords: the variety of species found in a habitat
protection and management of natural resources to prevent damage and maintain biodiversity
development that meets the needs of people today without damaging the environment or reducing resources for future generations
tips: There are videos from tourists recording highlights of their ecotourism visits to Costa Rica on YouTube (including the zip line).

6754.name: Using GIS to visualise and analyse deforestation
6754.outcome: I can use GIS to visualise deforestation and analyse the causes of deforestation.
points: GIS uses remote sensing to investigate spatio-temporal changes in rainforests.
Remote sensing includes satellite imagery and aerial imagery.
Historical satellite imagery and aerial imagery can be studied using swipe tools such as the Esri Wayback App or 3D GIS.
Remote sensing can be used to monitor and manage deforestation.
Remote sensing can be used to analyse a range of economic activities which can contribute to causes of deforestation.
keywords: a type of remote sensing which uses observations by aircraft of selected parts of the electromagnetic spectrum to monitor terrestrial, oceanic or atmospheric features and processes
the collection of data at a distance reflected or emitted by objects, living things or areas on different wavelengths of the electromagnetic spectrum, observed by satellite or aircraft
a type of remote sensing which uses observations by satellites of selected parts of the electromagnetic spectrum to monitor terrestrial, oceanic or atmospheric features and processes
tips: You can familiarise yourself with the activities by watching the 'GIS guides' included in this lesson.

3671.name: Location and physical characteristics of hot deserts
3671.outcome: I can describe the location and physical characteristics of hot deserts.
points: Hot desert ecosystems are located at roughly 30°N and 30°S of the Equator.
Hot desert ecosystems have distinctive physical characteristics.
The climate influences other physical characteristics of hot deserts.
keywords: a large-scale ecosystem with specific climate, plants and animals
the average weather conditions in a region over a long period of time
arid areas experiencing low rainfall, generally below 250 mm/year, and high summer temperatures
tips: The physical characteristics of deserts can vary significantly: show students a range of desert landscapes and use GIS to explore desert surfaces - from sand dunes to desert pavements.

7288.name: The interdependence of biotic and abiotic components in hot deserts
7288.outcome: I can explain how biotic and abiotic components in a hot desert such as soil, climate, animals, plants and people are interdependent.
points: Hot desert ecosystems exhibit interdependence of climate, water, soils, plants, animals and people.
Food chains and food webs show how biotic and abiotic components are interdependent in a hot desert.
Nutrient cycles show how biotic and abiotic components are interdependent in hot desert.
keywords: the non-living elements of an ecosystem (e.g. water, nutrients)
the living elements of an ecosystem (e.g. plants, animals)
the transfer of water to the atmosphere through evaporation from surfaces and transpiration from plants
the connections between different components of the environment, where each component depends on or influences the others
tips: If pupils have a strong understanding of nutrient cycles from studying ecosystems earlier in the course, then it is appropriate to challenge them to explain how the nutrient cycle of hot deserts changes in response to environmental change, such as a reduction in rainfall or removal of vegetation.

3672.name: Plant and animal adaptations, issues relating to biodiversity
3672.outcome: I can explain that plants and animals are well adapted to the physical conditions in hot deserts and that there are issues related to biodiversity.
points: Hot deserts are home to a variety of plants and animals.
Plants in hot deserts are well adapted to the physical conditions.
Animals in hot deserts are well adapted to the physical conditions.
There are issues related to biodiversity in hot deserts.
keywords: An adaptation is a feature that organisms have to help them live in a particular place.
the variety of species found in a habitat
An ecosystem is made up of all the living organisms in a place, interacting with each other and their non-living surroundings.
Nocturnal means being active or happening at night rather than during the day.
tips: Short clips from wildlife programmes about animal and plant adaptations in the hot desert help reinforce learning. Episode 4 of Planet Earth 2 has several good examples.

3673.name: Development opportunities and challenges in the Kalahari Desert
3673.outcome: I can explain the opportunities and challenges of developing hot desert environments in the Kalahari Desert.
points: The Kalahari Desert is an example of a hot desert.
There are opportunities for development in the Kalahari Desert (mineral extraction, energy, farming, tourism).
There are challenges for developing hot desert environments in the Kalahari (extreme temperatures, water supply).
keywords: a climate with little to no rainfall
indigenous people are the original inhabitants of a specific area
the process of removing valuable minerals from the earth
the business of attracting and taking care of visitors to a place
tips: Set students the task of developing a fact file on this case study for homework, which they can then use for revision closer to the exam.

3674.name: Desertification – causes and strategies
3674.outcome: I can explain the causes of desertification and the strategies used to reduce the risk of desertification.
points: Desertification is a serious threat in hot desert environments.
There are several causes of desertification including climate change, population growth and removal of fuelwood.
There are several strategies used to reduce the risk of desertification including soil management and tree planting.
keywords: large-scale removal or clearing of forests
the process by which land becomes desert due to climate change, deforestation, or inappropriate agriculture
a long period of time with little or no rainfall, leading to a shortage of water
actions to reduce or prevent the emission of greenhouse gases
tips: GIS could be used in this lesson to help students make the link with climate change and changes in seasonality such as the migration of the ITCZ. Utilise Google Earth and search for the desertification of the Sahel 1990-2020 to show these changes.

6122.name: Location and physical characteristics of cold environments
6122.outcome: I can describe the location and physical characteristics of cold environments.
points: Cold environments (polar and tundra) and located at high latitudes close to the poles.
Cold environments have distinctive physical characteristics.
The climate influences other physical characteristics of cold environments.
keywords: a large-scale ecosystem with specific climate, plants and animals
the average weather conditions in a region over a long period of time
environments found at higher latitudes and higher altitudes; they include polar, tundra and alpine biomes
an imaginary line running east to west around the Earth's surface that is used to show how far north or south a place is
a vast, flat, treeless Arctic region where vegetation growth is hindered by extreme low temperatures and short growing seasons
tips: The British Antarctic Survey have produced useful layers in ArcGIS which are free to access, including "Bedmap3 - bed topography of Antarctica", which shows the land area and topography of Antarctica: what is underneath the ice sheets.

7438.name: The interdependence of biotic and abiotic components in cold environments
7438.outcome: I can explain how biotic and abiotic components in a cold environment such as soil, climate, animals, plants and people are interdependent.
points: Cold environment ecosystems exhibit interdependence of climate, water, soils, plants, animals and people.
Food chains and food webs show how biotic and abiotic components are interdependent in a cold environment.
Nutrient cycles show how biotic and abiotic components are interdependent in a cold environment.
keywords: the non-living elements of an ecosystem (e.g. water, nutrients)
the living elements of an ecosystem (e.g. plants, animals)
the transfer of water to the atmosphere through evaporation from surfaces and transpiration from plants
the connections between different components of the environment, where each component depends on or influences the others
tips: If pupils have a good understanding of nutrient cycles from studying ecosystems earlier in the course, then it is appropriate to challenge them to explain how the nutrient cycle of cold environments change in response to environmental change, such as a reduction in rainfall or removal of vegetation.

6123.name: Plant and animal adaptations in cold environments
6123.outcome: I can explain how plants and animals are well adapted to the physical conditions in cold environments and that there are issues related to biodiversity.
points: Cold environments are home to a variety of plants and animals.
Animals in cold environments are well adapted to the physical conditions.
Plants in cold environments are well adapted to the physical conditions.
There are issues related to biodiversity in cold environments.
keywords: An adaptation is a feature that organisms have to help them live in a particular place.
the variety of species found in a habitat
An ecosystem is made up of all the living organisms in a place, interacting with each other and their non-living surroundings.
a state that certain animals enter to save energy during periods of unfavourable weather conditions or food shortages
tips: Watching short clips from wildlife programmes about animal and plant adaptations in the cold environment as a class helps to reinforce understanding of the link between challenges and adaptations.

6124.name: Development opportunities and challenges in Northern Canada
6124.outcome: I can explain opportunities and challenges of developing cold environments in Northern Canada.
points: Northern Canada is an example of a cold environment.
There are opportunities for development in Northern Canada (mineral extraction, energy, fishing, tourism).
There are challenges for developing in Northern Canada (extreme temperatures, inaccessibility, provision of buildings).
keywords: indigenous people are the original inhabitants of a specific area
the process of removing valuable minerals from the earth
ground that stays frozen for two or more years in a row
the business of attracting and taking care of visitors to a place
tips: Set students the task of developing a fact file on this case study for homework, which they can then use for revision closer to the exam.

6125.name: Value of cold environments
6125.outcome: I can explain how cold environments are at risk from economic development and how they can be protected.
points: Cold environments are at risk from economic development.
Cold environments are valuable as wilderness areas and these fragile environments should be protected.
Strategies are used to balance economic development and conservation in cold environments.
keywords: the variety of species found in a habitat
protection and management of natural resources to prevent damage and maintain biodiversity
development that meets the needs of people today without damaging the environment or reducing resources for future generations
tips: Use GIS tools to analyse areas that have been mined and their impact on the environment. Students could map tundra or polar areas, identify regions most affected by mining or fossil fuel extraction and correlate them with changes in local biodiversity.

3933.name: UK landscapes - the role of geology and past processes
3933.outcome: I can explain how geology, tectonics and glaciation have influenced the UK's upland and lowland landscapes.
points: The UK has upland and lowland landscapes and river systems.
Geology affects the shape and type of UK landscapes.
Tectonic activity has helped form upland and lowland areas.
Glacial erosion and deposition shaped upland and lowland landscapes.
Geology is the study of the Earth.
keywords: the study of the Earth and its physical structure
rocks formed when molten magma cools and solidifies
all the visible features of an area of land, often considered in terms of their visual appeal
rocks changed by intense heat and/or pressure
rocks made from compacted sediment layers over time
tips: There are opportunities to relate landscapes mentioned in this lesson to OS map extracts and to map skills.

3937.name: Wave processes at the coast
3937.outcome: I can explain how wave processes shape the coast.
points: Different wave types (constructive and destructive) affect the coast.
The coast is shaped by processes of erosion (hydraulic power, abrasion and attrition).
The coast is shaped by transportation (longshore drift) of sediment.
The coast is shaped by deposition.
keywords: low waves, typically formed by distant storms, that deposit sediment onto beaches
high, steep waves, typically formed by local storms, that remove sediment from beaches
the wearing away of rocks along the coastline
ripples in the sea caused by wind blowing over the surface of the water
tips: The lesson in this unit called 'Using GIS to visualise the impact of physical and human processes on coasts' could be used to extend this lesson.

3938.name: Weathering and mass movement at the coast
3938.outcome: I can explain how weathering and mass movement shape the coast.
points: The coast is shaped by weathering processes (mechanical and chemical).
The coast is shaped by processes of mass movement (sliding, slumping and rock falls).
keywords: chemical breakdown of rocks usually involving slightly acidic rainwater
the downhill movement of material under the influence of gravity
physical disintegration of rocks, for example through freeze-thaw
the breakdown or disintegration of rocks at or close to the surface
tips: GIS could be used in this lesson to explore the impact of landslides and identify areas most at risk. The National Trust has an ArcGIS resource on climate hazards which could be used for this called Slope Failure (Landslides) Current.

3939.name: The role of geology at the coast
3939.outcome: I can explain how geology can affect the development of coastal landforms.
points: Rock type (hard/soft) affects the development of coastal landforms.
Geological structure can result in concordant and discordant coastlines.
keywords: where rock layers (hard and soft) run parallel to the coastline
where rock layers (hard and soft) run perpendicular to the coastline
the physical and chemical characteristics of rocks
tips: The lesson in this unit called 'Using GIS to visualise the impact of physical and human processes on coasts' could be used to extend this lesson.

6131.name: Coastal erosion landforms
6131.outcome: I can describe the characteristics and explain the formation of landforms resulting from coastal erosion.
points: Caves, arches and stacks have distinct characteristics and formation.
Cliffs and wave cut platforms have distinct characteristics and formation.
keywords: the wearing away of rocks along the coastline
waves compress air into cracks in the rock, putting pressure on it and causing it to break over time
the process where cliffs move backward over time as erosion wears away the base of a cliff
tips: GIS can be utilised to study an area's geology, helping to determine whether a coastline has the potential to develop these erosional landforms.

3940.name: Landforms of coastal deposition
3940.outcome: I can describe the characteristics and formation of landforms of coastal deposition.
points: Beaches have distinctive characteristics and formation.
Spits and bars have distinctive characteristics and formation.
Sand dunes have distinctive characteristics and formation.
keywords: low waves, typically formed by distant storms, that deposit sediment onto beaches
when material being carried is dropped due to loss of a river’s energy
movement of sediment along the coast by wave action in a zigzag pattern
tips: The lesson in this unit called 'Using GIS to visualise the impact of physical and human processes on coasts' could be used to extend this lesson.

3941.name: Examples of coastal landforms
3941.outcome: I can describe and explain landforms of coastal erosion and deposition on the Jurassic Coast.
points: The location of the Jurassic Coast in the UK and background information.
The section of coastline has distinctive landforms of coastal erosion.
The section of coastline has distinctive landforms of coastal deposition.
keywords: landforms resulting from a dominance of coastal deposition
landforms resulting from a dominance of coastal erosion
tips: GIS can be utilised to measure the extent of change at particular coastal landforms over time.

6132.name: Costs and benefits of coastal management strategies
6132.outcome: I can explain different types of coastal management strategies and evaluate their costs and benefits.
points: Coastal management aims to protect communities and environments.
There are three main types of coastal management strategy.
Different stakeholders may have different views on coastal management.
keywords: using artificial structures to protect coastlines from erosion and flooding
when areas of the coast are deliberately allowed to flood or erode naturally
making use of natural processes to reduce erosion and flooding in a way that minimies environmental impact
anyone who has an interest in or is affected by a decision or issue
tips: The lesson in this unit called 'Using GIS to visualise the impact of physical and human processes on coasts' could be used to extend this lesson.

3946.name: Example of a coastal management scheme
3946.outcome: I can explain the reasons, strategy, effects and conflicts associated with coastal management at Lyme Regis.
points: Location of Lyme Regis in the UK.
There are several reasons why Lyme Regis needs coastal management.
A range of coastal management strategies are used at Lyme Regis.
The management strategies used at Lyme Regis have a range of effects.
keywords: using artificial structures to protect coastlines from erosion and flooding
when areas of the coast are deliberately allowed to flood or erode naturally
making use of natural processes to reduce erosion and flooding in a way that minimies environmental impact
any groups or individuals involved in or interested in changes being made at the coast
tips: The lesson in this unit called 'Using GIS to visualise the impact of physical and human processes on coasts' could be used to extend this lesson.

6759.name: Using GIS to visualise the impact of physical and human processes on coasts
6759.outcome: I can use GIS aerial imagery and webmaps to visualise the impact of physical and human processes on coastal landscapes.
points: GIS uses historical imagery to visualise and analyse how the coastline changes over time. This is called temporal data.
GIS uses historical maps to analyse how the coastline changes using georeferenced older maps.
GIS apps which enable visualisation of temporal data include Esri Wayback and NLS Maps.
