GIS apps use historical imagery and historical maps to visualise and measure change such as the rate of coastal erosion.
keywords: information which has been tied to a particular location (geolocated), using an agreed system such as latitude and longitude
photographs from any time in the past which can be compared with more recent photographs including aerial, satellite or conventional
maps from any time in the past which can be compared with more recent maps
information which is tied to a particular point in time, so that data can be time-enabled (also known as spatiotemporal data)
tips: No matter what your level of experience is with GIS, go through all the steps yourself first until you feel confident and fluent. Don't worry if you make a mistake, everybody does, even experienced practitioners!

3947.name: Changes in river landscapes along the course of a river
3947.outcome: I can describe changes in the long profile and channel of a river along its course.
points: Rivers exhibit a distinctive long profile from source to mouth.
River and valley cross profiles change between their upper, mid- and lower courses.
River channel characteristics in the River Eden change with distance downstream.
keywords: an imaginary line that divides the court vertically into 3 sections
the inside view of a 3D object when cut straight through
The gradient on a displacement-time graph gives the instantaneous velocity.
the process where a river erodes the land on its sides (banks) rather than just the riverbed
tips: This lesson provides an opportunity to use OS maps to dentifying the key characteristics of the upper, middle and lower course, practising grid references and interpreting contour lines.

3948.name: River processes of erosion, transportation and deposition
3948.outcome: I can understand the processes at work in a river.
points: Rivers erode landscapes through the processes of hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution.
Rivers transport sediment through the processes of traction, saltation, suspension and solution.
Rivers deposit sediment in areas of low energy.
keywords: the volume of water that flows through a river at a given point over a specific period of time
the speed at which water flows in a river
A material deposited by water, wind or ice, such as pebbles or sand.
tips: Use of mini whiteboards to allow students to test understanding of these proceses will help to develop understanding for use in later lessons.

3949.name: River landforms caused by erosion and deposition
3949.outcome: I can explain the characteristics and formation of river landforms.
points: River erosion shapes distinctive landforms (interlocking spurs, waterfalls and gorges).
River erosion and deposition combine to form distinctive landforms (meanders and oxbow lakes).
River deposition forms distinctive landforms (levees, flood plains, estuaries and deltas).
keywords: when rocks and debris carried by a glacier scrape and wear away the surface beneath it
when material being carried is dropped due to loss of a river’s energy
the power of water eroding a river’s bed and banks
the process where a river erodes the land on its sides (banks) rather than just the riverbed
tips: This lesson provides opportunity to look at OS maps to find examples of these landforms, looking at change in contour patterns along the course of a river. Practical modelling of the landforms using playdoh can help pupils to develop understanding.

3950.name: An example of a river valley in the UK
3950.outcome: I can identify major landforms of erosion and deposition in the River Eden valley, and explain their formation.
points: The River Eden valley is located in the northwest of England.
The River Eden valley features landforms of erosion and deposition.
It has erosional landforms in its upper course including a V-shaped valley, Hell Gill, and a waterfall, Hell Gill Force.
It has depositional landforms in its middle and lower course including meanders across floodplains near to Carlisle.
keywords: when material being carried is dropped due to loss of a river’s energy
the wearing away of rocks along the coastline
the breakdown or disintegration of rocks at or close to the surface
tips: Looking at a specific example provides opportunities for mapskills practice, using OS maps to identify specific landforms and land uses in the river valley.

3952.name: The storm hydrograph
3952.outcome: I can explain the characteristics and factors affecting the shape of a storm hydrograph.
points: The storm hydrograph shows the relationship between precipitation and discharge.
Physical and human factors affect the shape of the storm hydrograph.
keywords: the volume of water flowing through a river channel at any given time, measured in cumecs
a measure of how many rivers and streams there are within a given area. A high drainage density indicates many streams and rivers in the given area
the process by which water on the ground surface enters the soil
the time between the peak rainfall and the peak discharge
tips: This provides an opportunity to look at drainage basins on OS maps. Pupils can identify human and physical characteristics and decide on the shape of hydrograph that would be likely following intense rainfall.

3955.name: Factors affecting flood risk
3955.outcome: I can explain the physical and human factors that affect flood risk, and why flood risk is increasing.
points: Physical and human factors increase flood risk.
Increased flood risk is due to several factors including increased storm frequency (and intensity) and land use change.
Increased river flooding threatens people and the environment.
keywords: a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
the probability of a flood event occurring and its potential impact
a sculptural technique where the designs are raised above a flat background
a rise in the proportion of people living in urban areas
tips: To ensure pupils have a full understanding of these factors it is useful to link it to the storm hydrograph - thinking about the impact on lag time and peak discharge.

3957.name: Example of a UK flood management scheme: Carlisle
3957.outcome: I can use an example to discuss reasons, strategies and issues connected to a flood management scheme.
points: Carlisle is located in northwest England. It lies at the confluence of three rivers.
Carlisle has experienced several major flooding events.
£25 million was invested in a flood management scheme, combining hard engineering and soft engineering strategies.
There were social, economic and environmental issues associated with the example flood management scheme.
keywords: using artificial structures to protect coastlines from erosion and flooding
the quality of being very serious
making use of natural processes to reduce erosion and flooding in a way that minimies environmental impact
tips: A throrough understanding of the costs and benefits of flood management strategies is important before this lesson. Students could then justify their own ideas for the flood management strategy.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

7530.name: Costs and benefits of river management strategies
7530.outcome: I can assess the costs and benefits associated with hard and soft engineering strategies used to manage river flooding.
points: Use of hard engineering strategies to manage rivers.
Use of soft engineering strategies to manage rivers.
There are costs and benefits associated with each type of river management strategy.
keywords: using artificial structures to protect coastlines from erosion and flooding
making use of natural processes to reduce erosion and flooding in a way that minimies environmental impact
development that meets the needs of people today without damaging the environment or reducing resources for future generations
tips: Use case studies to show real-world examples of cost-benefit analysis in action.

6760.name: Using GIS to analyse river catchments and profiles
6760.outcome: I can use GIS to analyse river catchments and profiles.
points: The GIS tool 'Trace Downstream' can be used to analyse the course of a river.
The GIS tool 'Create Watersheds' can be used to analyse the drainage basin (catchment) of a river.
The GIS tool 'Elevation Profile' can be used to find out if a river's long profile corresponds to a theoretical model.
keywords: a GIS tool which maps the drainage basin or catchment of a river and all of its tributaries
a GIS tool which visualises changes in height above or below sea level along a transect line
a GIS tool which maps the course of a river from a location such as its source to the end of the river
a range of GIS applications used to support the processing, analysing, and visualising of spatial data
tips: No matter what your level of experience is with GIS, go through all the steps yourself first until you feel confident and fluent. Don't worry if you make a mistake, everybody does, even experienced practitioners!

3958.name: Ice-shaping processes
3958.outcome: I can explain the processes by which ice shapes the landscape.
points: Ice covered large parts of the UK in the past.
Glacial processes have been responsible for shaping the landscape of the UK.
Glacial processes include freeze-thaw weathering, erosion, movement, transportation and deposition (till and outwash).
keywords: the break up of rocks caused by water regularly freezing and thawing
a large mass of ice that forms on land and moves slowly due to gravity
a vast, continuous expanse of ice covering a very large area of land
tips: There are useful online videos that present the changes in ice sheet coverage in the northern hemisphere over previous glacial maximums.

3959.name: Glacial landforms resulting from erosion and deposition
3959.outcome: I can explain the characteristics and formation of glacial landforms.
points: Glacial landscapes exhibit several distinctive landforms.
Distinctive landforms formed due to erosion including corries, aretes, pyramidal peaks, truncated spurs, glacial troughs
Distinctive landforms formed due to processes of transportation and deposition include erratics, drumlins and moraine.
keywords: when rocks and debris carried by a glacier scrape and wear away the surface beneath it
a valley reshaped by glacial erosion into a U-shape
accumulation of unsorted debris, such as soil and rock, deposited by a glacier
when a glacier pulls chunks of rock from the bedrock as it moves over it
tips: It is important to understand the role of erosional processes - abrasion and plucking - in creating the glacial landforms. Previous knowledge of erosion, transportation and deposition (e.g. rivers, coasts) may help students in this lesson.

3960.name: An example of an upland glaciated landscape in the UK: North Wales
3960.outcome: I can identify landforms of glacial erosion and deposition in North Wales.
points: North Wales in the UK is an example of a glaciated landscape.
Snowdonia in North Wales exhibits landforms of erosion.
Snowdonia in North Wales exhibits landforms of deposition.
keywords: Geographical Information System: software that create maps of spatial data, as well as digital tools to analyse it
period when ice sheets were at their largest extent, during the last Ice Age about 26 000 years ago
lines drawn on maps that connect points of equal height above sea level
a bowl-shaped hollow eroded by a glacier, typically forming at the head of a valley
tips: This lesson provides the chance to build in OS mapskills, e.g. identify features using grid references, drawing a cross section and practising sketch maps using photographs of landforms in North Wales.

6128.name: Economic activities in glaciated upland areas
6128.outcome: I can explain the economic activities that occur in glaciated upland areas and their impacts.
points: Glaciated upland areas provide opportunities for economic activities.
Economic activities in glaciated upland areas include tourism, farming, forestry and quarrying.
Economic activities have positive and negative impacts on glaciated upland areas.
keywords: the variety of species found in a habitat
anything to do with money, jobs, and resources
the science and practice of planting, managing and caring for forests
the process of extracting stone or other materials from a quarry
tips: Practical use of OS maps can be used to identify economic activities in these areas, and link them to the physical landscapes. GIS tools can be useful for this.

6129.name: Conflicts in glaciated upland areas
6129.outcome: I can explain how conflicts may exist between different land uses and between development and conservation in glaciated upland areas.
points: Conflicts can exist between different land uses in glaciated upland areas.
Conflicts can exist between development and conservation in glaciated upland areas.
keywords: an active disagreement between people with opposing opinions or principles
protection and management of natural resources to prevent damage and maintain biodiversity
improving and building on design ideas to make them better
anyone who has an interest in or is affected by a decision or issue
tips: Allow groups of students to research a development scenario from a specific stakeholder's viewpoint. This could lead to a class debate/discussion to deepen their understanding of the reasons for conflict.

6130.name: An example of a glaciated upland area used for tourism
6130.outcome: I can explain the impacts of tourism in Eryri National Park and how it is managed.
points: Location of Eryri National Park in the UK.
The Eryri National Park glaciated upland area has attractions for tourists.
Tourism can have social, economic and environmental impacts.
Strategies can be used to manage the impact of tourism.
keywords: a protected area of natural beauty, wildlife, and cultural importance, managed to preserve its environment while allowing public access for recreation and education
tourism that considers its current and future economic, social, and environmental impacts
tips: Give students the opportunity to research some of the tourist attractions, creating a short factfile about each to help them to feel more confident when describing the range of reasons why tourists visit. Use of OS maps and GIS can help with this as well.

6761.name: Using GIS to visualise glaciated landforms in upland areas
6761.outcome: I can use GIS to visualise glaciated landforms in upland areas.
points: GIS can be used to visualise glacial landforms of the physical geography of upland areas such as North Wales.
GIS can be used to assess the extent to which a landscape aligns with a theoretical model of a glaciated landscape.
GIS can be particularly helpful when using tools to change the orientation of a 3D map and using oblique views.
Data about industrial heritage in glaciated areas can be visualised and configured using pop-ups to analyse conflicts.
keywords: physical landscape features created by the action of glaciers during a glaciation
a view over a landscape from one side at an angle (also known as ‘perspective view’)
the way a rectangular page is positioned for normal viewing
in GIS, a read-only display of attribute information (e.g. text, images, charts) often linked to a location
tips: Practise the procedural steps yourself first until you achieve fluency and feel confident. Don't worry if you make mistakes - everyone does even after years of experience! Look at details about the Snowdonia Slate Trail (snowdoniaslatetrail.org).

4039.name: Global trends in urbanisation
4039.outcome: I can analyse global patterns in urbanisation.
points: The world is becoming increasingly urbanised.
Trends in urbanisation (past, present and future) vary between global regions.
Some urban areas have grown into megacities.
Some urban areas have disproportionate economic and/or political influence.
keywords: a city with a population of 10 million people or more
when one city politically and/or economically dominates a country or region
a rise in the proportion of people living in urban areas
tips: Plotting megacities on a map is a good opportunity to develop and revise students’ atlas skills.

4040.name: Factors affecting the growth of cities
4040.outcome: I can evaluate the factors that affect urbanisation.
points: Migration affects the rate of urbanisation.
Economic change affects the rate of urbanisation.
Natural increase affects the rate of urbanisation.
keywords: the loss of industry from an area
the difference between the birth rate and the death rate of a population; occurs when the birth rate is higher than the death rate
Pull factors refer to the attractive aspects or opportunities that draw individuals to a new destination.
negative things that make people want to leave an area, for example, war
tips: Allow students the opportunity to hear different migration stories first hand. This will substantiate the theory and avoid placing all migrants together in one context.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

4044.name: Living sustainably in urban environments
4044.outcome: I can evaluate different strategies for making urban spaces more sustainable and less congested.
points: Urban sustainability requires management of resources and transport.
The features of sustainable living include energy and water conservation, waste recycling and creating green spaces.
Urban transport strategies can be used to reduce traffic congestion.
keywords: an overcrowding of traffic in a particular space
a system where people can park their cars just outside the CBD and then take public transport into the centre
development that meets the needs of people today without damaging the environment or reducing resources for future generations
tips: Students can research urban transport strategies in their own area and talk to regular users to gauge if these have been successful.

6758.name: Using GIS to visualise global trends in urbanisation
6758.outcome: I can use GIS to visualise global trends in urbanisation.
points: For the first time ever, humanity became ‘urban’ around 2007.
GIS can help us to manage and visualise big data about world cities using filters and pop-ups.
GIS helps us to manage and visualise big data about trends in urbanisation using choropleth maps and pop-ups.
GIS choropleth maps use shapefiles which are ‘joined’ to attribute using place identifiers in the shapefiles.
GIS pop-us can be configured to visualise trends in big data about urban population.
keywords: a cartographical method used to visualise data for bounded areas (polygons) using shading or colours
the selection of some data in a GIS layer to visualise spatial patterns more clearly
in GIS, a read-only display of attribute information (e.g. text, images, charts) often linked to a location
in GIS, a vector data storage format used for location, shape and attributes of geographic features, e.g. borders of polygons showing the outline and area of a country
tips: No matter what your level of experience is with GIS, go through all the steps yourself first until you feel confident and fluent. Don't worry if you make a mistake, everybody does, even experienced practitioners!

4045.name: Location and importance of Jakarta
4045.outcome: I can describe the location and importance of Jakarta and explain reasons for its growth.
points: Jakarta is located on the island of Java and is the capital of Indonesia.
Jakarta is important nationally, regionally and internationally.
Jakarta has experienced rapid growth due to natural increase and migration.
keywords: the difference between the birth rate and the death rate of a population; occurs when the birth rate is higher than the death rate
the sinking or settling of land, often caused by human activities such as excessive groundwater extraction, which can increase the risk of flooding
a city with global influence, important in the world economy through finance, trade, culture and communication
tips: Esri's Geography Visualiser is a great tool for exploring Jakarta's location within Java.

4047.name: Social opportunities associated with urban growth
4047.outcome: I can describe how urban growth creates social opportunities in Jakarta.
points: There are social opportunities associated with urban growth in Jakarta.
Urban growth creates access to services such as health and education.
Urban growth creates access to resources, such as water supply and energy.
keywords: how easy it is for people to take part in an activity, especially if there are barriers
a positive feature or benefit that improves people's lives, such as access to clean water, jobs, healthcare or education
tips: Use the Geogrpahy Visualiser’s satellite view to explore different parts of Jakarta, e.g. the CBD, port area, kampongs and newer suburbs. Pupils can annotate patterns they notice (dense housing, commercial areas, green spaces) and link these to opportunities and challenges.

4048.name: Economic opportunities associated with urban growth
4048.outcome: I can explain how urban growth creates economic opportunities in Jakarta.
points: There are several important industrial areas located in Jakarta.
Urban industrial areas have stimulated economic development in Jakarta.
Urban growth has created a range of economic opportunities in Jakarta.
Employment opportunities are changing from manufacturing towards services and from informal to formal sector employment.
keywords: the availability of jobs and work for people, often used to measure economic opportunity and development
jobs which pay tax to the government and which come with legal contracts and benefits like a regular salary, sick pay and pensions
jobs which are not registered with the government and illegally avoid paying tax, and which do not have any protections for workers such as contracts, insurance against accidents, sick pay, holidays
tips: Indonesia's Central Bureau of Statistics has a wide range of data about employment in Jakarta (DKI Jakarta) which can be usefully compared with other provinces of Indonesia. The publications are all available in English.

4049.name: Challenges associated with urban growth: housing
4049.outcome: I can describe how urban growth has created challenges for managing housing and quality of life in Jakarta.
points: There are challenges associated with managing urban growth in Jakarta.
Rapid population growth has created housing shortages in Jakarta.
There are challenges associated with squatter settlements in Jakarta.
keywords: the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
an informal settlement in Indonesian cities that is self-built without planning permission. Homes are overcrowded, poorly constructed and lack basic services
tips: Students could use satellite images to locate areas of Jakarta where kampungs have been built along rivers and in other marginal areas such as along railway lines.

4050.name: Challenges associated with urban growth: people and the economy
4050.outcome: I can describe the challenges associated with providing services and reducing unemployment and crime in Jakarta.
points: There are challenges associated with providing clean water, sanitation systems and energy in Jakarta.
There are challenges associated with providing access to health and education services in Jakarta.
There are challenges associated with reducing unemployment and crime in Jakarta.
keywords: water found underground in soil, sand, and rock. It is stored in aquifers and can be used as a source of water for drinking or industry
presence of harmful substances in the environment, such as in the air, water or soil, which can damage ecosystems and human health
systems for removing human waste and managing rubbish and dirty water to prevent the spread of disease
tips: There are lots of YouTube videos recording Western travellers' impressions of Jakarta. Show one that focuses on the modern face of Jakarta today, and one that features the 'sinking slums' of Jakarta.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of discriminatory behaviour
guidance.description: Historic or outdated representations of people that may portray inequality or injustice.

4051.name: Challenges associated with urban growth: environmental issues
4051.outcome: I can describe the challenges associated with managing environmental issues in Jakarta.
points: There are environmental challenges in Jakarta.
There are challenges associated with waste disposal in Jakarta.
There are challenges associated with air and water pollution in Jakarta.
There are challenges associated with traffic congestion in Jakarta.
keywords: an overcrowding of traffic in a particular space
water found underground in soil, sand, and rock. It is stored in aquifers and can be used as a source of water for drinking or industry
presence of harmful substances in the environment, such as in the air, water or soil, which can damage ecosystems and human health
tips: There are several YouTube videos about Bantar Gebang landfill that show the scale of the landfill, and some that also interview those who make a living as waste pickers on the landfill.

4052.name: Urban planning: improving quality of life for the urban poor in Jakarta
4052.outcome: I can explain, using an example, how urban planning is improving quality of life for the urban poor in Jakarta.
points: The Kampung Akuarium project has improved quality of life for the urban poor in Jakarta by improving housing conditions.
Posyandu clinics have improved quality of life for the urban poor in Jakarta by improving access to healthcare.
There are advantages and disadvantages of 'bottom-up' strategies for improving health and education services.
keywords: small-scale projects led by local people to meet community needs, often supported by NGOs
a group of people working together to achieve shared goals. A housing cooperative is where residents help plan and manage their homes, often in partnership with local government or NGOs
development that meets the needs of people today without damaging the environment or reducing resources for future generations
tips: Use GIS to map the location of kampungs like Akuarium and Pulo, showing proximity to flood zones or lack of infrastructure.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

4062.name: Strategies for achieving sustainability: 'top-down' strategies
4062.outcome: I can assess the advantages and disadvantages of 'top-down' strategies for making Jakarta more sustainable.
points: There are advantages and disadvantages of 'top-down' strategies for managing water supply.
There are advantages and disadvantages of 'top-down' strategies for managing waste disposal.
There are advantages and disadvantages of 'top-down' strategies for managing transport and air pollution in Jakarta.
keywords: the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
development that meets the needs of people today without damaging the environment or reducing resources for future generations
development led by governments or large organisations, often with large-scale funding and limited community input
tips: ArcGIS Online features different layers for Jakarta including demography, poverty and flood risk which could be used to highlight different challenges facing the city.

4063.name: Strategies for achieving sustainability: 'bottom-up' strategies
4063.outcome: I can explain advantages and disadvantages of bottom-up strategies for achieving sustainability in Jakarta.
points: Bottom-up strategies involving community and NGO-led can make Jakarta more sustainable.
Bottom-up housing projects have been successful in improving housing.
Bottom-up housing projects have been successful in improving health and education.
There are advantages and disadvantages of 'bottom-up' strategies for improving health and education services.
keywords: small-scale projects led by local people to meet community needs, often supported by NGOs
a group of people working together to achieve shared goals. A housing cooperative is where residents help plan and manage their homes, often in partnership with local government or NGOs
development that meets the needs of people today without damaging the environment or reducing resources for future generations
tips: Students could make use of ArcGIS’s Wayback feature to explore changes in Jakarta's residential areas.

3962.name: UK cities and population distribution
3962.outcome: I can locate major cities of the UK and describe and explain the UK's uneven population distribution.
points: There are 76 cities in the UK and the majority of these are in England.
Population is unevenly distributed in the UK.
Population density varies between the countries of the UK and areas within them.
Human and physical factors can explain the differences in population distribution.
keywords: the number of people living in a defined area, e.g. 300 people per square kilometre
describes how the people in that population are spread out across the area
tips: Pupils are likely to have some prior knowledge about the location of UK cities but using an atlas for Task A would scaffold it for those needing additional support.

3966.name: Location and importance of Liverpool in the UK and wider world
3966.outcome: I can describe the location of Liverpool and justify, using evidence, why it is an important city both nationally and globally.
points: Liverpool is a coastal city in the north-west of the UK.
Evidence of Liverpool’s importance can be categorised into historical, socio-economic, demographic and economic.
Liverpool is nationally important for its diversity, city economy, role in the Industrial Revolution and population.
Liverpool is globally important for trade, sporting and cultural events and its link to the slave trade and migration.
keywords: where a shape or action is placed, e.g. a starting position
tips: Promote local location knowledge by adapting the example of Grimsby to your location. Pupils could respond to this verbally to increase oracy skills.

3967.name: Impacts of national and international migration on Liverpool
3967.outcome: I can detail the main historic and recent, national and international migrations affecting Liverpool and describe the impacts on demography, economic growth and character.
points: Liverpool's migrations can be divided over time (historical and recent) and over space (national and international).
Significant national, historical inflows have been from Ireland and Wales.
International inflows have been both historic and recent.
Demographic impacts include changes to population, structure and ethnic composition.
All migrations have impacted on the economic growth and character of Liverpool.
keywords: migration of people to a place
moving from one place to another with the intention of staying there
migration of people away from a place
tips: To secure the information in the first learning cycle, call out the origins of the significant migrant groups and get pupils to identify their combinations: national/international, historic/recent.

3968.name: Opportunities created by urban change: people
3968.outcome: I can identify the social and economic opportunities for people in Liverpool as a consequence of urban change.
points: Urban change has created social and economic opportunities for people in Liverpool.
Social opportunities include entertainment and recreation opportunities.
Social opportunities include the benefits of a cultural mix.
Economic opportunities are in the form of a varied employment sector.
Tech companies are attracted to Liverpool due to the workforce, supportive environment and links to similar companies.
keywords: in population, a community of people from different backgrounds with their own beliefs and traditions
facts and figures which are particular to a place
changes that occur in a city due to its growth or decline
tips: Exploring the Albert Dock and other areas mentioned on Streetview would bring the case study to life.

3969.name: Opportunities created by urban change: infrastructure and urban greening
3969.outcome: I can explain how urban change has created environmental opportunities in Liverpool including the development of integrated transport systems and urban greening.
points: Urban change has created environmental opportunities to develop integrated transport systems and urban greening.
Integrated transport systems encourage people to use public transport through making journeys smoother.
Future development of the integrated transport system includes becoming more integrated, sustainable and accessible.
Urban greening can help Liverpool achieve its 2040 net-carbon zero ambitions.
Examples of urban greening include the investment from URBAN GreenUP, St John's Shopping Centre and Mersey Forest.
keywords: an interconnected urban transport network, with interchange hubs linking different forms of transport, such as bicycles, buses and cars
the greening of urban areas, involving planting trees and the creation of green areas and parks
tips: To add further depth to the misconception get pupils to think in detail about how investment in e.g. hydrogen fuelled buses is not only environemntally beneficial but also supports the economy and brings social benefits to people too.

3970.name: Challenges created by urban change: social and economic
3970.outcome: I can use data to describe deprivation across the Liverpool City Region and identify how this relates to inequalities at a variety of scales.
points: Urban change has created social and economic challenges in Liverpool linked to high relative levels of deprivation.
The Index of Multiple Deprivation measures relative deprivation at local authority and smaller scales.
The six local authorities in the Liverpool City Region are all in top 60 most deprived in England. Knowsley ranks 2nd.
Deprivation has a cause and effect link to inequalities in housing, health, employment and education.
High deprivation in Liverpool correlates with poor housing, poor health, unemployment and low educational attainment.
keywords: low standard of living caused by low income, poor health and low educational attainment, sometimes described as living in poverty
when things are not fair or equal for everyone
tips: The Index of Multiple Deprivation contains a wealth of rich data and adding comparisons to your local area could be a useful comparison. The misconception remains critical in this and the avoidance of stereotyping is paramount.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

3971.name: Challenges created by urban change: environmental
3971.outcome: I can identify how urban change has led to environmental challenges for Liverpool and use place-specific detail to evidence the problems.
points: Urban change has led to challenges with industrial and residential dereliction such as deterioration of buildings.
Urban change has led to challenges in the redevelopment of brown and greenfield sites to meet housing demand.
Urban change has led to challenges in waste disposal due to low rates of recycling.
The environmental challenges have been and continue to be addressed by the Liverpool City Region local authorities.
keywords: an area of land that was formerly used for something but which is now abandoned or derelict
when buildings or land degrades into a state of poor condition, having been abandoned
land, often rural or on the edges of urban areas, which has not been built on before
tips: Get pupils to conisder how suitability for redevelopment of brownfield sites is assessed. They could be prompted to think about drainage, transport infrastructure, demographics, facilities such as schools and medical centres. Which of these do they think should be given highest priority?

3973.name: Impact of urban sprawl on the rural-urban fringe
3973.outcome: I can explain how urban change has led to pressure on areas of Liverpool’s rural-urban fringe.
points: Significant urban sprawl in the Liverpool City Region has been prevented by extensive greenbelt land.
Unprotected areas that have been developed include areas within and around Speke, Croxteth Park, Halewood and Aigburth.
Commuter settlements often develop in the rural-urban fringe and are desirable due to housing and good transport.
There are positive and negative impacts of urban sprawl on the rural-urban fringe.
keywords: a place, often a town or village, where people live and then travel to other places, normally a city, for work
land that is protected from development and surrounds major English cities
the outer edge of a city where it merges with the countryside
the physical outward expansion of a city into the surrounding countryside
tips: Development of greenfield and greenbelt land sparks lots of controversey. Search for examples of conflict in your local area so pupils can relate to the challenges of developing the urban-rural fringe.

3974.name: An example of an urban regeneration project
3974.outcome: I can describe the location of the Albert Dock and explain the reasons for its decline and features of its regeneration.
points: The Albert Dock is located in central Liverpool on the north shore of the River Mersey.
Maps at different scales and their features help describe location in detail.
The Albert Dock went into decline from the 1860s until it was abandoned in 1971.
Regeneration of the Albert Dock began in 1981 and was reopened in 1984.
The regeneration features mixed land use to support social, economic and environmental development.
keywords: the purpose or function of land, for example: residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural or recreational use
planned improvements to an area of deprivation within a town or city
tips: Central Docks and others to the north of the Albert Dock are about to undergo regeneration. Plans and newspaper articles are available online and pupils could review the land use intentions.

3975.name: Sustainable living in an urban area
3975.outcome: I can identify features of sustainable urban areas and understand how resources and transport can be effectively managed.
points: Balancing social, economic and environmental factors is necessary to achieve sustainability.
The management of urban resources involves consideration of land, water, waste and energy.
The management of urban transport should aim to reduce emissions and congestion.
Sustainability is at the forefront of urban development in Liverpool.
keywords: techniques used to reduce hazard risk, including short-term relief and long-term planning, preparation and prediction
using resources wisely so future generations can also meet their needs
tips: Urban development is happening all around the country. You could enrich this lesson by investigating local development plans and get pupils to consider how social, economic and environmental pillars are being considered.

3905.name: The structure of the Earth
3905.outcome: I can explain how Earth has different layers, each of which has distinctive characteristics.
points: Earth has a layered structure.
The layers of Earth have different physical properties (temperature, density, composition, physical state).
keywords: a semi-solid layer of Earth's upper mantle
the rigid outer layer of Earth which includes the crust
tips: Liaise with science colleagues to see what students have already been taught about this topic in KS3 and KS4.

7578.name: Impacts of volcanoes in a developed and an emerging country
7578.outcome: I can use located examples to assess the impacts of volcanic eruptions in a developed and an emerging country.
points: Primary impacts are immediate and caused directly by the tectonic hazard.
Secondary impacts are indirect impacts and occur in the hours, days and weeks after the hazard.
There is a range of reasons why primary and secondary impacts may differ between two volcanic eruptions.
Different indicators can be considered to assess the significance of primary impacts and secondary impacts.
keywords: the immediate impacts of a tectonic hazard which are directly caused by it
indirect effects that occur as a consequence of a tectonic hazard’s primary impacts
tips: The ArcGIS Geography Visualiser is a fantastic tool for exploring volcanoes and the areas around them, while ArcGIS Online features layers that identify key aspects of eruptions, for example hazard risk zoning and evacuation routes.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

7577.name: Impacts of earthquakes in a developed and a developing country
7577.outcome: I can use located examples to discuss the impacts of earthquakes in a developed and a developing country.
points: Primary impacts are immediate and caused directly by the tectonic hazard.
Secondary impacts are indirect impacts and occur in the hours, days and weeks after the hazard.
There is a range of reasons why primary and secondary impacts may differ between two earthquakes.
keywords: the point on Earth's surface that is directly above where an earthquake happens underground
a measure of the energy released by an earthquake
tips: ArcGIS Online features layers that identify key aspects of eruptions, for example hazard risk zoning and evacuation routes.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3916.name: Examples of management of volcanic hazards
3916.outcome: I can describe how volcanoes are managed differently at contrasting locations.
points: Management can reduce the impacts of volcanic hazards.
Management involves short-term relief and long-term planning, preparation and prediction.
Volcanic hazards may be managed differently at contrasting locations.
keywords: the likelihood that people or property will be harmed by a natural hazard
techniques used to reduce hazard risk, including short-term relief and long-term planning, preparation and prediction
tips: There are amazing drone videos of the 2024 eruptions in Iceland available on YouTube and expert information on the Icelandic Met Office website. Reminder: although Oak has resourced both, students study *either* volcanic hazards *or* earthquake hazards for this part of the Edexcel B specification.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3917.name: Examples of management of earthquake hazards
3917.outcome: I can understand how earthquakes are managed differently at contrasting locations.
points: Management can reduce the impacts of earthquake hazards.
Management involves short-term relief and long-term planning, preparation and prediction.
Earthquake hazards may be managed differently at contrasting locations.
keywords: techniques used to reduce hazard risk, including short-term relief and long-term planning, preparation and prediction
tips: Reminder: although Oak has resourced both, students study *either* volcanic hazards *or* earthquake hazards for this part of the Edexcel B specification.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

3925.name: Examples of preparation and responses to tropical cyclones
3925.outcome: I can explain how the effects of tropical cyclones depend on a country's ability to prepare and respond.
points: The impacts of tropical cyclones depends on a country's ability to prepare and respond to them.
Japan's methods of preparation and response as a highly developed country.
Bangladesh's methods of preparation and response as a developing country.
keywords: the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
the initial set of movements and position required before executing the throw
action taken to address the impacts of a disaster
tips: Looking at data about the level of development and ways of life in Japan and Bangladesh, together with examples of the impacts of recent tropical cyclones in each country, will help to set the scene for this lesson.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

2928.name: Biosphere resources
2928.outcome: I can explain that the biosphere provides important resources for local people and commercially.
points: The biosphere provides resources for local people.
The biosphere is an important source of commercial resources, such as energy, water and minerals.
keywords: life on Earth, encompassing all living organisms (plants, animals, bacteria, etc.) and the ecosystems they form
the extraction and trading of materials, such as wood, for profit
people who have inhabited an area from the earliest times before the arrival of colonists
economically-valuable material concentrated in the Earth's crust, such as copper and oil
materials available in the environment (such as water, food and wood) that support our wants and needs
tips: Consider using video clips to help learners to understand the daily lives of indigenous people.

2927.name: Understanding the regulatory functions of the biosphere
2927.outcome: I can explain how the biosphere regulates the atmosphere and provides important environmental services.
points: The biosphere regulates the composition of the atmosphere.
The biosphere maintains soil health and regulates water within the hydrological cycle.
The biosphere provides globally important services.
keywords: the mood created in a section or whole of a text
benefits gained from the day-to-day functioning of the world's ecosystems that support human life
the continuous recycling of water in its different states, for example via rainfall and evaporation
to control, for example, the flow of water in a pipe or the temperature in a room
the structure, composition and nutrient content of a soil; a measure of soil fertility
tips: Learners may need reminding of the components of the hydrological cycle.

2930.name: Population and resources
2930.outcome: I can describe the growth in demand for resources, understand its causes and consider different theories about the relationship between population and resources.
points: Global and regional trends show increasing demand for food, energy and water resources.
Increasing resource demand can be caused by population growth, rising affluence, urbanisation and industrialisation.
Theories can help to explain relationships between population and resources, e.g. Malthus and Boserup.
keywords: Ester Boserup (born 1910) took an optimistic view of the link between population growth and agriculture
Thomas Malthus (born 1766) took a pessimistic view of the link between population growth and resources
the wealth of individuals or societies, which rises with industrialisation and the creation of a middle class
where a mainly agricultural society changes and begins to depend more on manufacturing industries
a rise in the proportion of people living in urban areas
tips: There are opportunities for developing geographical skills (using graphs and maps showing global and regional trends). Some graphs, in particular may be explored using interactive versions online.

2939.name: Threats associated with climate change in the rainforest
2939.outcome: I can explain that tropical rainforests are indirectly threatened by climate change.
points: Climate change is affecting tropical rainforests.
How is climate change an indirect threat to tropical rainforests (ecosystem stress, drought).
keywords: a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
effects or consequences that are not immediately caused by an event or action but happen as a result of it
A threat is the possibility that something unwanted or dangerous will happen.
tips: The lesson in this unit called "Using GIS to visualise and analyse deforestation" gives students opportunities to explore and measure deforestation using accessible GIS tools.

2940.name: Biotic and abiotic characteristics of the taiga biome
2940.outcome: I can describe the interdependence of biotic and abiotic characteristics of the taiga biome.
points: The taiga is an example of a global biome.
The taiga has distinctive biotic (living) characteristics (plants, animals and humans).
The taiga has distinctive abiotic (non-living) characteristics (climate, soil and water).
Biotic and abiotic characteristics are interdependent.
keywords: the non-living elements of an ecosystem (e.g. water, nutrients)
a large-scale ecosystem with specific climate, plants and animals
the living elements of an ecosystem (e.g. plants, animals)
the average weather conditions in a region over a long period of time
tips: The lesson in this unit called "Using GIS to visualise and analyse deforestation" gives students opportunities to explore and measure deforestation using accessible GIS tools.

2941.name: Plant and animal adaptations in the taiga biome
2941.outcome: I can explain how plants and animals in the taiga are well adapted to the physical conditions.
points: The taiga is home to a variety of plants and animals.
Animals are well adapted to the physical conditions in the taiga, for example, by being migratory.
Plants are well adapted to the physical conditions in the taiga, for example, needles instead of leaves.
keywords: a feature or behaviour that helps an animal or plant survive in its environment
the variety of species found in a habitat
the natural place where a plant or animal lives and grows
tips: A BBC Teach video on "Coniferous forests - Finland" provides a useful introduction to some specific plant and animal adaptations in the taiga / boreal forest.

2942.name: Nutrient cycling and biodiversity in the taiga biome
2942.outcome: I can explain that, compared to tropical rainforests, the taiga has low productivity, a lower rate of nutrient cycling and supports lower levels of biodiversity.
points: The taiga has a lower rate of productivity than tropical rainforests and less active nutrient cycling.
The taiga support much lower levels of biodiversity than tropical rainforests.
keywords: the variety of species found in a habitat
when two or more biotic features, like plants or animals, depend or rely on each other to survive
chemical substances found in all biotic features which are important for survival
tips: Ensure students are familiar with the concept and features of nutrient cycle diagrams by comparing the nutrient cycle diagram for the taiga with one for a tropical rainforest and explaining the differences.

2943.name: Threats to the taiga from commercial development
2943.outcome: I can explain ways in which the taiga is threatened by commercial development.
points: The taiga is increasingly threatened by commercial development.
Threats include logging, pulp and paper production, fossil fuel extraction, mining and HEP development.
An example of threat to the taiga from development is the commercial exploitation of tar sands in Alberta, Canada.
keywords: the variety of species found in a habitat
a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
A threat is the possibility that something unwanted or dangerous will happen.
tips: Recap with students what factors make the taiga biome unique and vulnerable to development, for example slow rates of decomposition, poor soil nutrients. slow tree growth.

2944.name: Causes of biodiversity loss in the taiga biome
2944.outcome: I can describe how acid precipitation, forest fires and pests and diseases contribute to a loss of biodiversity in the taiga.
points: The taiga is vulnerable to biodiversity loss.
The taiga is experiencing a loss of biodiversity.
Acid precipitation is contributing to a loss of biodiversity.
Forest fires and pests and diseases are contributing to a loss of biodiversity.
keywords: the variety of species found in a habitat
a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
A habitat is the place where an organism lives. It must provide food, shelter and a place to reproduce.
tips: The "Mountain Pine Beetle" layer from Esri Canada is available on ArcGIS Online, and shows changes in distribution over time in Canada's Rocky Mountains.

2945.name: Creating and protecting wilderness areas in the taiga biome
2945.outcome: I can explain challenges of creating and maintaining wilderness areas in the taiga.
points: Wilderness areas are found within the taiga biome.
There are challenges in creating protected wilderness areas, national parks and sustainable forestry in the taiga.
There are challenges in maintaining protected wilderness areas, national parks and sustainable forestry in the taiga.
keywords: development that meets the needs of people today without damaging the environment or reducing resources for future generations
large, undisturbed natural areas protected to preserve biodiversity and natural processes
tips: Use GIS to show students the vastness of taiga wilderness areas and illustrate how factors like terrain, climate, and accessibility affect management and conservation efforts.

2946.name: Conflicting views on protecting/exploiting resources in the taiga biome
2946.outcome: I can explain why there can be conflicting views on protecting and exploiting forest and natural resources in the taiga.
points: There are conflicting views on protecting forest and natural resources in the taiga.
There are conflicting views on exploiting forest and natural resources in the taiga.
keywords: anyone who has an interest in or is affected by a decision or issue
using resources wisely so future generations can also meet their needs
tips: Canada provides a good source of news stories that illustrate conflicts between those wishing to develop taiga resources, and those (including First Nations groups) looking to conserve them.

3935.name: Characteristics and distribution of UK rock types
3935.outcome: I can describe the characteristics and distribution of rock types in the UK.
points: Rock types have distinctive physical and chemical characteristics.
Igneous, metamorphic and sedimentary rocks are found in the UK.
Igneous rocks form from cooling molten magma.
Sedimentary rocks form from accumulated sediments.
Metamorphic rocks change due to heat and/or pressure.
keywords: a soft white sedimentary rock found in southern England
a hard igneous rock found in upland UK areas
rocks formed when molten magma cools and solidifies
rocks changed by intense heat and/or pressure
rocks made from compacted sediment layers over time
tips: It would be useful to have samples of different rock types in the classroom for students to look at.

3936.name: Processes creating distinctive landscapes
3936.outcome: I can explain how distinctive upland and lowland landscapes result from physical processes and human activity.
points: Physical processes shape landforms through interaction with geology.
Weathering, rivers and slope processes shape the land.
Climate affects the formation of landscapes over time.
Human activity also changes how landscapes look and function.
keywords: the average weather conditions in a region over a long period of time
the wearing away of rocks along the coastline
actions like farming, forestry and building that alter landscapes
processes that move material downslope due to gravity
the breakdown or disintegration of rocks at or close to the surface
tips: Use of GIS could be used to investigate different lowland and upland areas to consider the processes involved in their development. A good understanding of key processes will help ideas to be developed in this lesson.

3951.name: Interaction of human and physical factors in river landscapes
3951.outcome: I can explain how physical and human factors interact to affect river landscapes, sediment load and flood risk.
points: Physical and human factors interact to affect river landscapes.
Physical and human factors interact to affect sediment load.
Physical and human factors interact to affect flood risk.
keywords: large-scale removal or clearing of forests
an area of low-lying ground adjacent to a river, formed mainly of river sediments and subject to flooding
the total amount of sediment transported by a river
a rise in the proportion of people living in urban areas
tips: Make sure students are confident with key terms associated with the rivers topic: erosion, deposition and transportation, and have an understanding of how and where different river landscapes are found.

7532.name: Costs and benefits of managing flood risk
7532.outcome: I can assess the costs and benefits associated with hard and soft engineering strategies aimed at reducing river flooding.
points: There are costs and benefits of management strategies to reduce river flooding.
Hard engineering strategies include flood walls, embankments and flood barriers.
Soft engineering strategies include flood plain retention and river restoration.
keywords: using artificial structures to protect coastlines from erosion and flooding
making use of natural processes to reduce erosion and flooding in a way that minimies environmental impact
development that meets the needs of people today without damaging the environment or reducing resources for future generations
tips: Use case studies to show real-world examples of cost-benefit analysis in action.

3953.name: Example of a river flood: River Eden, Cumbria (2015)
3953.outcome: I can explain how physical and human factors interacted to cause the River Eden flooding in Cumbria in 2015.
points: The River Eden valley is located in the northwest of England.
In December 2015, Carlisle and surrounding towns were flooded.
Physical and human factors interacted to cause the flooding.
keywords: structures built to protect areas from flooding
an area of low-lying ground adjacent to a river, formed mainly of river sediments and subject to flooding
Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons as they contain only single bonds between carbon and hydrogen atoms.
tips: As this is a located example in the Edexcel B specification, make use of OS maps, video clips and news articles to support learning and bring it to life.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

6493.name: The role of geology in coastal erosion
6493.outcome: I can explain how geology can affect the development of coastal landforms.
points: How resistant rock is to erosional processes is influenced by its rock type (hard/soft).
Geological structure can result in concordant and discordant coastlines.
Coastal erosion creates distinctive landforms.
keywords: the wearing away of rocks along the coastline
refers to rocks that are less likely to be eroded or weathered
the process where cliffs move backward over time as erosion wears away the base of a cliff
tips: The lesson in this unit called 'Using GIS to visualise the impact of physical and human processes on coasts' could be used to extend this lesson.

6494.name: The role of climate, marine and sub-aerial processes in coastal erosion
6494.outcome: I can explain the role climate, marine and sub-aerial processes play in coastal erosion.
points: Climate (seasonality, storm frequency, prevailing winds) affects the rate of erosion along coastal landscapes.
Marine processes (destructive waves) affect coastal landscapes and the rate of coastal retreat.
Sub-aerial processes (mass movement, weathering) affect coastal landscapes and the rate of coastal retreat.
keywords: low-energy waves that result in the buildup of sediment along the coastline
high-energy waves that result in the removal of sediment along the coastline
the wearing away of rocks along the coastline
the downhill movement of material under the influence of gravity
the breakdown or disintegration of rocks at or close to the surface
tips: GIS could be used in this lesson to overlay different data sets, such as historical maps, on current OS maps to explore rates of coastal erosion.

6495.name: The influence of sediment transportation and deposition on coastal landscapes
6495.outcome: I can explain the role sediment transportation and deposition play in forming coastal depositional landforms.
points: Sediment transportation (longshore drift) and deposition (constructive waves) operate at the coast.
Processes of transportation and deposition influences coastal landforms (spits, beaches, bars).
keywords: when material being carried is dropped due to loss of a river’s energy
the most frequent wind direction a location receives
refers to the vertical section of water from the surface to the sea bed
tips: The lesson in this unit called 'Using GIS to visualise the impact of physical and human processes on coasts' could be used to extend this lesson.

3942.name: The effect of human activities on coastal landscapes
3942.outcome: I can explain the effect of human activities on the coast.
points: A variety of human activities take place at the coast (development, agriculture, industry and coastal management).
Human activities can have direct effects on coastal landscapes.
Human activities can have indirect effects on coastal landscapes.
keywords: improving and building on design ideas to make them better
the wearing away of rocks along the coastline
A habitat is the place where an organism lives. It must provide food, shelter and a place to reproduce.
tips: Students could study an OS map of a specific area and identify human activity taking place along the coast and research the direct and indirect impacts for the specific coastal landscape.

3943.name: Change in a named coastal landscape
3943.outcome: I can use knowledge of a location to explain how physical and human processes interact to cause change at the coast.
points: Happisburgh is experiencing some of the fastest coastal erosion rates in the UK.
Physical processes make the Happisburgh coastline vulnerable to erosion.
Human processes play a significant role in the rate of coastal erosion at Happisburgh.
keywords: a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
the protection of coastlines from erosion and flooding through artificial or natural methods
the wearing away of rocks along the coastline
tips: GIS can be used in this lesson to investigate the coastal erosion of area by comparing historic and modern maps.

3945.name: Risks from coastal flooding
3945.outcome: I can explain the risks from coastal flooding.
points: There are several causes of coastal flooding.
The risks from coastal flooding are increasing due to climate change.
Coastal flooding brings threats to people and the environment.
keywords: a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
A habitat is the place where an organism lives. It must provide food, shelter and a place to reproduce.
being more susceptible or exposed to the harmful impacts of a natural disaster
tips: Students could use GIS to map areas that are most at risk of coastal flooding in a particular country or around the world.

3956.name: Costs and benefits of management strategies
3956.outcome: I can explain different types of coastal management strategies and evaluate their costs and benefits.
points: Coastal management aims to protect communities and environments.
There are two main types of coastal management strategy.
Different stakeholders may have different views on coastal management.
keywords: using artificial structures to protect coastlines from erosion and flooding
making use of natural processes to reduce erosion and flooding in a way that minimies environmental impact
anyone who has an interest in or is affected by a decision or issue
how important an area is either socially, economically or environmentally
tips: The lesson in this unit called 'Using GIS to visualise the impact of physical and human processes on coasts' could be used to extend this lesson.

3963.name: Impacts of migration on the UK's population
3963.outcome: I can assess the impact migration has had on the UK's population.
points: National migration has altered the population geography of the UK (numbers, distribution, age structure).
International migration has altered the population geography of the UK (numbers, distribution, age structure).
UK and EU immigration policy has contributed to increasing ethnic and cultural diversity.
keywords: someone who seeks permanent or temporary protection in another country from the persecution or danger they experience in their home country
the act of moving out of a source location
the act of moving into a new host location
someone who has successfully sought asylum in another country and is henceforth protected by international law
tips: The topic of migration is a great opportunity for students to practise interview and active learning skills by talking to an international migrant about their migration story.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

3964.name: Changing economic sectors in urban and rural areas
3964.outcome: I can compare the changes that have occurred in different economic sectors.
points: There has been a decline in the primary and secondary sectors in rural and urban areas.
There has been a rise in the tertiary and quaternary sectors in rural and urban areas.
This decline and growth has affected the economy and employment structures of particular areas of the UK.
keywords: a tertiary sector industry that deals with banking, investments, pensions and insurance
the movement of manufacturing industries from developed countries to emerging and developing countries
the development of machinery and technology in industries such that it reduces the need for human labour
an area of land dedicated to businesses specialising in science and technology
tips: Students can use old maps to look at how farming and urban landscapes have changed over time and how these changes are indicators of economic sector decline or growth.

3965.name: Economic impacts of globalisation
3965.outcome: I can assess how FDI and TNCs have affected the UK.
points: Globalisation has increased foreign direct investment in the UK.
Free-trade policies have increased foreign direct investment in the UK.
Privatisation has increased foreign direct investment in the UK.
TNCs play a significant role in the UK economy.
keywords: foreign direct investment. Investment in a business that operates in another country
transnational corporation. A company that operates in more than one country
trade between countries or economic regions where no tariffs (tax) exist on imported or exported goods
the increased interconnectedness of the world, economically, politically and culturally
the takeover of state-run industries by private corporations
tips: Students can look into the origin of an international brand they know well and see when and how it became a TNC.

3976.name: Context of the city – site, situation and connectivity
3976.outcome: I can describe the location of Liverpool through the features of site, situation and connectivity and use these to explain Liverpool’s national, regional and global importance.
points: Liverpool is a coastal city sited on flat land in NW England and situated about 300 km NW of London.
Liverpool is connected to the rest of the world through rail, road, sea and air links.
Liverpool's importance nationally and globally is a consequence of its site, situation and connectivity.
Liverpool is nationally important for its diversity, city economy, role in the Industrial Revolution and population.
Liverpool is globally important for trade, sporting and cultural events and its link to the slave trade and migration.
keywords: a measure of how well connected (by transport and other forms of communication) a place is
the point on the ground where a settlement is built
the description of a place in relation to its human and physical surroundings
tips: Promote local locational knowledge by adapting the example of Norwich to your location. Pupils could respond to this verbally to increase oracy skills.

3977.name: Liverpool's structure and functions
3977.outcome: I can use a model of city structure to describe characteristics of different areas of Liverpool.
points: Liverpool exhibits characteristic urban forms (CBD, inner city, suburbs and rural-urban fringe).
Liverpool's structure (urban form) is determined by building age and density.
Liverpool's structure (urban form) is determined by land use and environmental quality.
keywords: commonly, the centrally-located commercial and business district in a city with a dominance of offices and shops
located between the city centre and the suburbs and often an area of high density terraced housing
the outer edge of a city where it merges with the countryside
suburbs are areas on the outskirts of a city or town where people live
tips: Bring the places in Liverpool to life by using Google Street View to take a closer look.

3978.name: Causes of migration that influence the growth and character of the city
3978.outcome: I can detail the main historic and recent, national and international migrations affecting Liverpool and describe their influences on age structure, ethnicity, housing, services and culture.
points: Liverpool's migrations can be divided over time (historical and recent) and over space (national and international).
Significant national, historical inflows have been from Ireland and Wales.
International inflows have been both historic and recent.
Liverpool's population, age structure, economy, ethnicity, housing, income, services and culture have been influenced.
Toxteth, Calderstones and Halewood have been influenced in different ways
keywords: a term that refers to the backgrounds or shared experiences of a group of people, including language, religion and beliefs
migration of people to a place
moving from one place to another with the intention of staying there
migration of people away from a place
tips: To secure the information in the first learning cycle, call out the origins of the significant migrant groups and get pupils to identify their combinations: national/international, historic/recent.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

3979.name: Inequalities in employment, services, education and health
3979.outcome: I can use data to describe deprivation across the Liverpool City Region and identify how this relates to inequalities at a variety of scales.
points: Inequalities exist in Liverpool linked to high relative levels of deprivation.
The Index of Multiple Deprivation measures relative deprivation at local authority and smaller scales.
The 6 local authorities in the Liverpool City Region are all in the top 60 most deprived in England. Knowsley ranks 2nd.
Deprivation has a cause and effect link to inequalities in services, health, employment and education.
High deprivation in Liverpool correlates with poor housing, poor health, unemployment and low educational attainment.
keywords: low standard of living caused by low income, poor health and low educational attainment, sometimes described as living in poverty
when things are not fair or equal for everyone
tips: The Index of Multiple Deprivation contains a wealth of rich data and adding comparisons to your local area could be a useful comparison. The misconception remains critical in this and the avoidance of stereotyping is paramount.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

3980.name: Liverpool CBD and inner city: challenges and opportunities from decline
3980.outcome: I can describe how 20th century decline in Liverpool’s CBD and inner city led to challenges and opportunities for the population and economy.
points: Deindustrialisation in the 20th century triggered depopulation in Liverpool's CBD and inner city.
The CBD and inner city experienced decline from the 1930s to 1990s followed by growth due to regeneration efforts.
Decline in the CBD and inner city led to challenges including dereliction, unemployment and economic recession.
21st century economic and population growth led to significant investment in the CBD.
Studentification, gentrification and e-commernce have brought challenges and opportunities.
keywords: decline in importance of the industrial sector, for example, the closure of factories
reduction in the population of an area, typically involving out-migration following deindustrialisation
the upgrading of areas (typically housing) often in the inner city, making them more desirable but often more expensive
areas with a high concentration of students, typically in sub-divided rental properties
tips: Bring inner city Liverpool during the slum clearances of the 1960s and 1970s to life by adding further images of the city at this time.

3981.name: Liverpool suburbs and rural-urban fringe: challenges and opportunities of growth
3981.outcome: I can describe how 20th and 21st century changes in Liverpool’s population and economy led to challenges and opportunities for the suburbs and rural-urban fringe.
points: Between 1931 and 2021, population in some local authorities in the Liverpool City Region grew, e.g. Halton.
The 1960s saw decentralisation from the declining CBD and inner city in favour of the suburbs and rural-urban fringe.
Developments in transport enabled decentralisation, e.g. new motorways.
Economic growth was a result of the development of retail and business parks and out of town shopping from the 1970s.
Urban sprawl in the suburbs and rural-urban fringe presents challenges, e.g. congestion and countryside destruction.
keywords: the outward movement of businesses and administrative organisations from the city centre to the outskirts or beyond
land that is protected from development and surrounds major English cities
the physical outward expansion of a city into the surrounding countryside
tips: Development of greenfield and greenbelt land sparks lots of controversey. Search for examples of conflict in your local area so pupils can relate to the challenges of developing the rural-urban fringe.

3982.name: The impacts of regeneration and rebranding on people
3982.outcome: I can explain how Liverpool has approached rebranding and regeneration since the 1980s and describe the positive and negative impacts on people.
points: Rebranding and regeneration began in Liverpool in the 1980s to reverse the decline of the city.
Significant regeneration has occurred in the centre including areas around the waterfront, RopeWalks and Lime Street.
Liverpool has been rebranded as a cultural hub due to sports, music, ethnic diversity and maritime and historical sites.
Positive impacts include greater job diversity, new leisure facilities and a higher quality urban environment.
Negative impacts include a loss of community, a persistent wealth gap and focus on tourist over local needs.
keywords: a planning and marketing strategy aimed at creating a new image of a city to encourage growth
a planning strategy aimed at addressing problems associated with decline, often involving improvements to infrastructure and encouraging new industries to an area
tips: To reinforce the importance of extended explanations, respond to brief statements with "so what?" or get pupils to bounce this phrase between themselves to encourage further explanation.

3984.name: Sustainable urban living
3984.outcome: I can describe how recycling, employment, green spaces, transport and affordable and energy-efficient homes are improving sustainability and quality of life in Liverpool.
points: Liverpool has a number of strategies involving housing such as affordability and energy efficiency.
Liverpool has low rates of recycling. To address this it is using strategies such as education campaigns.
Some employment in Liverpool is low paid. Strategies to address this include paying the real national living wage.
Green spaces have been considered in Liverpool’s city centre though the URBAN GreenUP project.
Liverpool is developing integrated transport systems to encourage use of public transport.
keywords: wellbeing of individuals or groups of people measured by criteria other than wealth such as housing, employment and environmental factors
using resources wisely so future generations can also meet their needs
tips: Urban development is happening all around the country. You could enrich this lesson by investigating local development plans and get pupils to consider how social, economic and environmental pillars are being considered to ensure sustainability and improvements to quality of life.

3985.name: Consequences of interdependence of Liverpool and accessible rural areas
3985.outcome: I can identify ways in which Liverpool and Aughton are interdependent and categorise costs and benefits for both places (social, economic or environmental).
points: Cities are interdependent with accessible rural areas. An example of this is Liverpool and the village of Aughton.
Interdependence involves flows of goods, services and labour between urban and accessible rural areas.
Interdependence leads to economic, social and environmental benefits for Aughton and Liverpool.
Interdependence leads to economic, social and environmental costs for Aughton and Liverpool.
keywords: easy to get to and from
a place, often a town or village, where people live and then travel to other places, normally a city, for work
when two or more biotic features, like plants or animals, depend or rely on each other to survive
tips: Google Street View provides good opportunities for further investigating the functions of villages like Aughton.

3986.name: Links to Liverpool: changes in a rural area
3986.outcome: I can explain the social and economic changes to Aughton as a result of its links to Liverpool.
points: Aughton is a rural village easily accesible from Liverpool.
Aughton has experienced economic and social changes as a consequence of counter-urbanisation which began in the 1950s.
Counter-urbanisation led to social changes in Aughton to do with its total population and population structure.
The demand for homes in the area has led to a pressure on housing affordability.
The affluence of the area has led to high-end restaurants and increased visitors have put pressure on the area.
keywords: the movement of people away from a city and into the countryside, which may lead to a reduction in the city's population
to do with money and wealth
to do with people individually or as a community
tips: Compare Aughton to a village which has experienced signficiant decline in services due to its proximity to a city. A local example to your context would support understanding and could be used as an opportunity for primary or secondary research.

3987.name: Challenges of living in rural areas
