3987.outcome: I can use knowledge about the area of Eden to explain the challenges facing the area and their impact on the young and the elderly.
points: Eden is a very rural district within the rural county of Cumbria.
Eden has the highest percentage of green space and lowest population density of any district in England.
Eden ranks 186 on the Index of Multiple Deprivation. This masks areas of high deprivation such as barriers to services.
Eden faces four challenges: housing, provision of education and healthcare and decline in primary employment.
The young and elderly are more likely to be affected by challenges due to dependency on parents or the state for income.
keywords: reduction in the population of an area, typically involving out-migration following deindustrialisation
jobs involving the extraction of raw materials including farming, fishing and mining
wellbeing of individuals or groups of people measured by criteria other than wealth such as housing, employment and environmental factors
tips: Explore the Index of Multiple Deprivation in greater detail by looking into what measures are used to calculate the rank of each of the indicators.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

3988.name: Economic opportunities and environmental impacts in rural areas
3988.outcome: I can identify ways in which rural areas generate income through tourism projects and rural diversification, and recognise the environmental impacts of these opportunities.
points: Economic challenges from the decline in farming have led to new economic opportunities in rural areas.
Tourism projects and rural diversification support the local multiplier effect which strengthens the local economy.
An example of a tourism project in Eden is the Herdwick Stones and of rural diversification, Waterside House.
Economic opportunities have environmental impacts which can be positive and negative.
keywords: increase the spread of commercial activities, for example, by creating new enterprises on a farm such as a shop or a B&B
planned initiative designed to attract tourists such as new attractions, improvements to infrastructure, promotion of sustainable tourism and the development of tourism-related businesses
tips: Add a local component to this by finding an example of a local development which had some arguments around environmental impact within it. Or set up conflict more generally with a debate around the following motion: "This House would prioritise environmental protection over economic growth".

1197.name: Formulating an enquiry question
1197.outcome: I can use research frameworks to create good enquiry questions.
points: An enquiry question helps geographers to learn more about the world when they do fieldwork.
A good enquiry question guides the geographer through the enquiry process, is linked to place and uses precise language.
Enquiry questions come from different ways of conducting fieldwork known as research frameworks.
keywords: An enquiry is an investigation to find out more about something.
an idea, for example an idea about an outcome of an experiment, based on observations and understanding
the type of geographical research on which the enquiry will focus
tips: You may wish to highlight how many geographical facts and concepts students have already experienced have come about because geographers of the past used geographical enquiry questions. Top geographers working in universities today continue to use enquiry questions to direct their research.

guidance.label: Risk assessment required - outdoor learning
guidance.description: Fieldwork.

4019.name: Collecting human geographical data
4019.outcome: I can use questionnaires and surveys to collect a variety of human geographical data.
points: Geographers can collect lots of different types of data during fieldwork.
Questionnaires can be used to measure people's opinions.
Specific surveys can be used to measure activity in, and the quality of, a settlement.
keywords: data that is collected in person during fieldwork
A test in which the result is based on an observation.
Refers to a measurement of quantity. A numerical value.
data that has previously been collected by someone, usually unknown to the person doing the fieldwork
tips: If students design their own questionnaire, they should test it on peers and family first. This is known as a pilot study. Students can then edit their questionnaire to remove or change any questions that are found to be ambiguous.

guidance.label: Risk assessment required - outdoor learning
guidance.description: Fieldwork.

4020.name: Collecting physical geographical data
4020.outcome: I can use sampling strategies to help me measure the shape and characteristics of a landscape.
points: Geographers use different techniques to sample data during fieldwork.
There are a variety of ways that we can measure the morphology (shape) of the land.
There are a variety of ways that we can measure the characteristics of the land.
keywords: Inclination or prejudice for or against one person or group, especially in a way considered to be unfair.
the measurement of a sound wave at a point in time
the number of individual pieces of data that are studied in a geographical enquiry
the process of creating and using a sample
an imaginary line along which samples of data are collected
tips: Different sampling strategies can be demonstrated by using colourful buttons. Students can try to create random, systematic and stratified samples of the buttons based on their colours and size.

guidance.label: Risk assessment required - outdoor learning
guidance.description: Fieldwork.

4021.name: Presenting geographical data
4021.outcome: I can present quantitative and qualitative data and use maps to present spatial data.
points: Quantitative data can be presented using a variety of graphs and charts.
Qualitative data can be presented using a variety of text based graphics.
Geographers frequently use maps to show how data varies spatially.
keywords: data that sits on a continuum from low to high values
data that can be arranged into exclusive categories
data that is assigned to a specific location
tips: Using geography textbooks, ask students to identify by name some of the data presentation techniques they can see. Some students may even be able to suggest data presentation methods for data that is given in its raw form in tables.

4022.name: Analysing geographical data
4022.outcome: I can analyse geographical data and use my findings to create different types of conclusions.
points: Quantitative data can be analysed using the GRaDE framework and simple statistical tests.
Qualitative data can be analysed through coding and discourse analysis.
Geographical conclusions are made through careful analysis of all the data geographers have collected.
keywords: concluding what one believes to be true by basing one's ideas on some, but not all, of the evidence collected
a relationship or pattern between two or more variables
evidence collected through direct observation and experience rather than through logical thinking
tips: Students can think about data evidence along a sliding scale, with ‘fact’ at one end, ‘assumption’ in the centre and ‘inconclusive’ at the other end. As they look at different types of data they can suggest where on the scale they should place their evidence if they wish to make a conclusion.

4023.name: Evaluating geographical enquiries
4023.outcome: I can evaluate the effectiveness of the different stages of a geographical enquiry.
points: There are many stages of a geographical enquiry that can be evaluated.
Conclusions should be evaluated to show how reliable and valid the data is.
Geographical research is often evaluated to see how ethically and morally considerate it is.
keywords: a value within the data set that does not appear to follow the general pattern or trend
not influenced by personal feelings or opinions when representing facts
reliable is another word for trustworthy and accurate
describes something that's based on a person's opinions, individual experiences, and biased influences
valid data is data that allows the geographer to answer their enquiry question successfully
tips: Give students a short opinion editorial newspaper article that covers a geographical idea. They can then highlight objective and subjective data and make suggestions on how the ideas could be better researched.

4024.name: Coastal fieldwork
4024.outcome: I can collect primary and secondary data at the coast to help me answer a geographical enquiry question.
points: There are many geographical enquiry questions that you can investigate at the coast.
Data collection techniques at the coast look at beach and wave morphology and coastal management.
Secondary data can provide contextual information about particular coastlines and comparable data.
keywords: a hand-held device used to measure the gradient of a slope
the physical shape and size of a beach, a cliff, waves and beach sediment
A quadrat is a square frame used to sample populations of plants or slow-moving animals.
a metal pole (traditionally red and white striped) that is used to mark a point in a survey
an imaginary line along which samples of data are collected
tips: It is important to remind students that beaches and waves change their size and shape constantly. This means that any data collected is a representation of these features at that particular time rather than how they appear every day.

guidance.label: Risk assessment required - outdoor learning
guidance.description: Fieldwork.

4026.name: River fieldwork
4026.outcome: I can collect primary and secondary data in a river environment to help me answer a geographical question.
points: There are many geographical enquiry questions that you can investigate along the course of a river.
Data collection methods in a river landscape can examine flood management and a river's agreement to the Bradshaw model.
Secondary data can provide contextual information about particular rivers and comparable data.
keywords: the physical size and shape of a river channel, including the sediment (bedload) it carries
strategies used to prevent a river over topping its banks following a period of intense rainfall
a theory about how river processes change from source to mouth
tips: River fieldwork is an excellent opportunity for students to develop teamwork and leadership skills. Multiple variables have to be measured using different pieces of equipment so roles can easily be rotated between group members.

guidance.label: Risk assessment required - outdoor learning
guidance.description: Fieldwork.

4027.name: Urban fieldwork
4027.outcome: I can collect primary and secondary data in an urban area to help me answer a geographical enquiry question.
points: There are many geographical enquiry questions that you can investigate in urban areas such as towns and cities.
Data collection techniques in an urban area can investigate quality of life, sustainability and regeneration.
Secondary data can provide contextual information about urban populations and spaces and how these have changed.
keywords: a score scale that uses both positive and negative values
a variable which indirectly suggests that another variable may be true
a planning strategy aimed at addressing problems associated with decline, often involving improvements to infrastructure and encouraging new industries to an area
tips: Cities can be thought of as dynamic beings with multiple, complex variables interacting together at once. Students need to recognise that urban spaces are meeting points of lots of areas in geography. Students should understand the links between these topics before they start some urban fieldwork.

guidance.label: Risk assessment required - outdoor learning
guidance.description: Fieldwork.

4028.name: Rural fieldwork
4028.outcome: I can collect primary and secondary data in a rural area to help me answer a geographical enquiry question.
points: There are many geographical enquiry questions that you can investigate in rural areas.
Data collection techniques in a rural area can investigate inequality, service provision and lived experience.
Secondary data can provide contextual information about rural populations and spaces and how they have changed.
keywords: a person or animal in a story
the everyday, personal experience that someone has of living in a place
anyone who has an interest in or is affected by a decision or issue
tips: The slower pace of life that is often witnessed in rural areas can make some aspects of data collection challenging. For example, questionnaires may have to be redesigned to take into account that there may be fewer members of the public on the street to ask.

guidance.label: Risk assessment required - outdoor learning
guidance.description: Fieldwork.

7613.name: Using 3D GIS for physical geography fieldwork
7613.outcome: I can use 3D GIS to visualise and analyse physical geography fieldwork data.
points: 3D GIS can be used to visualise and configure primary georeferenced data attributes from physical geography fieldwork.
3D GIS visualisations can use attributes including bearing data to create proportional, orientated symbols.
3D GIS visualisations can be time-enabled using temporal data attributes to enhance the visualisation.
3D GIS visualisations of secondary data attributes such as flood risk data can be used to support fieldwork enquiry.
keywords: A bearing is an angle measured in degrees from North in the clockwise direction and written with three figures.
a GIS tool which visualises changes in height above or below sea level along a transect line
properties or characteristics of an entity
information which has been tied to a particular location (geolocated), using an agreed system such as latitude and longitude
tips: No matter what your level of experience is with GIS, go through all the steps yourself first until you feel confident and fluent. Don't worry if you make a mistake, everybody does, even experienced practitioners!

7596.name: Using GIS for human geography fieldwork
7596.outcome: I can use GIS to visualise and analyse human geography fieldwork data.
points: GIS can be used to visualise and configure primary georeferenced data attributes from human geography fieldwork.
GIS visualisations can use attributes including bearing data to create proportional, orientated symbols.
GIS visualisations can be time-enabled using temporal data attributes to enhance the visualisation.
GIS visualisations of secondary data such as government data about deprivation can be used to support fieldwork enquiry.
keywords: A bearing is an angle measured in degrees from North in the clockwise direction and written with three figures.
properties or characteristics of an entity
information which has been tied to a particular location (geolocated), using an agreed system such as latitude and longitude
tips: No matter what your level of experience is with GIS, go through all the steps yourself first until you feel confident and fluent. Don't worry if you make a mistake, everybody does, even experienced practitioners!

guidance.label: Risk assessment required - outdoor learning
guidance.description: Fieldwork.

3989.name: Defining development
3989.outcome: I can define quality of life and development and understand how their definitions have changed over time.
points: Quality of life has multiple aspects, some of which are subjective such as life satisfaction.
Development is a contested term often linked to a limited (Eurocentric), outdated view of economic progress.
Its definition has broadened over time to include human welfare, social and environmental justice.
The process of development is neither inevitable nor apolitical.
keywords: the human-made spaces around us that create our local environment
improving and building on design ideas to make them better
a subjective measure of happiness used to compare countries
wellbeing of individuals or groups of people measured by criteria other than wealth such as housing, employment and environmental factors
tips: You might try to highlight the way in which our understanding of the way quality of life varies around the world is coloured by our own experiences and the Eurocentric nature of our culture. Some aspects of quality of life are subjective and difficult to interrogate at a distance.

7130.name: Measuring development
7130.outcome: I can explain the different ways in which social and economic development is measured, and the limitations of individual economic and social measures used.
points: There are global variations in economic development and quality of life.
There are a range of different measures of level of development.
There are limitations of both economic and social measures.
keywords: a UN measure of development calculated using education, life expectancy and income data
improving and building on design ideas to make them better
a measure of goods and services produced by a country, including income earned abroad; may be divided by the total population to give ‘GNI per head’
the average number of years a person is expected to live
tips: Skills: There is an opportunity to reinforce understanding of averages (mean, mode, median) and categorisation of data as quantitative or qualitative.

3990.name: Development and demography
3990.outcome: I can explain the links between levels of development and demography.
points: Countries at different levels of development have differences in their demographic characteristics.
The different demographic characteristics include birth rate or fertility rate, death rate and population structure.
A population pyramid enables us to compare population structure of different countries.
The economic impact of different population structures may be understaod by calculating the dependency ratio.
There are links between the stages of the Demographic Transition Model and the level of development.
keywords: the number of births for every 1000 people in a population per year
a theoretical model that suggests how birth rate, death rate and total population change over time
the study of population: its size, composition and change over time
the difference between the birth rate and the death rate of a population; occurs when the birth rate is higher than the death rate
an age-sex graph used to present the structure of a population (that may resemble a pyramid)
tips: This topic provides the opportunity for students to practise interpreting bar graphs and line graphs; and link the data to the 'story' of a country's development. You may wish to set a research task using online resources.

3991.name: Causes of global inequalities
3991.outcome: I can explain a range of causes of global inequality, including physical, historical, economic and political causes.
points: There are global inequalities in development.
There are physical/environmental causes of global inequality.
There are economic causes of global inequality.
There are historical/political causes of inequality.
keywords: the occupation, management and control of one country by another, often involving exploitation of its people and resources
the way in which nations interact with and regard each other, in relation to politics, economics and culture
being surrounded by land of other countries, having no coast
the indirect control of one country by another via economic power or cultural influence
the shape and height of the land
tips: Find out about the content of key stage 3 history in your school. To what extent is colonialism and the impact of the British Empire taught?

3992.name: Consequences of global inequalities
3992.outcome: I can explain what the consequences of global inequalities are.
points: There are consequences of global inequality.
Uneven development can result in disparities in wealth, health and education.
Uneven development can result in different types of international migration.
keywords: a person who moves to another country with better working or living conditions
an illness that may be passed from one person to another
poverty is the state of being extremely poor
someone who has successfully sought asylum in another country and is henceforth protected by international law
payments sent home by migrants to members of their family or community
tips: There are several opportunities to reinforce locational knowledge in this lesson. Make use of atlases or online map resources.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

3996.name: Strategies to reduce the development gap: industry and investment
3996.outcome: I can explain how industry and investment strategies reduce the global development gap.
points: Various strategies exist to reduce the development gap.
The development of manufacturing industries can help to reduce the gap.
The development of services industries, including tourism, can contribute to economic development.
Foreign direct investment in infrastructure can promote economic growth.
Microfinance loans allow people to set up small businesses and become self-sufficient.
keywords: the widening difference in standards of living and wellbeing between the world’s richest and poorest countries
the secondary economic sector, involving making goods from raw materials or other manufactured products (for example motor vehicles)
the provision of small-scale loans given to people in LICs to help them start a small business
the tertiary economic sector, which includes tourism, banking, education and health
tips: There are further opportunities to explore the strategies of industrial development and investment: in this unit; and within the case study of a newly emerging economy.

7509.name: Strategies to reduce the development gap: Fairtrade, debt relief and aid
7509.outcome: I can explain how Fairtrade, debt relief, aid and intermediate technology can reduce the global development gap.
points: Various strategies exist to reduce the development gap.
The global system of trade is not free or fair as trade blocs, tariffs and quotas hamper the flow of goods.
The Fairtrade movement aims to address some of the problems of the global trade system by supporting producers in LICs.
Debt relief enables the government in LICs to invest in public services and support the poorest.
International aid can support the development of essential infrastructure via the use of intermediate technology.
keywords: an organisation dedicated to improving the income and lives of farmers in lower income countries by making trade fairer
help given by a group or country to support development in another country or for disaster relief
when debt is cancelled or reduced
technology suited to the needs, skills, knowledge and wealth of local people in the environment in which they live
Trade is the exchange of goods, commodities and services.
tips: There is a further opportunity to explore the benefits of intermediate technology in the Global pattern of resources unit, when teaching about an example of a local food, water or energy scheme.

3997.name: Example of how tourism can reduce the development gap
3997.outcome: I can explain how the growth in tourism has helped to reduce the development gap in Bali as well as concerns about overtourism.
points: Bali is an island province in Indonesia (an NEE) where international tourism has developed since the 1960s.
Tourism provides 60 per cent of Bali’s income, with many new jobs created.
Life expectancy in Bali is higher than average for Indonesia; Bali ranks fifth of 38 provinces for human development.
Tourism has some negative impacts, including eroding local culture, pollution and reduced water supplies.
The government plans to develop five new destinations elsewhere to address concerns about ‘overtourism’ in Bali.
keywords: An attraction is a force that acts to pull one object towards another.
the shared ideas, customs, and art of a group of people
all the visible features of an area of land, often considered in terms of their visual appeal
when too many people visit a place, so that it is spoiled and life becomes difficult for people who live there
presence of harmful substances in the environment, such as in the air, water or soil, which can damage ecosystems and human health
tips: Go online to find images of Bali's tourist attractions to help students picture this distant place. Using 'time hop' photography online can also be a great way to help students understand the pace of change.

6763.name: Using GIS maps to analyse links between inequality and migration
6763.outcome: I can use GIS maps to analyse links between inequality and migration.
points: GIS maps can be used to visualise and analyse inequalities in measures of development such as HDI.
Benchmarks are often used to compare inequalities in measures of development such as HDI.
GIS visualisations can be used to support analysis of reasons for migration.
GIS can be used to visualise and analyse migration trends over time, supported by configured pop-ups.
keywords: the Human Development Index (HDI) is a composite measure of development using income, life expectancy and education, ranging between 0 and 1
a starting point or measurement you can compare to later
in GIS, a read-only display of attribute information (e.g. text, images, charts) often linked to a location
tips: The GIS knowledge and skills can be difficult at first and most errors will happen because students skip an important step. It's therefore important to rehearse the steps first yourself so that you can confidently demonstrate the steps as in the video. Encourage peer support, as appropriate.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

3999.name: Location and importance of Indonesia
3999.outcome: I can describe Indonesia's location and explain why it is important in its region and globally.
points: Indonesia is the largest country in Southeast Asia and is an archipelago consisting of over 17 000 islands.
Indonesia is important regionally and globally.
Indonesia is placed within a wider political, social, cultural and environmental context.
keywords: the Association of Southeast Asian Nations is a group of 10 nations who cooperate on trade and security with the aim of boosting their economic, social and cultural development
Context concerns the circumstances in which a text was written; context helps us to understand the writer’s intentions further.
tips: The ASEAN website includes information about ASEAN's aims and history, as well as the flags of its members (which some students may enjoy identifying), and a video of the ASEAN anthem which could be an interesting resource to use in starting the lesson.

4000.name: Changing industrial structure of Indonesia
4000.outcome: I can explain how Indonesia's economic sectors have changed since 1990.
points: Indonesia has experienced a changing industrial structure.
In Indonesia, the balance between different sectors of the economy has changed.
Manufacturing industry can stimulate economic development.
keywords: the part of an economy that involves using natural resources directly from the land or sea, for example, agriculture, fishing, forestry and mining
the part of an economy that involves manufacturing goods from raw materials or other manufactured goods, for example factory work, construction and food processing
the part of an economy that provides services to people and businesses rather than goods, for example teachers, doctors, shop workers and delivery drivers
tips: Students could use the Esri World Imagery Wayback app to compare land use and economic activity in Indonesia over the last decade. Land reclamation in Jakarta Bay is a good example.

4001.name: TNCs in Indonesia
4001.outcome: I can describe the role of TNCs in Indonesia's development and some of the advantages and disadvantages they bring to the country.
points: TNCs have boosted economic growth in Indonesia.
TNCs can bring advantages to Indonesia.
TNCs can bring disadvantages to Indonesia.
keywords: (FDI) foreign countries invest in businesses or industries in another country, often by setting up or buying local companies
TNCS are large companies that operate in several countries; they often have headquarters in one country and factories or offices in others
tips: Students could use Google Street View in urban centres in Indonesia to identify makes (brand) of cars on the streets, and see if it is true that Japanese makes dominate. Looking at the availability of Street View on different islands could be a way of introducing core and periphery.

4002.name: International aid in Indonesia
4002.outcome: I can describe different types of international aid and assess their impacts on Indonesia.
points: There are different types of international aid.
Indonesia receives different types of international aid.
Receiving international aid has impacts on Indonesia.
keywords: a non-profit, voluntary group of citizens who work on a local, national or international level to achieve an aim; they are not controlled by the Government, but will often work closely with it
help given by a group or country to support development in another country or for disaster relief
aid given directly from one country to another for specific projects
aid from multiple countries or international organisations, like the UN or World Bank, for development
tips: Students could research aid provided to Indonesia following recent earthquakes by visiting the websites of organisations such as the Disasters Emergency Committee, Red Crescent, Red Cross, and ActionAid.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
guidance.description: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

4003.name: Environmental impacts of economic development in Indonesia
4003.outcome: I can explain how economic development has led to air, water and land pollution and deforestation in Indonesia.
points: Economic development in Indonesia has had environmental impacts.
Environmental impacts in Indonesia include air, water and land pollution.
keywords: a long-term change in Earth’s climate patterns
An ecosystem is made up of all the living organisms in a place, interacting with each other and their non-living surroundings.
presence of harmful substances in the environment, such as in the air, water or soil, which can damage ecosystems and human health
tips: The Mongabay website provides detailed information about wildfires in Indonesia which students could investigate to add further details to their notes on environmental impacts.

4011.name: Causes of economic change
4011.outcome: I can describe the main causes of economic change in the UK.
points: There have been major changes in the economy of the UK.
De-industrialisation and the decline of traditional industrial base have caused economic change in the UK.
Globalisation has caused economic change in the UK.
Government policies have caused economic change in the UK.
keywords: the loss of industry from an area
the increased interconnectedness of the world, economically, politically and culturally
the takeover of state-run industries by private corporations
labour-intensive industries such as coal mining, steel and textile production and ship building
tips: It can be difficult for students to understand what life was like in areas dominated by traditional industries. Using short clips from films can help them to see the dependence families had on particular industries.

4012.name: The post-industrial economy
4012.outcome: I can describe the features of a post-industrial economy.
points: The UK is moving towards a post-industrial economy.
The development of information technology has contributed to a post-industrial economy in the UK.
The growth of service industries, finance and research has contributed to a post-industrial economy in the UK.
Science and business parks have contributed to a post-industrial economy in the UK.
keywords: money that people earn that is left over after they have paid their bills is called disposable income
a tertiary sector industry that deals with banking, investments, pensions and insurance
term used to describe a city after it has changed from being centre of manufacturing to a place where most people work in services
an area of land dedicated to businesses specialising in science and technology
tips: Look at maps, satellite images and street views of Cambridge Science Park to show students what the modern face of industry looks like.

4013.name: Impacts of industry on the physical environment
4013.outcome: I can describe how industry can both negatively and positively affect the physical environment.
points: Industrial development can have negative impacts on the environment.
Newer industries can be more sustainable.
The Nissan plant in Sunderland illustrates how modern industrial development can be environmentally sustainable.
keywords: the process by which bacteria are transferred from one area to another
being able to produce the same level of output but through the use of less energy
development that meets the needs of people today without damaging the environment or reducing resources for future generations
tips: Hold a debate amongst students as to whether the manufacturing of electric cars is environmentally sustainable.

4014.name: Social and economic changes in the rural landscape
4014.outcome: I can assess the impacts of rural population growth and decline.
points: The rural landscape in the UK has experienced social and economic change.
The rural landscape in South Cambridgeshire has experienced social and economic changes due to population growth.
The rural landscape in Gwynedd has experienced social and economic changes due to population decline.
keywords: someone who lives a distance from where they work and has to regularly travel between the two locations
the movement of people away from a city and into the countryside, which may lead to a reduction in the city's population
land that is protected from development and surrounds major English cities
the difference between the birth rate and the death rate of a population; occurs when the birth rate is higher than the death rate
tips: Discussing population growth and decline provides opportunities for students to practise calculating percentage increase and decrease from raw data.

4016.name: Improvements and new developments in transport
4016.outcome: I can analyse the impacts and potential impacts of new developments in transport infrastructure.
points: There have been improvements in the UK's transport infrastructure.
There have been improvements in road and rail infrastructure in the UK.
There have been improvements in port and airport capacity in the UK.
keywords: compensation is something given to make up for loss or harm
the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
transatlantic means crossing the Atlantic Ocean
tips: It is hard to imagine the scale of Liverpool2. Examine a satellite image of the site from which students can see individual containers and gain a better understanding of its size.

4017.name: The north-south divide
4017.outcome: I can evaluate strategies that attempt to resolve regional differences in the UK.
points: Regional differences exist in the UK between the north and the south.
Social and economic indicators can be used to identify a north-south divide in the UK.
There are strategies for resolving regional differences.
keywords: the group of muscles in the abdomen, lower back, hips and pelvis that provide stability, strength and control for movements
the outer edges or boundary of something
differences in the standard of living and wealth between two areas of the same country
tips: Students can look at current ONS data for areas in the north and south and evaluate if these have been successful in reducing regional inequality.

4018.name: The place of the UK in the wider world
4018.outcome: I can compare the UK's links with the wider world.
points: The UK has significant links with the wider world.
The UK has links to the wider world through trade, culture, transport and electronic communications.
The UK has economic and political links with the EU and the Commonwealth.
keywords: a voluntary association of 56 independent and equal countries, many of which were formerly colonised as part of the British Empire
the connections between different components of the environment, where each component depends on or influences the others
the movement of people from one country to another
tips: Students can make a list of their five favourites from different categories such as music artists, items of clothing, or foods and map where these things originate from to see how their lives link to other places.

4064.name: The importance of food, water and energy for human development
4064.outcome: I can explain the significance of food, water and energy to well-being and describe global inequalities in supply and consumption of these resources.
points: Food, water and energy affect economic and social well-being and are fundamental to human development.
There are global inequalities in the supply and consumption of: food, water and energy resources.
Around 10% of people worldwide face hunger; between 740-780 million people.
There is overlap between regions in which many face hunger and those in which many lack safe water and/or electricity.
Supply (or lack of resources) limits consumption in some locations, as does poverty.
keywords: materials available in the environment (such as water, food and wood) that support our wants and needs
systems for removing human waste and managing rubbish and dirty water to prevent the spread of disease
having an intake of energy and/or nutrients below what is needed
tips: There will be opportunities to reinforce key ideas about inequality and resource management in later lessons looking at global resources; choose between food, water and energy for your students key focus.

4065.name: Food resources in the UK
4065.outcome: I can explain how changing demand for food in the UK creates opportunities and challenges.
points: Changing demand for food in the UK creates opportunities and challenges.
There is growing demand for high-value food exports from LICs, seasonal food (all-year) and organic produce.
There is a move towards local food sourcing to reduce carbon footprints.
There is a trend towards agribusiness.
keywords: an intensive farming system often involving high capital costs to maximise profits
the total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases released into the atmosphere by an individual, product, process, country, etc
Food miles are the distance between the place where food is grown or made and the place where it is eaten.
food grown without the use of artificial chemicals, such as fertiliser and pesticide
tips: Your students' understanding of agribusiness and the impacts of different methods of food production on the environment will be further developed, if you do the food option within the global resources topic. If not, this is a key lesson for help students understand their role as consumers.

4066.name: Water resources in the UK
4066.outcome: I can explain how changing demand for water in the UK creates opportunities and challenges.
points: Changing demand and provision of water in the UK creates opportunities and challanges.
Demand for water is changing and there are issues matching supply to demand.
There is a need for water transfers within the UK to maintain supplies.
There are various causes of water pollution including agricultural runoff, industrial discharges and sewage spills.
Pollution management is needed to maintain water quality and protect the environment.
keywords: whether what is in a supply of water (e.g. its chemical or biological contents) make it suitable for a particular kind of use
when the demand for water exceeds the available amount during a certain period or when poor quality restricts its use
the movement of water (through pipes or via canals or rivers) from areas of water surplus to areas of water deficit
tips: If you plan to study the water lessons, within the Global pattern of resources topic, you will have opportunites to reinforce the impact of water quality on water security. If not, this is the opportunity to discuss the link water quality and the environment with your future domestic consumers.

4067.name: Energy resources in the UK
4067.outcome: I can discuss opportunities and challenges resulting from the UK's changing energy mix.
points: Changing demand and provision of energy in the UK creates opportunities and challanges.
The energy mix in the UK is changing.
There are reduced domestic supplies of coal, gas and oil.
There are economic and environmental issues associated with energy exploitation.
keywords: volume of carbon produced contributing to global warming
the combination of different energy sources used by a country or a region. The energy mix can change over time
natural sources of energy that will run out because they cannot be reproduced, such as fossil fuels (coal, oil and natural gas) and nuclear power (uranium)
natural sources of energy that will never run out, such as wind, water and solar energy
tips: GIS offers excellent opportunities to identify and assess (e.g. measure change over time) environmental impacts of energy extraction and generation in the UK landscape.

4077.name: Global patterns of energy consumption and supply
4077.outcome: I can interpret patterns in global energy security and describe the impacts of energy insecurity on people and economies.
points: Demand for energy resources is rising globally.
Globally, there are areas of surplus (security) and deficit (insecurity).
Impacts of energy insecurity include exploration in sensitive areas, economic and environmental costs.
keywords: the amount of something that is bought and used
a measure of how much of something people want to buy
the uninterrupted availability of energy sources at an affordable price
the amount of something that is available to buy
tips: The Our World in Data website has a wide range of excellent maps and other resources related to energy consumption and production.

4079.name: Energy consumption and supply
4079.outcome: I can explain reasons for increasing energy consumption and factors that affect energy supply.
points: Energy consumption is increasing due to economic development and technology.
Energy consumption is increasing due to population increase.
Physical, technological, economic and political factors affect energy supply.
keywords: how easy it is for people to take part in an activity, especially if there are barriers
the growth of a country’s wealth, leading to better jobs, higher incomes and improved living standards
a known amount of oil or gas that can be taken from underground and used
tips: Ofgem publishes typical energy usage figures with descriptions of the user groups which can be useful for developing students' understanding of factors that increase energy consumption.

4080.name: Strategies to increase energy supply
4080.outcome: I can assess strategies used to increase energy supply and use an example to support my answer.
points: Different strategies can be used to increase energy supply.
Strategies to increase energy supply include developing renewable and non-renewable sources of energy.
The USA is developing new sources of oil and gas in Alaska, which has advantages and disadvantages.
keywords: Dry mass of a living organism.
volume of carbon produced contributing to global warming
the process of using moving water to generate electricity: also known as hydroelectric power (HEP)
tips: Understanding nuclear power and biomass is sometimes challenging for students: YouTube videos about the process of generating nuclear power (and reprocessing spent nuclear fuel), and of turning biofuels into energy sources work well in consolidating understanding here.

4081.name: Sustainable use of energy
4081.outcome: I can explain how energy efficiency and energy conservation can reduce the demand for energy, and use an example to discuss a local renewable energy scheme in Togo, an LIC.
points: Many countries are taking action to use energy more sustainably.
More sustainable energy use includes energy conservation and energy efficiency.
Togo provides examples of local renewable energy schemes using solar power.
keywords: the total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases released into the atmosphere by an individual, product, process, country, etc
protection and management of natural resources to prevent damage and maintain biodiversity
working in an organised way that doesn't waste time and resources
tips: A video of the PRAVOST rural electrification project is available on Vimeo at https://vimeo.com/1036792638: it is in French with English subtitles.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

4073.name: Global patterns of water security
4073.outcome: I can describe the inequalities in global water security and the impacts of water insecurity on people and economies.
points: Globally, there are areas of surplus (security) and deficit (insecurity), and inequalities in access to water.
Water insecurity has impacts on people when they use polluted water or contract waterborne diseases.
Water insecurity has impacts on the economy including food production and industrial output.
There is potential for conflict where demand exceeds supply.
keywords: dispute between regions or countries about the distribution and use of freshwater
when water availability is not enought to ensure the population of an area enjoys good health and earnings; caused by lack of suppy or poor water quality
the reliable availability of an acceptable quantity and quality of water for health, livelihoods and agricultural or industrial production
disease transmitted in contaminated water; contracted by bathing, washing, drinking or the consumption of infected food, e.g. cholera
tips: There are lots of links between this lesson and the next (Water resources: demand and supply) meaning there will be opportunities to reinforce new terminology.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

4074.name: Water resources: demand and supply
4074.outcome: I can explain reasons for the increasing demand for water and factors that affect water supply.
points: Globally, water consumption is rising.
Water consumption is increasing due to economic development.
Water consumption is increasing due to population increase.
There are physical factors that affect water availability, such as climate and geology.
Human factors affecting water availability include pollution, over-abstraction, limited infrastructure and poverty.
keywords: the extraction of water from a water source, such as a river or aquifer
occurs when the extraction exceeds recharge by precipitation
poverty is the state of being extremely poor
tips: When considering factors that affect availability of water, there are opportunities to drill down to a local scale and consider contrasts within countries. This return to a more concrete, experienced scale may be welcomed by students after the 'global-scale' questions of the first learning cycle.

4075.name: Strategies to increase water supply
4075.outcome: I can describe different strategies used to increase water supply and outline the advantages and disadvantages of California's water project.
points: Different strategies can be used to increase water supply.
Strategies to increase water supply include diverting supplies, increasing storage and desalination
The California State water project is a large-scale water transfer scheme with advantages and disadvantages.
keywords: the process of removing salt from seawater to make it suitable for drinking and irrigation
the movement of water (through pipes or via canals or rivers) from areas of water surplus to areas of water deficit
tips: ArcGIS Online provides a wide array of useful layers related to water supply, including for example location of desalination plants in Saudi Arabia.

4076.name: Sustainable use of water resources
4076.outcome: I can explain how sustainable strategies can increase water supply while protecting the environment for future generations, and explain how the Turkana water scheme in Kenya is sustainable.
points: Sustainable strategies to increase water supply include water conservation, groundwater management and recycling.
The Turkana County water project, in Kenya, is an example of a local scheme to increase sustainable water supplies.
Groundwater management and improved water access has helped the community to adapt to the impacts of climate change.
keywords: water from sinks, showers and washing machines that, whilst not suitable for drinking, can be used for other purposes
regulation and control of water levels, pollution, ownership and use of groundwater
development that meets the needs of people today without damaging the environment or reducing resources for future generations
reducing waste, such as through leakages, and unnecessary use e.g. using drinking water to flush toilets
tips: It may be possible for students to assess the water conservation methods used in your school or college and make suggestions for improvements.

4069.name: Global patterns of food security
4069.outcome: I can describe inequalities in global food security and explain the impacts of food insecurity on people, economies and the environment.
points: Globally, there are areas of food surplus (security) and food deficit (insecurity).
There are global inequalities in food supply and calorie intake.
30% of the global population is affected by moderate or severe food insecurity.
Impacts of food insecurity include famine, undernutrition, soil erosion, rising prices and social unrest.
keywords: a famine is a situation in which there is not enough food for a great number of people, causing illness and death, or a particular period when this happens
being without reliable access to sufficient, affordable, nutritious food
when people lack secure access to sufficient amounts of safe and nutritious food for normal growth and development and an active and healthy life
having an intake of energy and/or nutrients below what is needed
tips: Dollar Street is particularly useful for this lesson about global patterns and the next which builds on ideas about how and why consumption is linked to access (specifically income). Allowing students time (with technology) to explore the site is invaluable: a picture paints a thousand words.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

4070.name: Food resources: demand and supply
4070.outcome: I can explain the reasons for increasing demand for food and factors that affect food supply.
points: The global demand for food is rising.
Food consumption is increasng due to economic development.
Food consumption is increasing due to population increase.
Factors affecting food supply include climate, technology, pests and disease, water stress, conflict and poverty.
keywords: a long period of time with little or no rainfall, leading to a shortage of water
a method of supplying water to crops to help them grow
poverty is the state of being extremely poor
when the demand for water exceeds the available amount during a certain period or when poor quality restricts its use
tips: If you have studied the (optional) hot deserts topic you might remind students about the way drought and poverty lead to soil erosion and desertification, affecting food supplies.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

4071.name: Strategies to increase food supply
4071.outcome: I can describe different strategies used to increase food supply and outline the advantages and disadvantages of Kenya's Mwea irrigation scheme.
points: Different strategies can be used to increase food supply.
Strategies to increase food supplies include irrigation, aeroponics and hydroponics.
Biotechnology has a role, for example, producing genetically-modified crops that are drought-resistant.
A new green revolution is needed to increase the production of smaller farms without harming the environment.
Mwea Irrigation Scheme, Kenya, is a large-scale agricultural development with advantages and disadvantages.
keywords: growing plants in a mist environment without the use of soil
technology suited to the needs, skills, knowledge and wealth of local people in the environment in which they live
use of technology to modify organic products or processes, for example, genetically-engineering crops
growing plants using mineral nutrient solutions in water and without soil
approach to boosting food production that seeks to benefit poor farmers bypassed by the original green revolution and conserve the environment
tips: This lesson builds on students' understanding of agribusiness introduced in the lesson about food resources in the UK.

4072.name: Sustainable food production
4072.outcome: I can explain how sustainable strategies can increase food supply while protecting the environment for future generations, and use a local-scale example.
points: There is a move towards sustainable strategies to increase food supply.
Sustainable strategies to increase food supply include organic farming, seasonal food consumption and reduced waste.
Around nine per cent of people in Bangladesh live in extreme poverty, without enough food to eat.
Sandbar-cropping in Rangpur region is a local-scale example of how sustainable supplies of food can be increased.
keywords: when food is grown without the use of artificial chemicals, such as fertiliser and pesticide
a system of farming based upon or directly using patterns and features observed in natural ecosystems, such as increased biodiversity and intercropping
when food is produced in ways that avoid damaging natural resources, provide social benefits and contribute to local economies
the growing of crops and the raising of animals in towns and cities; includes processing and distributing food, as well as collecting and reusing food waste
tips: Encourage pupils to investigate local initiatives that promote sustainable food production, e.g. urban farming.

4095.name: Evaluating geographical issues
4095.outcome: I can evaluate different sources of evidence to justify a decision about a geographical issue.
points: Geographical issues link different parts of geography together and involve decisions about how land is used.
There is a wide range of data that can be used when evaluating geographical issues, including graphs and maps.
Data can be used to understand the issue and as evidence to support an argument.
Geographers use evidence to make decisions and aim to balance the needs of people and the environment.
keywords: Context concerns the circumstances in which a text was written; context helps us to understand the writer’s intentions further.
resources that are released prior to an examination, which include maps, graphs and text that give information about a geographical issue
a dam built across a bay or estuary that uses the movement of the tides to generate electricity
tips: This lesson provides a framework to help students understand and engage with the pre-release material. Once the pre-release is available, you may wish to revisit this lesson and break it into smaller parts that directly link to the specific content of the booklet.

3993.name: Rostow’s and Frank’s theories about development over time
3993.outcome: I can explain Rostow's and Frank's theories about how and why countries develop over time.
points: There are different theories that can explain how countries develop over time.
Rostow's modernisation theory suggests that the introduction of manufacturing causes countries to develop.
Frank's dependency theory suggests that the development of a core and periphery leads to inequality.
keywords: a socialist view that explains how the core (developed countries) exploit the periphery, proposed by Frank
living on less than $2.15 a day
the secondary economic sector, involving making goods from raw materials or other manufactured products (for example motor vehicles)
a view that suggests that countries move through five stages of economic development, proposed by Rostow
tips: The Gapminder website and others provide excellent visualisations of change over time that may be used to good effect from the front of class or on student devices.

3998.name: Top-down strategies to reduce global inequalities
3998.outcome: I can describe the advantages and disadvantages of top-down strategies used to reduce global inequalities.
points: Top-down and bottom-up strategies to reduce global inequalities differ in scale, aims, funding and technology.
Strategies such as foreign direct investment contribute to globalisation, but some countries benefit more than others.
Foreign direct investment by TNCs can lead to large-scale, economic change; but profits leak and jobs may be short-term.
Loans from IGOs for large infrastructure projects can deliver technological solutions, but also risk debt problems.
keywords: the increased interconnectedness of the world, economically, politically and culturally
IGOs are established by a treaty or agreement between countries pursuing a common goal, e.g. World Bank
TNCs are firms that own or control productive operations in more than one country
tips: The case study of an emerging country will provide further opportunities to explore why some countries have benefited more than others from globalisation.

7610.name: Bottom-up strategies to reduce global inequalities
7610.outcome: I can describe the advantages and disadvantages of bottom-up strategies used to reduce global inequalities.
points: Top-down and bottom-up strategies to reduce global inequalities differ in scale, aims, funding and technology.
Aid takes different forms, from NGO-supported, small-scale projects to larger IGO donations and bilateral aid.
NGOs can help communities to develop and maintain essential infrastructure, using intermediate technology.
In Nepal, Practical Action’s gravity ropeway has improved the lives of people in a remote, rural community.
keywords: technology suited to the needs, skills, knowledge and wealth of local people in the environment in which they live
a non-profit, voluntary group of citizens who work on a local, national or international level to achieve an aim; they are not controlled by the Government, but will often work closely with them
tips: The topic of intermediate technology provides the opportunity to consider human agency in developing countries as well as the concept of sustainable development.

4004.name: Introduction to Indonesia
4004.outcome: I can explain how Indonesia’s situation creates both opportunities and challenges for development.
points: Indonesia is the largest country in SE Asia and is an archipelago consisting of over 17 000 islands.
Indonesia is significant nationally (environmental and cultural), regionally and globally.
Indonesia is placed within a wider political, social, cultural and environmental context.
keywords: improving and building on design ideas to make them better
the point on the ground where a settlement is built
the description of a place in relation to its human and physical surroundings
tips: Use interactive maps to help students explore Indonesia's location and its neighbouring countries. Highlight its proximity to major global trade routes and ASEAN members, allowing students to better understand how its site and situation influence both regional and global relations.

4006.name: Key economic trends in Indonesia since 1990
4006.outcome: I can explain how Indonesia's economic sectors have changed since 1990.
points: Indonesia has experienced rapid economic change.
In Indonesia, there has been rapid economic change in GDP and per capita GNI since 1990.
In Indonesia, there have been changes in the importance of economic sectors since 1990.
In Indonesia, there have been economic changes in the type of foreign direct investment since 1990.
keywords: total value of goods and services produced within a country, divided by its population
GDP plus income from foreign investments and remittances, divided by the population
improving and building on design ideas to make them better
(FDI) foreign countries invest in businesses or industries in another country, often by setting up or buying local companies
tips: Youtube has several useful videos about Batam Special Economic Zone, which students could study to identify the types of industries investing in Batam and the infrastructure improvements made by the Indonesian government to boost economic development in the island.

4007.name: Globalisation in Indonesia
4007.outcome: I can explain the role of globalisation and government policy in Indonesia’s development.
points: Globalisation has had an important role in the development of Indonesia.
Government policy has had an important role in the development of Indonesia.
International aid has helped Indonesia develop and take part in globalisation.
keywords: help given by a group or country to support development in another country or for disaster relief
(FDI) foreign countries invest in businesses or industries in another country, often by setting up or buying local companies
when a company hires another business, often in a different country, to carry out work such as manufacturing or customer service
TNCS are large companies that operate in several countries; they often have headquarters in one country and factories or offices in others
tips: Use GIS to map where different types of aid are going in Indonesia (e.g. education in rural areas, energy projects like the Mentarang dam, or infrastructure like the high-speed railway).

4008.name: Effects of economic development on people in Indonesia
4008.outcome: I can explain how rapid economic change has had positive and negative impacts on people in Indonesia.
points: Rapid economic growth in Indonesia has had positive and negative impacts.
Rapid economic change has contributed to demographic change (fertility and death rates).
Rapid economic change has caused urbanisation and created regional disparities in Indonesia.
Economic development and globalisation have had positive and negative impacts on different age and gender groups.
keywords: number of deaths per 1000 people per year
average number of children per woman in a population
when things are not fair or equal for everyone
tips: Students could use GIS layers for population density and for city size to further investigate how economic development affects where people live in Indonesia.

4009.name: Effects of economic development on the geopolitical influence of Indonesia
4009.outcome: I can explain how rapid economic development has changed Indonesia's international role.
points: Rapid economic development has changed Indonesia's regional role.
Indonesia is seen as a middle power, not a superpower.
Indonesia uses trade to strengthen its role in Southeast Asia and beyond.
keywords: the way geography, economics and politics influence a country’s power and relationships with other countries
a country that is strong and influential in its part of the world but not necessarily globally dominant
Trade is the exchange of goods, commodities and services.
tips: The ASEAN website includes comic strips in ASEAN initiatives which students could explore as a way of understanding more about ASEAN's role in the region.

4010.name: Costs and benefits of changing international relations
4010.outcome: I can explain costs and benefits of changing international relationships and the role of foreign investment in Indonesia.
points: There are costs and benefits of changing international relationships.
TNCs have brought benefits to Indonesia.
There are costs to relying on TNCs for Indonesia.
keywords: the increased interconnectedness of the world, economically, politically and culturally
the action of putting forward money, time or effort with the aim of making a profit or other benefit
TNCS are large companies that operate in several countries; they often have headquarters in one country and factories or offices in others
tips: You could search for GIS layers that compare regions of Indonesia in terms of foreign investment, export industries and infrastructure access, such as Java versus rural islands, manufacturing hubs like Karawang, and areas with better road or port development.

4041.name: Contrasting urban economies in developing, emerging and developed countries
4041.outcome: I can explain the links between a country's level of development and the nature of employment there.
points: There are four sectors of employment.
Different urban economies are defined by these sectors.
Formal and informal employment create different working conditions in urban economies.
keywords: a category of economic activity where jobs are grouped together based on their type of work
employment that is officially recognised and regulated
employment that lacks official recognition and has no regulation
tips: Use online search engines to find examples in images of employment in other countries. Question with students the extent to which the images conform to stereotypes or reflect the actual employment opportunities in a country.

4042.name: Urban change over time
4042.outcome: I can analyse how, and the reasons why, urban areas change.
points: Urban areas change over time.
Urban population numbers, distribution and spatial growth change over time.
Processes of urban change include urbanisation, suburbanisation, de-industrialisation and regeneration.
Counter-urbanisation is a process leading to urban change.
keywords: the loss of industry from an area
a planning strategy aimed at addressing problems associated with decline, often involving improvements to infrastructure and encouraging new industries to an area
the movement of people from more central urban areas to the outskirts of an urban area
the physical outward expansion of a city into the surrounding countryside
tips: Urban sprawl can be demonstrated well through students comparing old maps of cities to those of today.

4043.name: Characteristics and factors influencing different urban land uses
4043.outcome: I can describe and explain different urban land uses.
points: There are a variety of urban land uses.
Urban land uses (commercial, industrial and residential) have different characteristics.
Several factors influence urban land use, including accessibility, availability, cost and planning regulations.
keywords: central business district; the commercial centre of an urban area
an area of land that was formerly used for something but which is now abandoned or derelict
a land use category used for areas that trade goods and services
land that is protected from development and surrounds major English cities
tips: Where possible, contextualise the ideas in this lesson by using a town or city that the students are likely to know well.

4053.name: Location and national, regional and global context of Jakarta
4053.outcome: I can describe the location and context of Jakarta.
points: Jakarta is a global megacity located on the island of Java and is the capital of Indonesia.
Jakarta has distinctive characteristics of site, situation and connectivity.
Jakarta is important nationally, regionally and internationally.
keywords: a city with a population of 10 million people or more
the sinking or settling of land, often caused by human activities such as excessive groundwater extraction, which can increase the risk of flooding
a city with global influence, important in the world economy through finance, trade, culture and communication
tips: Use GIS to map Jakarta’s transport links and flood risk areas, helping students understand its national and global connectivity, as well as why environmental challenges like subsidence and flooding are driving the capital’s relocation.

4054.name: The structure of Jakarta
4054.outcome: I can explain factors influencing Jakarta's urban structure.
points: Jakarta exhibits characteristic urban forms (CBD, inner city, suburbs and rural-urban fringe).
Jakarta's structure (urban form) is determined by function and buildling age.
Jakarta is rapidly expanding into surrounding rural areas, changing land use dramatically.
keywords: the CBD is the commercial and business centre of a city, usually with high land values, tall buildings and a concentration of shops, offices and services
the purpose or function of land, for example: residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural or recreational use
the outer edge of a city where it merges with the countryside
tips: Use Google Earth or GIS platforms such as ArcGIS to explore land use in Jakarta’s suburbs and rural-urban fringe.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

4055.name: Trends and causes of population growth in Jakarta
4055.outcome: I can explain factors that have contributed to Jakarta's population growth.
points: Jakarta is a rapidly growing megacity.
Natural increase has contributed to population growth.
National and international migration has contributed to population growth.
Economic investment and growth has contributed to population growth.
keywords: a city with a population of 10 million people or more
moving from one place to another with the intention of staying there
the difference between the birth rate and the death rate of a population; occurs when the birth rate is higher than the death rate
tips: Students could use Street View to explore BSD City and identify features that might make it attractive for companies looking to relocate or invest there.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

4056.name: Effects of population growth on spatial growth, functions and land use
4056.outcome: I can describe how population growth has affected the pattern of spatial growth and changing urban functions and land use in Jakarta.
points: Population growth has affected the pattern of spatial growth in Jakarta.
Population growth has affected changing urban functions in Jakarta.
Population growth has affected land use in Jakarta.
keywords: areas of grass, trees, or plants within urban environments, like parks or gardens
informal settlements in Indonesian cities built by residents, often on derelict or unsafe land
a city with a population of 10 million people or more
tips: GIS can help students see how Jakarta’s land use changed from 2000 to 2020. They can use maps to spot green space loss, urban sprawl, and link it to data like population or flood risk.

4058.name: Opportunities for people living in the city
4058.outcome: I can explain how population growth has created opportunities for people in Jakarta.
points: Rapid population growth creates opportunities for people in Jakarta.
Rapid population growth has provided opportunities to access resources in Jakarta.
Rapid population growth has provided employment opportunities in Jakarta.
keywords: how easy it is for people to take part in an activity, especially if there are barriers
the availability of jobs and work for people, often used to measure economic opportunity and development
a positive feature or benefit that improves people's lives, such as access to clean water, jobs, healthcare or education
tips: Use GIS to map the locations of schools, universities, hospitals, and health centres in Jakarta alongside population and income data. This shows where education and healthcare facilities are concentrated, helping to identify where new opportunities could be developed.

4059.name: Challenges caused by rapid urban population growth: housing
4059.outcome: I can explain how rapid population growth in Jakarta has led to housing issues.
points: There are challenges for people living in Jakarta.
Rapid population growth has created housing shortages in Jakarta.
Rapid population growth has led to the development of squatter and slum settlements in Jakarta.
keywords: a waterborne disease caused by bacteria in contaminated water or food. It spreads quickly in areas with poor sanitation and can cause severe diarrhoea and dehydration
the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
an informal settlement in Indonesian cities that is self-built without planning permission. Homes are overcrowded, poorly constructed and lack basic services
tips: Students could use Street View to compare housing types and quality in different areas of Jakarta.

4060.name: Challenges caused by rapid urban population growth: services
4060.outcome: I can explain how rapid population growth creates challenges for service provision in Jakarta.
points: Rapid population growth creates challenges of clean water supply in Jakarta.
Rapid population growth creates challenges of waste removal in Jakarta.
Rapid population growth creates challenges of limited service provision in Jakarta.
Rapid population growth creates challenges of traffic congestion in Jakarta.
keywords: water found underground in soil, sand, and rock. It is stored in aquifers and can be used as a source of water for drinking or industry
presence of harmful substances in the environment, such as in the air, water or soil, which can damage ecosystems and human health
Recycling is when we collect and sort our rubbish instead of throwing it away. These items then get changed into something new for us to use.
tips: By thinking first about the services that their own settlement relies on, and then considering what the challenges of service provision would be if the population of their settlement were to increase rapidly, students can get a clearer understanding of systemic pressures.

4061.name: Urban patterns in Jakarta
4061.outcome: I can describe how rapid population growth in Jakarta has created significant inequalities and challenges in managing the city.
points: There are significant inequalities in Jakarta's residential areas.
There are differences in quality of life in Jakarta's residential areas.
Managing Jakarta involves political and economic challenges.
keywords: informal settlements in Indonesian cities built by residents, often on derelict or unsafe land
the number of people living in a defined area, e.g. 300 people per square kilometre
wellbeing of individuals or groups of people measured by criteria other than wealth such as housing, employment and environmental factors
tips: Students could use Street View to survey different areas of Jakarta to identify and describe features of higher-income and lower-income areas.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

4082.name: Classification of energy – non-renewable, renewable and recyclable
4082.outcome: I can classify sources of energy into non-renewable, renewable and recyclable energy.
points: Energy sources can be classified as non-renewable, renewable and recyclable.
Non-renewable energy resources include fossil fuels: coal, oil and gas.
Renewable energy resources include flows of solar, wind and HEP.
Recyclable energy resources include nuclear and biofuels.
keywords: energy sources, such as fossil fuels, that cannot be replaced and will eventually run out
sources of energy that can be reused and so will last into the future, such as biofuels and nuclear energy
energy from natural sources that are constantly replenished, like wind and solar
tips: Understanding what makes nuclear power and biofuels recyclable is sometimes challenging for students: YouTube videos about the process of generating nuclear power (and reprocessing spent nuclear fuel), and of turning biofuels into energy sources work well in consolidating understanding here.

4083.name: Environmental impacts of energy extraction
4083.outcome: I can explain environmental impacts associated with non-renewable, renewable and recyclable energy extraction and use.
points: Energy extraction has environmental consequences.
Mining and drilling can have environmental impacts, such as landscape scarring, oil spills and carbon emissions.
Renewable energy can have landscape impacts including from HEP flooding and land use for wind turbines and solar panels.
keywords: volume of carbon produced contributing to global warming
visible damage to a landscape caused by human activities such as mining or construction
tips: GIS offers excellent opportunities to identify landscape scarring and measure the impact of changes in landscapes due to energy extraction and production over time.

4084.name: Factors affecting access to energy resources
4084.outcome: I can explain how access to energy resources is affected by physical resources and access to technology.
points: Access to energy resources is not evenly distributed.
Access to energy resources is affected by physical resources, such as geology, accessibility, climate and landscape.
Access to energy resources is affected by access to technology.
keywords: how easy it is for people to take part in an activity, especially if there are barriers
a method of drilling into the Earth to extract oil and natural gas by injecting high-pressure fluids to crack rocks and release the resources trapped inside
the study of the Earth and its physical structure
a known amount of oil or gas that can be taken from underground and used
tips: Use this topic to refresh and develop students' skills in use and interpretation of world maps showing the distribution of energy resources.

4085.name: Global patterns of energy use and causes of variations
4085.outcome: I can describe the global pattern of energy use and explain reasons for the variations in energy use per person.
points: There are variations (inequalities) in the global pattern of energy use.
Level of economic development is a cause of variations in the global pattern of energy use.
Demand from different economic sectors cause variations in energy use.
Energy poverty has negative economic, social and environmental implications.
keywords: the growth of a country’s wealth, leading to better jobs, higher incomes and improved living standards
the different types of jobs and industries in an economy, divided into primary (e.g. farming), secondary (e.g. manufacturing), tertiary (services) and quaternary (e.g. research)
